PROPOSAL BY Mr. SPEAKER TOWARDS EFFECTING ECONOMY IN THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In view of the extremely severe financial pressure due to the present war, I have thought it proper to endeavour to effect such economies in con-

nection with the management of the business of the House as may be secured without injuriously affecting its prompt and efficient conduct. To this end I appointed a committee of three of the senior officers of the House to look into the question of the parliamentary printing. This committee has made a report recommending that the Votes and Proceedings and the. Journals should toe consolidated* The committee believes that in this way, while a full and proper record of the proceedings of the House would be preserved, that a very large saving would result. I beg to suggest, therefore, that the House appoint a small committee of three experienced members to consider whether this proposal should be adopted. It is not intended to make any change this session, but during the coming recess to work out the details of the scheme, and to begin the new arrangement next session.
I may also, inform the House that I purpose, myself, to immediately make a very full inquiry into the duties and organization of the staff of the House, the result of which I shall communicate to the House in due course.

Is it the intention of the Government to urge the repeal of the Act of 1896 so that Canadian cattle will be allowed into Great Britain?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The information called for by this question is set forth in the following extract from a discussion on the subject which took place at the Imperial War Conference on the 26th day of April, 1917. This discussion' was embodied in a return laid before the Parliament of the United Kingdom in September last, and also laid before the Parliament of Canada at the last session, and which reads:
Imperial War Conference, 1917.
Extracts from Discussions at the Imperial War
Conference on the Admission of Canadian
Cattle into the United Kingdom.
Note.-The discussion took place on the Fourteenth Day, Thursday, 26th April 1917. (See p. 113 of Minutes of Proceedings in [Cd 8566.].)
Mr. Rogers :	Mr. Chairman, yesterday, when
the Resolution presented by Sir Albert Stanley from the Board of Trade came before this Conference, a Resolution which was, in my judgment, very proper and very desirable from
all points of view, he was able to make no mention of beef imported from the Dominion of Canada, and my purpose in bringing the matter up is to draw attention to the fact that this was entirely due to the action on the part of the Board of Agriculture in placing an embargo-as against Canadian cattle because of alleged pleuro-pneumonia in a shipment of Canadian cattle to England in the year 1892. Now, as I understand, it was shown conclusively that the allegation was erroneous, and that it was irregular to create the embargo and to put it in force; but later it was made statutory. Since that date I may say, for the information of the Conference, that over 3,000,000 head of cattle have been shipped from Canada and slaughtered on arrival in Great Britain, and no single case of disease has been discovered. Now you can understand that this is a condition which we complain of very seriously, and we have made several appeals with respect to it. Later on we got an answer -through his Excellency the Governor General of that day, Lord Grey, giving us a copy of a letter from the Board of Agriculture, in which it was stated that the experience of foreign countries had shown how suddenly and unexpectedly foot-and-mouth disease made its appearance, irrespective of an efficient veterinary organisation.* That goes to show that the Board of Agriculture were not able to support the ground upon which they placed an embargo against all Canadian cattle originally, and shifted their ground in making this statement that in foreign countries experience went to show that very suddenly and unexpectedly foot-and-mouth disease could develop. This has had a very detrimental effect in Canada. This, of course, intensifies the feeling that a great injustice has been done by the Board of Agriculture as against the Dominion of Canada in respect of the cattle industry, and when this Resolution was presented by Sir Albert Stanley, we felt that it was an opportune moment to bring this matter to the attention of the Conference, in order to see if it would be possible for us to have redress. I may say that our Minister of Agriculture, in a letter on the question, states that our cattle are as healthy as any cattle in the world, and during the three outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease in the United ^States, which have occurred since the embargo was placed, Canada has been able to maintain her herds absolutely free from infection. From the point of view of disease, therefore, I feel very strongly that there is every justification for the removal of this embargo. Of course, we naturally argue that this embargo has been placed as a matter of policy by the Board of Agriculture for the purpose of the development of the British live cattle industry. If the Board of Agriculture conceive it to be their duty and to be in the public interest of Great Britain to have a policy of protection of their live cattle industry, then we would have no complaint and offer no objection; but we do seriously complain in that an embargo is placed against our cattle which supplies this protection and carries with it the stigma that they are liable to have pleuro-pneumonia, and, therefore we suffer not only in this market but more or less in the markets of the United States. I think it is due to Canada-and I think this is the proper time when we should ask this Conference-to take some definite action in order that this wrong may be remedied, so that our Canadian cattle shall have the same consideration and be received in Great Britain without having to go through the embargo that has been placed upon them by the action of the Board of Agriculture.

You, Mr. Long, were good enough to suggest that you would like to see present here a representative of the Board of Agriculture when the matter came up, and the discussion on the point was adjourned from yesterday for that purpose.
I am glad that the representatives of that Department are here to-day, and if they have any explanation to offer, or any reason why this embargo should be continued in the future, then of course we would like to [DOT]know it and to understand it in order that we may be able to explain it, at all events, when we go back to Canada, because it is a very very very live question and one in which our people take the very deepest interest. Probably you will remember, Mr. Long, that I *had this matter up with you some days ago, and you sent me a letter to say "Mr. Prothero suggests, therefore, that further discussion on the matter should be deferred until after the War, when the representations of the Canadian Government can be brought forward for reconsideration." But we do not like to feel that we are misunderstood or that our cattle industry is suffering from a reputation that never did exist, and a stigma which never ought to have been attached. Therefore, if there is any explanation to be given on the part of the Board of Agriculture, we shall be very glad indeed to hear it.
Mr. Prothero: Of course you know in this country we are very panicky about outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease and pleuro-pneumonia, and you quite correctly state that the case on which the policy was founded dates right back to 1892. I had up the papers which relate to the alleged outbreak in 1892, and as far as I could see it was not a case of pleuro-pneumonia at all. The case upon which this embargo was founded1-it is not quite correctly stated as an embargo, because cattle are allowed to be landed provided they are slaughtered at the landing-dates right back to 1892. As I say, I had the papers up before me this morning, and I think the papers show that the alleged case on which the embargo was founded is extremely doubtful as to its being pleuro-pneumonia. I also believe that at the present moment and for many years past, as far as I can make out, Canada has been free from the disease, and on those grounds therefore we should receive the present suggestion for the removal of the embargo very sympathetically. As far as I personally am concerned, and so far as the English Board of Agriculture is concerned, after the War is over, of course, because it is not an economical mode of bringing meat to this country during the War to bring over live animals, we should, I consider, be wise to remove the embargo, and I think for this reason in the main:	The home
demand for store cattle in the eastern counties has been rather imperfectly met for many years past. On the other hand, there has been a considerable increase in breeding in this country; but if we have, what I think we shall have, a large extension of the arable farming in this country, we shall want to increase our reservoir for store cattle. Of course, your Canadian cattle will co;ne over as what we call "stores/' that is to say, they are to ;be fed and fattened here in England. We shall want a great many more store cattle if we have this great extension of arable farming; we shall want more animals to trample the straw and eat the root crops. At the same time there are signs that we shall not get the same number of store cattle from Ireland as heretofore. fSir Robert Borden.]
You will understand-I do not know whether there is a representative of the Irish Department here-that the main opposition, at least one strong line of opposition, to the introduction of Canadian stores is that the Irishman is afraid that it is going to cut into his trade in store cattle with this country. Well, Ireland is advancing most rapidly 'in its agricultural development. If we get cattle from Ireland they will increasingly come over here in the form of finished, fully fed cattle. Therefore the supply of Irish store cattle is likely to diminish, and in that case again the fact that we can turn to Canada for store cattle will be of great advantage to us, and I can assure you that so far as the English Board of Agriculture is concerned, we are in favour of the removal of the embargo. We do not believe that there is now, or has been for a good many years past, the slightest ground to exclude Canadian cattle on the score of disease. I do not know-I am afraid you know a great deal better than I do-but any statistics I have seen as to disease in Canada show me that you have been remarkably free from it. That is so, is it not?
Sir Robert Borden:	That is absolutely so.
Mr. Prothero: Therefore, that is the answer that I would like to make you. I am afraid I ought to consult the Irish Department, because they may make difficulties, but I do not think they will, because, as I say, the whole development of Irish farming is in favour of the breaking up of these great grass ranches on which the store cattle were grazed, and from which they were sent over. Instead of that they are adopting the finishing system, upon which, of course, there is very much more money to be made and much more profit agriculturally in other ways to the farmer.
Sir Robert Borden : Mr. Prothero, may I ask a question purely for information:	Is the
'statute or the regulation which constitutes the so-called embargo applicable to all countries or is it only applicable to certain countries?
Mr. Prothero: It is applicable to all countries. I believe it was passed by Mr. Walter Long in 1896.
Chairman: It was.
Mr. Rogers:	Are you quite sure, Mr. Prothero, that it applies to all countries?
Mr. Prothero: It does. I mean that it is a broad general principle, but we can admit animals in exceptional cases from time to time. I think that is the case.
Sir Robert Borden: We appreciate very much your sympathetic attitude with regard to the matter, Mr. Prothero. As to postponing it until after the end of the War, I am not so much impressed by the consideration put forward, because, assuming the absence of tonnage, nothing would come forward in any case until that shortage is relieved. As far as Canada is concerned, I do not want it understood that we desire to interfere in any way with the fiscal policy of the United Kingdom. 'If it is thought desirable here that the cattle industry should be protected, whether in Ireland, or England, or Scotland, or Wales, that is a matter of domestic concern for the United Kingdom, about which we do not desire to make any suggestion; but what has been felt in Canada, whether rightly or wrongly, is this, that under the guise of a sanitary regulation you have succeeded in carrying out a fiscal policy-	,
Chairman ; It was said just now that I was responsible for this policy, for advising the

Government. It certainly was not that at all, nor did we accept the view (which my friend Mr. Prothero has said obtained twenty years afterwards) that we had not abundant evidence. There was a difference of opinion between your scientific people and ours. Our people held a strong view about it. There was a great agitation in this country about disease, particularly pleuro-pneumonia, and our scientific people differed from yours.
Mr. Rogers:	A Commission was appointed
to go into the facts of the whole case, and they decided that there was no ground for the action which was taken.
Chairman: Your people held one view and ours the other.
Sir Robert Borden:	I think Mr. Prothero
has put it very moderately when he says that it was at least a doubtful case. I should say there was not any substantial evidence at all of disease in Canada. There was only one instance adduced, and the experts were divided upon that. We sought an independent investigation outside Canada, and that investigation convinced us that there was absolutely nothing in it, and from that time up to the present not a single case has developed in Canada so far as I am aware, whereas numerous instances of disease have developed in the United Kingdom during that time. As far as sanitary regulations are concerned, there would be far more reason for us to put an embargo against British cattle coming to Canada than there would for Great Britain to impose an embargo upon Canadian cattle coming here. Whether rightly or wrongly, the impression does exist in Canada, that it was more the carrying out of a fiscal policy than the enforcement of a sanitary regulation. I know that view impressed itself upon the members of the late Administration, and we are not free from it ourselves.
Chairman:	Sir Charles Tupper held that
view.
Sir Robert Borden:	Yes, and the members
of the late Administration held that view; the Canadian (Minister of Agriculture I am quite sure held that view. If it is desired to protect the cattle industry in the United Kingdom, let it be done; that is a matter of domestic concern; but do not accomplish it by the enforcement of a regulation which casts an undeserved slur upon conditions in Canada.
I am sure we are all very much obliged to Mr. Prothero for the sympathetic consideration he has given to the subject, and, as it is a matter of sentiment with us as well as a matter of material consideration, I hope it may be possible for him to reach the conclusion that it is not necessary to await the termination of hostilities before taking action for this purpose; but that, of course, is for him to decide. I only offer a strong suggestion along that line.
Chairman : Of course you could get publicity given to the thing by having a question asked in the House of Commons, without passing any statute. As far as I am concerned, as my name has been brought into it I can only say that I entirely agree with Mr. Prothero's policy. I think the time that has elapsed has shown that Canada has had a complete and dean bill of health during that time. I am not concerned to defend my share of the policy, though I was personally responsible as Minister, but it is fair to my advisers at that time-I am sorry to say I am afraid they are no longer alive even-to say that they disagreed with the advisers of the Canadian Government. Sir
Charles Tupper was Minister for Agriculture,
I think.
Mr. Rogers: No, he was the High Commissioner.
Chairman: Perhaps I mean his son.
Mr. Rogers: He was never Minister of Agriculture. It was Sir Charles Tupper, the High Commissioner, who took the matter up and took a deep interest in it.
Chairman: That is our old friend who died the other day.
~Mr. Rogers : Yes.
Chairman: No, I mean another Tupper, one of the sons. I thought he was Minister for Agriculture. He came over here, saw Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, Secretary for the Colonies, and then came to see me. There was a difference between the technical experts on both sides. In Canada they held that there was no justification; whereas our experts took the opposite view, and they held further that as it was possible for cattle to pass from the United States of America into Canada and they frequently did pass, and as in the United States there was risk of disease, they ought to be fortified here. That was the view that prevailed, and it was really a case for the experts, who were not fiscal reformers at all; they differed, and we followed our experts. I think, however, subsequent experience has shown that Canada has an absolutely clean bill of health.
Mr. Rogers: Yes, and we had it even in that case. They slaughter them now at the dock immediately they arrive.
Mr. Prothero: There is one point I might mention. I think, if I might use a slang phrase, we were rather "jumpy" at that time about cattle plague, because just before 1896, when this new legislation was made, we had been bringing in cattle from Argentina, and on the voyage a whole shipload of cattle were discovered to be actually suffering from foot-and-mouth disease. That was no doubt one of the reasons why we made this more drastic alteration, but we could, not by legislation but merely by an order of the Board of Agriculture, put Canada into the free list to-day.
Mr. Rogers: Then' for Heaven's sake why do not they do it?
Chairman: I think that is not so. I have not looked into this thing for twenty years, and I think that that was exactly the sin I committed from the point of view of Canada. I think before the passing of the Act of 1896, to which we are now referring, you could do this by Order in Council. At that time, as Mr. Prothero has said, there was the gravest apprehension here with regard to our cattle industry. It was extremely important to our English cattle-breeders to increase the number of cattle in the country. We had from the year 1865 or 1866, right away down to the nineties, a succession of outbreaks of various diseases, foot-and-mouth and pleuro-pneumonia, and the demand of the cattle-breeders in this country was that they should be protected against disease, however slight the risk might be. That was a demand which was backed by experts. That was the real history of it. I think that removed from the Board of Agriculture the power to put countries on the free list. I think you will find that you will have to repeal the Act of Parliament, but I speak subject to correction.
Mr. Prothero: I am afraid I have not looked at the Act on this specific point. I was not quite sure what point I was supposed to

address myself to, but I will look into it, and if we do take any action I do not see why it should not be taken at once, especially if we cannot put it into operation until after the war is over.
Mr. Rogers: How do you mean, you cannot put it into operation?
Mr. Prothero: Because there are no ships.
Mr. Rogers: We do not object to that, but remove the stigma against us from which we are suffering.
Chairman: Now the position is that the restriction is to be removed, and the Board of Agriculture will take such steps as are necessary for this purpose, but upon the understanding that, there being no tonnage, there cannot be any arrivals.
Mr. Rogers: I do not want to have any understanding about it. If there is no tonnage, that follows.
Chairman: No, I do not want it to be a misunderstanding.
Sir Robert Borden: It cannot become effective because there is no tonnage.
Chairman: We cannot do it; I am quite sure that the Shipping Controller would stop it at once, and he would say, 'We cannot let live cattle come because they take up too much room."
Sir Robert Borden: We perfectly understand that.	[DOT]
Mr. Rogers: Yes, but still, we do not want to be placed in a false position. This is an old sore and an old grievance, and now is the proper time to have it cured, because the facts are all in our favour.
Chairman: The Minister of Agriculture has undertaken to do it.
Mr. Rogers: Do not you think we should have a Resolution about it?
Chairman: You do not want a Resolution, do you-or if you like you can simply move that the embargo on Canadian cattle be removed as speedily as possible.
Mr. Rogers: I beg to move that.
Chairman: Mr. Prothero accepts that, and there is an end of it.
Mr. Hazen: I think as we have a statement from the President of the Board of Agriculture that this restriction will be removed, and that he does not see why it should not be done at once, we might leave it there.
Mr. Massey: Does this embargo apply to Canada only, or to all overseas countries?
Chairman: All overseas countries.
Mr. Hazen: You do not ship cattle from New Zealand; it is too far.
Mr. Massey: They did ship cattle from Australia, but we never ship them from New Zealand.

subtopic: THE PRIME MINISTER GIVES DETAIDS OF WAR EXPENDITURE AND MAJOR GENERAD MEWBURN EXPDAINS MILITARY ESTIMATES.

speechtext:
Right Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 38 for granting to His Majesty aid for military and naval defence.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I proposed the second reading of a Bill very much the same as this in February, 1917, and I had then great hope that it would never be necessary tjo propose in this House a vote for war purposes of so large an amount. Unfortunately, the duration of the war has greatly exceeded the anticipations we had at that time, and the present is a moment v hen the greatest effort of the nation seems to be required.
It is not necessary, I hope, for me to say anything in support of the principle which this Bill embodies. It is, however, most desirable-indeed, absolutely necessary- that full information as to expenditure during the past year and estimates, for the coming year should be afforded to the House in order that they may consider whether or not the Bill in its present form should be approved. It is precisely in the same form as the Bill which passed this House last year. I propose, therefore, if it meets the view of hion. gentlemen opposite and of the House in general, that the House go into committee on the Bill, whereupon I shall give such information as is available with regard to the expenditure
of the past and the estimate for the future.
I shall endeavour to have that information placed upon Hansard in a form which will be quite intelligible. After I have discharged that duty, the Minister of Militia and Defence will give a statement to the committee setting forth information more especially upon the military side of the questions that are involved. We shall then be very glad to have suggestions from hon. gentlemen as to any further information that may be desired. I would then propose that the committee should rise and report progress, in order that the information thus spread upon the pages of Hansard may be taken into account with a view to further consideration of the Bill in committee on another day.

The grounds upon which they based their request seemed to be reasonable, and I believe that the request has since been acceded to by the Commonwealth of Australia and the Dominion of New Zealand. The ground was this: at the time the arrangement was made no one had any conception of the tremendous expenditure for ammunition, especially ammunition for the field guns; there was

Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia and Defence):	I feed somewhat
diffident, in appearing before the House to give an explanation of the war policy of the Government, because I realize fully the magnitude of the task, and I would, - Therefore, bespeak for myself the usual generous indulgence extended to a new member. This is the fifth-occasion since the war began on which war estimates have been presented to the House. In dealing with the whole situation, I should like, if possible, to transfer the minds and imagination of hon. members to our troops in France. On what is known as the western front there is a Canadian army of not far short of 150,000 men. The existence of that army is the reason for my being here to-day. Its presence there gives us a high status among the nations of the world even at this early date in the history of our young country. It is our business and it is our pride as a nation to maintain that army. I venture'to suggest that, in all our thoughts about our policy, we should keep our army constantly first in mind. Its efficiency should be the standard at which we should aim, and by keeping its wellbeing ever in mind, we shall preserve a sense of proportion in weighing the details of our national effort The .heroic deeds of the Canadian Expeditionary Force are a sacred pride to every true Canadian.
I think I am justified in giving to the committee an outline of our organization in France, and I ask that the committee do not require certain detail which it would not be advisable in the allied interest to give.	>
'The Canadian Army Corps, as it exists in France, as hon. members are all well aware, is under the immediate command of Lieut.-General Sir Arthur Currie. It consists of four divisions, comprising an. establishment of about 78,000 men and corps troops, largely artillery, amounting to about 11,000 more.

reserve units are also included men in hospitals; that is3 when a man is evacuated from France as a wounded man, he is immediately taken 'off the strength of the base in France and taken on the strength of his reserve battalion or unit in England. He is shown as either in hospital undergoing treatment, or in a convalescent home, or in one of the reserve units which he may join after his convalescence is over. We have, therefore, those men in the various categories, and at one time what was known as category "A" was down to a very low ebb, particularly after the battle of Passchendaele, when the casualties were very heavy. Our men go from one category to another, and when they work up to category " A," they become available for reinforcement.
We also had the Fifth Division which was at first intact, but which it unfortunately became necessary to break up in order to ensure a steady flow of reinforcements for the other divisions in France.
That was one of the most highly trained divisions we ever had since the commencement of the war. But it was conceded, and it must be conceded, the way recruitment is, that iCanada could not maintain and keep up more than four divisions at .the front. It was 'believed to be far better that we should maintain four divisions up to strength than attempt to maintain five divisions that were only partly up to strength. Therefore, for military reasons, sad and disappointing as it was to the officers, it was conceded to be essential *that the divisions should be (broken up and the men put into the various reserves whilst gradually flowing on to France.
In addition, we have what is known as the administrative units which take in all the business end of the organization in England, training schools, Canadian Army Service Corps, Canadian Army Medical Corps, Dental Corps, Ordnance and Pay Corps, Record, Discharge, General and Command Depots. These various establishments in England aTe most important connecting links between our army in the field and our efforts here. In .addition to that there are the hospitals.
There are several training reports coming in from time to time in connection with the overseas work in France which show what is being done from month to month. There is not much information in these reports that J can give the House as they are purely matters of detail in regard to the training but there are one or two reports which I think may be interesting and if I
[Major-General Mewburn.]
may digress -for a moment I would like to quote them to show, for instance, what is being done by the chaplain services in France, I read:
FRANCE:	The Chaplains of the Canadian
Corps have continued to prosecute their work with unabated loyalty and devotion. An estimate of the service they have set themselves to accomplish may be gained from the programme carried out by the Chaplains of the First Division during a recent offensive.
These officers have had considerable experience at the front and promptly seized the opportunity for service which they realized a sharp engagement made (possible. Knowing the nature of the operations to be carried out by the Division they made preliminary arrangements for the establishments of soup kitchens and coffee stalls in the most strategic places close to the front line in order that they and their helpers might minister to the wounded and also to the weary men going to, and coming from the battle-front. This work was carefully planned to the last detail. One of the Chaplains reporting on the four days activities states:
" We worked hard all day and most of the night serving the wounded and others. We carried hot coffee, tea and soup in petrol tins to the roadside where we distributed it together with biscuits and cigarettes. Infantry men, artillery men, tunnellers, engineers, Royal Flying Corps men, anti-aircraft personnel, stretcher bearers, and others were ministered to in large numbers."
It is estimated by the Chaplain in charge that in the four days twelve thousand were in some way served. Thousands of cigarettes were given away and great quantities of coffee and other refreshments were served out.
Another bright spot in connection with the chaplain work in France is disclosed by a report to the senior chaplain. In a report to the senior chaplain by an officer commanding one of the units of the Third Division, the following comment is made on the work of the chaplain:
In a report to the Senior Chaplain by an officer commanding one of the units of the 3rd Division, the following comment is made on the work of the Chaplain " He was tireless in his efforts to evacuate wounded and bury dead. It was mainly through his efforts that we were able to hand over our quarter of the battlefield cleared of both our own, and enemy dead. Since then his work has been most excellent. What is therein stated concerning one Chaplain can be applied with equal truth to the zeal and devotion of most of the Chaplains of the Corps.
I am just reading these extracts to show how that work is carried on by those splendid men at the front.
I now come to 'Canada with which I am more familiar. I can probably speak with a greater degree of certainty of our efforts here to procure mens to equip them and to get them overseas as soon as possible. Within the last nine months we have

thought it wise to give up any attempt to go into any detailed training. Our chief aim and obligation has been to get men over to England as soon as the ships are available and when they get over, their organization and training are completed.
Speaking generally, our efforts in Canada are to procure men, equip them, give them their preliminary organization and such an amount of training as is possible, and despatch them to England as ships are available. The Overseas authorities complete their organization and training and forward them to Prance. Conversely, the Overseas department sends back unfit or superfluous men and the Militia Department to-day are confronted with the large and serious task of evacuating our wounded and sick from England, the treatment and care thereof, and carrying out their discharge from the army; Up to a year ago we were enthused by the large number of recruits coming forward and the task that was undertaken by the citizens as a whole. It was a pleasant task to provide positions for the men going overseas, but we are now confronted with the most serious- aspect of the war, viz., the return of our magnificent men, many maimed and injured for life, broken down in health, and with shattered nerves. In other words, we are to-day confronted with the enormous task of demobilization and all that it means, of which I will speak later.
I would like to speak for a moment of the change in organization here-. What I am about to say is not at all by way of criticism because when wre look back and see the wonderful results that we have accomplished we cannot have any feeling other than that of admiration, but in the very large number of battalions that we have raised, and which were authorized, and which it must have been known could never get to the 'front, we find the reason for the very large number of surplus officers of whom I am going to speak later.
Last year it became necessary to re-organize our method of supplying reinforcements for overseas. Up to the fall of 1916, and in the early spring of 1917, we were still raising complete overseas- units. It was conceded by many of those who were vitally interested in recruiting, that complete units could not all get to the front and in the judgment of many officers, who had devoted a great deal of time and energy, that instead of raising so many C. E. P. Battalions, it might have been better, from the first, had the old militia units, through whom the first, second and third divisions were raised, been able to retain their old
numerical numbers, thereby keeping up the esprit-de-corps of the old Canadian militia units and sending forward reinforcements for the battalions that would have then been at the front. There is, of course, a great deal to be said for the system of raising complete battalions, as it was done voluntarily and it was by this means that the large number of volunteers were obtained. When the policy of sending complete units overseas, ceased, it was then necessary to organize within Canada, Depot Battalions throughout the various military districts, into which recruits were taken, and from these Depot Battalions, organized on the Territorial system and linked up with the Territorial system in vogue in England and the front, our men are forwarded in drafts to England.
The soldier to-day begins his military career in the Depot Battalion in his district in Canada. After he has gone through the preliminary training, medical examination, inoculation and vaccination, he proceeds to England with a draft and is taken on the strength of the same territorial regiment or battalion there.

How long after being enlisted?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Just as
quickly as we can get him over. Ordinarily speaking, it would be much more preferable if a man could be trained here for some months before he left. To-day, within two or three weeks after the recruit is enlisted, vaccinated and inoculated, he should proceed overseas, not that it is desirable that he should do -so, but because it is a question of ships. When we can get ships we feel that we should get our men into England as rapidly as possible for the sake of getting them over and getting them trained there.
Eventually the man finds himself in France still in the same regiment which he first joined. This system has replaced the earlier method of raising battalions. For instance, we have the first and second Quebec regiment, and the first and second Ontario regiment, and so on. They are organized terri-torically by provinces, as well as could be done, although it was rather late to do it, and it has not worked out as well as we hoped it would have, because there are many men to-day from all over Canada who are in different regiments at the front. There are men from Manitoba who are in Quebec regiments, men from Ontario in New Brunswick regiments, and -so forth. It could not help but be so. It is simply a case of filling

those really necessary. Thirdly, we have 'depot units for the reception, administration and disposal of returned soldiers who are to return to civil life. These last mentioned units are absolutely essential for the purpose of carrying on demobilization, and every man 'before being discharged must have his documents and records completed and a final medical examination held before final discharge.
This question of training presupposes the procuring of men. The past year has been the introduction of the Military Service Act. I wish to make lit very elear'here that the Military Service Act is administered by the Department of Justice. The task of approaching the civil population and selecting therefrom a proper number of men to be recruits is committed, very properly in my opinion, to a civil department. When the Department of Justice has made tha selection, has decided that it is equitable and advantageous, considering alike the interests of the nation and the circumstances of the individual, that a given man should serve the country, we in the Militia Department receive him, outfit him, train, him and send him overseas.
The business of tribunals and exemptions i6 very largely outside of our sphere, although we naturally have a deep interest in the matter, and our administration touches that of the Military Service Act at numerous points. Our interest in the matter, indeed, is SO' strong that I do not hesitate to say that in my opinion there must he a decided- speeding up of the tribunals. In view of the recent events, the need for men is more apparent than ever. Canada must produce the men; she must bear her part in the great work set before civilization. The Military Service Act has produced, so far, recruits enough to keep our splendid divisions up to strength, but in order to maintain them it must produce more.
As is well known, the Military Service Act provided for the raising oif one hundred thousand reinforcements. I had no part in bringing into operation the Military Service Act. I have felt, and still feel, that we have got to get reinforcements overseas. I realize there are difficulties to he overcome, and in that connection I was much interested in the debate which took place here the other night with respect to the unfortunate occurences in the province of Que- , bee. Nevertheless I have always felt, and I still feel, that the province of Quebec will do its duty.	.

Hear, hear.

Major-General MEWBURN: I may be wrong, I hope I am not, and I regret as deeply as one can regret the events that took place in the city of Quebec, but I feel satisfied that that province will yield her quota to keep up the number of Quebec battalions at the front. I may be wrong but that is my own conception. The Military Service Act is not the only source from which we have been obtaining recruits. We have in the United States what is known as the British-Canadian Recruiting Mission. Before the United States entered the war their Government consented to the Imperial authorities recruiting men within the Union. At first the idea was to get men for the British Expeditionary Force. Afterwards we were asked to join them and endeavour to secure recruits for the Canadian Expeditionary Force. We did so in a very small way, but gradually the movement.grew. The officers we have sent down there were all returned officers who had seen service at the front.
We do not obtain all our recruits from the Military Service Act. Up to ,a short ' time ago, . voluntary recruiting was per-

mitted to continue and a considerable number of men were obtained for technical services. A large number of young men, who had riot attained the age of legal obligation, joined the Royal Flying Corps; youth being [DOT]a great asset in this new and strange way of fighting.
I wish to utter a word of appreciation of the activities of the Royal Flying Corps in the Dominion. As is well known, it is an Imperial organization. Canada having followed the policy of assisting in every way possible - this organization, everything has been done by the Government, and by my department in particular, to assist the officers of the Royal Flying Corps in their arduous undertaking. Some five thousand Canadians, the flower of our youth, have joined this corps. Much glory has come to Canada through its contribution. On the other hand, the officers of the Royal Flying Corps have maintained correct and congenial relation with the Canadian military authorities. It is thought by some Canadians that we should have started, and should start even now, a flying corps of our owm but in my opinion that would be a mistake for more reasons than one. Some gentlemen also think that Canada should contribute certain squadrons to the Royal Flying Corps. Whether or not such a thing is advisable is a question to be considered. It is known that the Imperial Government have established throughout Canada a tremendous organization, and, as I have already stated, some five thousand of our young men have joined the Royal Flying Corps, and we all know what a name they have made for themselves. In one of our camps, Camp Borden, the work that was accomplished by that Flying Corps last year was wonderful. Camp Borden is recognized [DOT]as one of the best Flying Corps camps in the world. The young Canadians who received their initial training there and passed through the various courses of instruction, were considered] fit to go to the front, I am advised, as technically qualified 'Flying Corps officers after a very short period1 of further training in England. They have done so, and have made a name for themselves.
The British Canadian Recruiting Mission, as I have already said, assisted in obtaining recruits for the Imperial and Canadian Expeditionary Forces and the Royal Flying [DOT]Corps. British subjects residing in the United 'States for the Canadian Expeditionary Force. In adition to these, a large number of men have been obtained for the British Expeditionary Force as well as for the Royal Flying Corps.

such a large number of mien naturally, at a time like the present, greatly added to the difficulties of those officers entrusted with transportation duties. We are up against this situation, not only as regards transports for troops going overseas, but we are now face to face with the problem of invalids coming back, and also of men unfit for further service at the front being brought back. There have been some complaints, probably some of them just and many unjust, as to the transports coming

back. We are not responsible here for bringing the troops back to Canada so far as berthing and arranging for ships is concerned. That is entirely under the Admiralty. So many troops, who are collected at the Buxton Discharge Depot, where they undergo their examination, and the returned and hospital cases, are notified on very short notice to proceed to the embarkation point and get on board ship. So far, the Canadian Government have been unable to charter a complete ship, and men complained, in .some instances, that berths were empty, and that they were not permitted to use those berths. An investigation is going on now. Some time ago an officer proceeded overseas to see if some better co-ordination could be brought adopt. The steamship companies sold passages and berths in England to civilians, and in some instances the berths were not occupied. Canada was paying so much per capita for the transport of the men, and when the ship sailed with empty staterooms, there was complaint by a few of the men; but the majority realized the difficulty about transports, and that there was bound to be a little trouble. But I think it has practically all passed away and better and more definite arrangements are being made. Probably we will be able to charter complete ships, and bring our men back as troops and not as civilians. It is a difficult thing to handle men coming back when they are not organized as units but as individuals, collected on short notice. For in- -stance, I have known of men hurried- down to the port of embarkation, and held twelve and fourteen days before they were allowed to leave. These conditions have arisen and will arise in the future, but arrangements have been made that will gradually and effectually overcome all of these little annoyances. After all, as many officers and men have told me, these are only petty annoyances and discomforts, and they realize that there is a war on, and that they must put up with some discomforts.
I would like to speak, if I may take up the time of the House for a few minutes, regarding the surplus officers returned to Canada. I feel it is my duty to say something in regard to that, and I would like to call to the attention of hon. gentlemen, who may not have seen or read it, an article which appeared a short time ago in the Military Gazette entitled "Mental Crucifixion of Officers." I shall not wade through the whole article, but I think hon. members will appreciate it if an explanation is made, and some of these unfortunate offi-


errs will have more decent consideration than they have had in the past:
It is about time that the indignities and mental torture endured' by offioers ordered back to Canada, because of age and senior rank, were put an end to by a strong and clear announcement from the Militia Department, published, at advertising rates, if necessary in every single paper, great and small, in the country.
Owing to the system of recruiting by means of oounty and district corps, so long in vogue, and so wonderfully fruitful in result, a very large number of senior officers found themselves in England, without a chance to serve with their rank in Franoe, and with but little chance, even in the lower grade, to see service there. These gentlemen had enlisted in perfectly good faith, fully expecting to accompany their respective corps to the front, only to find on crossing the seas that the exigencies of war required the battalion to be broken up for reinforcements, with the result that their connection with it was severed forever. Now, there is in England very useful employment for a great many officers. All the reserve battalions need them, to say nothing of suoh big departments as the Pay Corps, the Records Office, and a dozen minor ones. These various positions absorbed many officers or disbanded' units, who thus did useful work, releasing younger men for the front.
But as the war went on, and the number of returned' wounded offioers increased', it was felt that these men who had suffered much should be given these positions in England, their vacated posts in France being filled, wherever possible, by men from the ranks who had seen much service there.
With this plan surely no one can quarrel. As a result a gradual displacement has taken place, so hundreds of officers, of the county corps class, have been superseded by returned casualties, and find themselves without employment. What could these unfortunates then do? IF BELOW FORTY YEARS OF AGE they could revert to a lieutenancy and go to the front. Hundreds have done so, but hundreds of others, in fact, nearly all of the rank of Major and Lt.-Colonel, with many Captains, too, were above the age limit, and could not be used in this way.
I may say that that age limit has since been reduced from forty to thirty-five year?.
The writer has known many who have fairly gone on their knees to headquarters to be excepted from the general rule, and allowed to go over, though past forty. Naturally, headquarters has been deaf to these appeals, for to open the door to one would make trouble with scores of others.
Nor could1 an officer "grab up a rifle and rush to the front," as some melodramatic people at home have recommended. War is no longer a "rush to the front," but a highly organized business in which headquarters has the say as to who shall and shall not "rush" there.
As an officer said to me: "This is an awful war. It takes an awful long time to get to it." He had been in England for a year and a half. The article continues:
And so in due course, an officer who has sacrificed much in helping to raise a corps, who
has given up a lucrative profession or business, who has done his best to go and fight, and has not been allowed to do so, finds himself ordered back to Canada, and at home once more.
And then the horrible thing happens, at least it has often happened, and may again. His fellow citizens actually send a committee to ask him to apologize for not having been killed. The bitter humiliation of such a visitation can only be appreciated by one who has had to endure it.
I regret that there is a good deal of truth in what the writer of this article says. The whole trouble experienced in 'Connection with returned surplus officers is simply the by-product of voluntary recruiting. Two hundred and fifty-eight battalions were raised, each having from thirty-six to forty officers, senior and otherwise. Many of these officers had given years of their lives to training; others had joined the forces only since the outbreak of war. With very little financial assistance from the Government; they raised these battalions and took them overseas. I know one man not many miles from Ottawa who was asked to raise a battalion and assured that he would be allowed to take command of it at the front. He sacrificed his business, raised the battalion, and went over to England. There his unit was broken up and ultimately he was returned as a surplus officer. There have been many such cases, but it is difficult to know what to do under circumstances like that. In these various- battalions there were some three or four thousand officers; what was to become of them? Hon. gentlemen must bear in mind that as we were accumulating this mass of officers in England, officers without war experience and war testing, the divisions in France were advancing men who had shown ability and leadership on the field of battle. Much is to be said in favour of making promotion in war time depend upon war service. But what of our officers fresh from 'Canada? The easy reply is, " Let them revert." For the younger men this is possible to some extent, though only to some extent; for there is a limit to the number of lieutenants needed, and the battalions at the front have many deserving non-commissioned) officers of proved worth whom they desire to promote. For older men reversion becomes very difficult. When a man is past 40 he is not likely to make a very good platoon leader. That is a young man's job. Then an order was issued that no officer over 35 years of age could revert. I put it to every honourable member: if he were colonel of a battalion in the trenches and had his choice for the leadership of one of his platoons between a man of 45 who has never been in action, who was formerly a major or a colonel, and a young man of

How long has the Militia Council been in existence?
Major-General MEWBURN: I think since 1904. Since the war started, the scope of the Militia Council has been greatly enlarged, and one can imagine that the work of the council is very much greater than

it has ever been before. It is an advisory council, matters of a very technical nature come before it, and before decisions 'are given, reports are made to it by the heads of the different branches of the Militia Department.

There is no longer a Parliamentary Secretary.
Major-General MEWBURN: No, I wish sometimes there were two or three of them. I should like to bear testimony to the very efficient work of several of the officers who have carried on this burden since the "war started. In the first place there is my deputy minister who is present now. I shall not say what I think of him at the present time, 'but certainly his long experience of both military and administrative work, his military services in South Africa, and his faithful and unceasing work, not only before the war but since, are wonderful, and he is deserving of the greatest possible credit. There is another officer of whom I should like to speak, and I do so with the greatest admiration and respect. I refer to the Chief of the General Staff, Major-General W. G. Gwatkin, who has been directly responsible for all the training and military operations of the troops. He has also had numerous other responsibilites thrust upon his shoulders. The public do not and probably never will realize the magnificent work that has been performed by this hard-working, patient and faithful officer. He has 'been responsible for all the confidential correspondence and cables with the War Office and has been directly in touch with the Admiralty on naval matters in connection with the war, as far as my department is concerned. The country owes a heavy debt to both General Fiset and General Gwatkin for their faithful and efficient work performed since the war started. There are other officers who are working day and night in that department. I wish to tell the hon. gentlemen present that the (Militia Department is overworked. It has no complaints to make. The only regret we had when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) brought in the Daylight (Saving Bill was that he could no(t increase the number of hours per day to twenty-four so that we might proibahly have heavier (production. fPhe duties of the Adjutant-General which are now performed hy Major-General Ashton, are tremendous. Under the Adjutant General the following officers have shown wonderful ability and have devoted all their best efforts to the prosecution of the war;
[.Major-General Mewburn.]
I refer particularly to Brigadier-General Gwynne, in charge of mobilization, Colonel C. S. Maolnnes, in charge of organization, Colonel A. Z. Palmer and Major S. T Blackwood, and others, who have worked night and day faithfully and honestly, not for the small pay which they have been receiving, but simply for the honour and glory of doing something for their country.
The organization of the department has been undergoing certain changes. My hon. friend asked me last night if 'I had the details of it; I have a draft of it here hut I shall not burden the House with the details. But the organization in the different departments is under the (Minister of Militia, the deputy minister, the chief of the general staff, the Adjutant (General, the Quartermaster General, the Master General of the Ordnance, who goes into all the technical work of the 'branches and the whole service generally, and who has a much heavier task than many hon. gentlemen realize. Then we have, under the Adjutant General, what is known as the Record Office which has developed since, the war started. That office is responsible for. all the documents and information pertaining to every officer, non-commissioned officer and mian who has gone overseas or who has returned from overseas.	'

Both officers and men?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Yes. Of
course, the records of all officers are also in the militia headquarters. The Record Office in London, England, has grown to an enormous extent. It has a large staff which is responsible for getting out all the returns, the statistics relating to every individual man and all the casualty lists. As the casualties come forward, one can realize the heavy strain on that department. I have been endeavouring to make some changes in various departments, and while I am not boasting in (any way, within the last few months I have, by reorganization undertaken by a very efficient man who came from overseas, who has seen service at the front, and who. is familiar with that work, succeeded in reducing the sltaff by over 400 and in showing a saving of over $250,000 in that one department alone. There has I understand been criticism in the press and elsewhere in regard to the dismissals of employees in the record office.
There has been no person peremptorily dismissed. I want, if I can accomplish it, to get the highest efficiency and economy in my department. I do. not ever expect to reach that objective, but I am endeavouring

to do so. It is necessary in my judgment, if you are running a department, to get an efficient head, put the responsibility on that head and make him, livie up to it. If you do that, you will accomplish something. There will (be no dismissals except foT cause. In the Record Office the correspondence and the magnitude of the work is enormous. There are over two thousand five hundred telegrams and letters coming in daily that the 'branch has to deal with. Every time there is a casualty the Record Branch deals with it and conveys the news to the next of kin, promptly.
One of the largest departments under the Paymaster General is the Assigned Pay and Separation Allowance Branch. When I took charge of the department I found, the work of that branch to be something in the nature of an enormous financial (transaction and I made up my mind-to put it on a proper financial ibasis. I succeeded in getting an officer who had 'been at the, front and who, simply loaned his services until he got it running smoothly. Then, he went back to civil life. I have been assisted by financial men who have voluntarily given their service's, with (the result that I think I am getting the, efficiency in that department that I am getting in many others.
I would like to give a few facts relating to the Separation and Assigned Pay Branch in, order that hon. members may realize the magnitude of work carried on there. During the year 1917, the average number of cheques issued each month was 254,400. Since the Separation and Assigned Pay accounts have been consolidated, the average number of combined cheques is about 180,000 monthly, although, of course, action has to Ibe taken on 265,000 accounts. To write out the cheques for one month would ' take am average clerk, working full working hours, over four years. With the new printing machinery which is now being installed in the 'Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay Branch, it would be possible, if necessary, to write these cheques in two and one-half days. This new equipment also automatically prepares the mailing list for the poet office and the Return tor the Auditor General. The average number of letters received and replied to during the year 1917 was about 425,000, or about 1,350 per working, day. Some days the correspondence received is as high as 5,000 letters.
So you can realize when some hon. member writes to know why one of his constituents has not received her separation allowance why the devil he does not get a
reply by next mail that it is very difficult to comply with every request of this -kind as speedily as otherwise might :be possible.
During the year 1917, 18,000 new Separation Allowance accounts and 56,000 Assigned Pay accounts were opened. During the same period 14,000 Separation Allowance accounts and 26,000 Assigned Pay -accounts were closed. Also, 8,000 soldiers changed the amount of their assignment, through the Chief Paymaster, overseas. Change of address has been one of the great troubles.
The number of clerks employed in the branch is 872. The total expenditure during the year 1917 was $59,561,299, or an average of almost $5,000,000 per month. It is difficult to realize the work which is done by the S. A. & A. P. Branch, unless one visits their office and makes a close inspection.
During the year 1917 almost every one of the 80,000 separation allowance accounts has been investigated to see that the separation allowance was being properly paid. The enormous amount of work entailed can only be imagined. The dependents live from coast to coast, and each investigation had to be carried on in the locality in which the dependent resided. This, of course, was only rendered possible by the co-operation of the Canadian, Patriotic Eund. Such investigation was- necessary, as no business firm would think of paying out money unless they knew that the payee was entitled to it.
The hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) has been instrumental in rendering the greatest possible assistance, through the Patriotic Fund, to the Militia Department in getting information regarding these thousands of accounts.
Every payment of assigned pay from the S. A. & A. P. Branch amounting to some 170,000 accounts each month, has been checked over with deductions made in the Chief Paymaster's Office, London, England, and the organization is now so perfect that a casualty in the field affecting a soldier's assigned1 pay is acted on in the S. A. & A. P. Branch within seven days from the date of casualty being reported. I think we are improving, and that probably in a short time the department will be working more smoothly and without much cause for complaint.
The country, as far as the Militia Department is concerned, is divided into eleven military districts, the division not in all cases being in conformity with provincial boundaries. The districts are as follows:
No. 1, Western Ontario, Brigadier-General L. W. Shannon; No. 2, Central Ontario, Major-General W. A. Logie; No. 3, Eastern Ontario, Brigadier-General T. D. R. Hemming;

No. 4, Western Quebec, Major-General E. W. Wilson; No. 5, Eastern Quebec, Brigadier-General J. P. Landry; No. 6, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, Major-General F. L. Lessard; No. 7, New Brunswick, Brigadier-General A. H. Macdonell; No. 10, Manitoba and a portion of New Ontario. .Major-General John Hughes; No. 11, British Columbia, Major-General R. G. E. Leckie; No. 12, Saskatchewan, Major-General J. C. MacDougall; No. 13, Alberta, Colonel G. Macdonald.
Each of these districts has a general officer commanding, with the necessary staff. That staff is qualified to perform administration duties as well as to handle all recruits, train and mobilize the same. During the past year these district staffs have disbursed in the neighbourhood of $75,000,000, under the direction and authority of headquarters.	-
As I said before, I am a great believer in decentralization. With a country the size of Canada, it is absolutely impossible to carry out the enormous amount of work by centralizing at headquarters. As heavier and greater responsibilities have been and will be put on the shoulders of G. O. C.'s of districts, some changes have taken place and other changes will likely be made. No permanent appointments have or will be made at present, as it is recognized1 as things develop that appointments to these positions will be made by officers who have seen service at the front. In all districts in Canada, there have been officers who have been carrying on the drudgery work since the war started and magnificent service thqy have performed. I know of no single instance where an officer who has been employed at headquarters has not desired to go. overseas. In some instances there have been officers who have been medically unfit and for this reason unable to proceed overseas. There are many other instances of officers, whose hearts have almost been,, broken with the idea of being held back, but in order to cope with the tremendous situation in Canada it was absolutely essential to retain certain officers in Canada to carry on the work, as Canada is the base and foundation of all our overseas forces.
Just here I wish to bear testimony to the faithful, loyal support and help that has been given by the G. O. C.'s of various military districts and their splendid staffs and I would particularly mention General Shannon at Military District No. 1, General Logie at Military District No. 2, General Hemming at Military District No. 3, General Wilson at Military District No. 4, General
[Major-General Mewburn.]
Fages at Military District No. 5 (Quebec), General Benson at Military District No. 6, General Ruttan at Military District No. 10 (Winnipeg), Colonel Macdonald at Military District No. 13 (Calgary, Colonel Duff Stuart at Military District No. 11 (Vancouver).
It is a difficult matter to single out any one officer for special recognition, as with very few exceptions all officers employed both at headquarters and at districts are performing and have performed their arduous duties with the greatest satisfaction, and the names I have mentioned are those who are the responsible heads of departments and districts.
It is my intention to carry the idea of decentralization very much further than it has ever been carried before and on the same principle as I have spoken of in regard to some of the other branches. In each military district, a good general officer commanding should be responsible for the whole organization, administration and discipline within his military district. If that is carried out, it is going to save the headquarters from a great deal of labour and it is going to make for greater efficiency because everything that is centralized in headquarters tends to weaken the efficiency of the militia service. It is difficult in a country extending three thousand six hundred miles from Halifax to Esquimalt to administer military affairs from headquarters. It is physically impossible, and the machinery will play out if it is attempted. I hope that in the near future we will have a strengthening of the various military districts by the adoption of a policy of decentralization and everything it means.
There are two branches of the service I would like particularly to bring to the attention of the House. One is the Medical Services.
The devotion of the Canadian Army Medical Corps has been magnificent, both overseas and in Canada. The following extract is from a report made by Mr. McPherson to the House of Commons in England, as to the work of the Army Medical Corps, and is significant:
In the Napoleonic Wars the percentage ot deaths from disease was 97 and from death on the battlefield three; Even as late as the South African Campaign there were 67,000 cases of disease admitted to hospital and over 8,000 deaths. Four times as many men died from disease in South Africa as there were cases in France up to the beginning of November last. Sir W. Cheyne, than whom there was no greater authority, had made It clear how, although In a stationary army epidemics of disease were most liable to break out. skill and medical science, care and forethought had made the incidence of disease in the British Forces in

France less than in the history of any army in the world."
The Canadian Dental Corps has performed marvellous work. During the past eighteen months, 1,042,000 dental operations have been performed, and I am making a conservative estimate when I say that at least forty per cent of the Canadian soldiers now serving in France, would never have been permitted to leave Canada, had it not been for the magnificent service rendered by the Dental Corps.
From the reports from overseas, on the .work of the Canadian Army Dental Corps up to the 31st of December, 1917, we learn that the Dental Corps in England and France, performed' 1,375,629 different dental operations and treatments.	-

How many men have you in that dental corps?	.
Major-General MEWBURN: It is distributed all over. In Military District No. 2, at Camp Borden and at Niagara, the dentists and their assistants have a corps of, I think, not over 35 or 40, and I know, frbim the figures I checked as A.A.G. of that district, that 10,000 men proceeded overseas to France who would have been rejected had not the Army Dental Corps given their services.
If any further information is desired I will be delighted to give it at any time.
