speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I merely thought we would resume this evening for the purpose of ascertaining if there was any subject which occurred to hon. gentlemen on. the other side which has not yet been placed before the Committee, and as to which they desire information. It would be useful to have any suggestions of that kind in order that the information necessary might be prepared and be immediately available. However, as no question seems to arise for the moment, perhaps we had better adjourn the debate forthwith.

I have one
question to ask. Can the Minister of Militia and Defence give us the number of men conscripted! in Canada?
Major-General MEWBURN- The number of men that are in. Canada?

Yes.
Major-General MEWBURN:	I do not
think it- is desirable to give details as to the actual number of troops of the Canadian Expeditionary Force that are in this country, but on the 31st March there were approximately 30,000 troops in Canada, including conscripted men. If my right hon. friend would 'like to get any further information I will be very glad to give ilt to him confidentially, because I do not think it is wise to disclose the places where all these troops are. They are, as hon. gentlemen know, moving overseas very rapidly. As I stated this afternoon, we are desirous of getting them there as quickly as possible, or as soon as ships are available. We 'have distributed in the various military districts both the men who have reported to these depot battalions, and others who have come from the United States .as recruits raised by the recruiting mission that has been at work there, and they are categorized in the various branches as infantry, cavalry, artillery, engineers, medical and dental organizations, railway construction corps, veterinary units, and -so forth. Thos"

5M

are not immediately available for duty overseas by any means, unfortunately. A rigorous medical examination is now required. In the first >and second years of the war men did go overseas, and broke down under training in England or at the front; they were unable to stand the severe test of the arduous work there. Therefore we have found it necessary ithat, after the men get into the depot battalions or regiments where we have them now, and .before sending them overseas, it is necessary , to have a final medical board. .It has been found inadvisable to allow men to proceed overseas who are not .absolutely in what we call technically class A, and fit for immediate service at the front. I regret to say _ that under the Military Service Act there have been many cases of men rwho have been found after re-medical examination, medically unfit. These men have had to be discharged and this has, in some instances, reduced our available reinforcements. Some of the men in question have -been placed, even after joining the colours, in the lower B category. They will, we hope in some instances/ come back to the higher category. Then, included in )the number given are a certain number of men whom we have had on special guard duties within Canada, and whom we have 'been forced to hold, including t'he garrisons at Halifax and other points. Approximately the total is as I have stated. Should my right hon. friend desire more details I would be very glad to give them to him.
Publicly or privately?

Privately.
T do not think it is in the public interest to give detailed information publicly.

The minister, wheji speaking this afternoon, said he thought a mistake had been mads in the early part of the war in sending over so many battalions officered by such a large number of officers-I think he toll us that each battalion had thirty-five or forty officers, if I remember correctly. He said that upon reaching the other side the men were drafted into other battalions and the officers were left in England with practically nothing to do. Now there has been a great deal of talk in the press and elsewhere with regard to this matter. I notice by the press that a large number of these officers have been returned to Canada, but there still must be many on the other side. Would it be possible for the minister to state the approximate number of such officers who are still in England?
[Major-General Mewburn.]

As regards the surplus officers in England, I am not in a position to give the exact number that are there at the present time. With respect to the regiments or battalions which were .raised in the early stages of the war, I did observe that I thought other arrangements might have been made, but there was this to he said with respect to the regiments in question: when these battalions *were authorized and organized, in 1915 and 1916 particularly, had it not been for the individual efforts of these officers in raising the battalions in question I do not think we wiould ever have got the number of men that we did get. Owing to the military situation those battalions went overseas up to their regular establishment, in round figures about 1,150. Each composite battalion had one hundred extra [DOT]men, but the strength was subsequently reduced to 1.050. I do not think all the officers were struck off, hut in many in stances when those battalions want overseas the officers were taken away from them. The men were put into t-ne or other of the numerous reserve battalions for training in England, which were then officered by officers who had been in England from the early stages of the war, as well as officers who' had been returned wounded from France and could not go back. Theie.were many instances where officers failed to find employment, 'but in 1916 they were all employed in England and they were employed in taking special courses. A very large number of those officers took various courses, qualifying them for the higher rank, such as field courses, and so on, with the object of giving them the higher training that would enable them to be utilized in France. Subsequently the policy was adopted under which non-commissioned officers and privates who had distinguished themselves in the field and who were recommended by their commanding officers weie given commissions. Therefore, there naturally was very little chance of some of the officers in question getting to the front. They had the privilege of reverting to the rank of lieutenant, tout in many cases officers who went from Canada did so with the rank of major and had held that rank in the Canadian militia for a long time. They had taken highly technical courses and were in command of double companies when they went to the front. There were many of those who did revert in rank and are to-day serving at the front as lieutenants, and all the more honour to them on that account. There was another class of officers who were over the age of thirty-five, and who, under the
APRIL 10, 101b
new order, were prohibited from going-" to the front. There were still others-and I think this is a great compliment to Canada -who accepted positions in the Imperial army. For a time the Imperial army were short of officers, but to-day they have a large surplus of junior officers. In some instances we had officers who were trained in the higher .branches of the service who were qualified for conducting open warfare, and who would, under the new order, be struck off and sent back to Canada as surplus. But I am glad to say that I know of two instances where Canadian officers were accepted by the British War Office and are to-day in France in command of British regiments with the rank of lieutenant-colonel. The British Army recognized their ability and were glad to accept their eervices. A very large number of officers returned to Canada. I .am not prepared to give the exact number because I have not the information available. Within the last six or seven months a large number of officers have been returned. A large number have gone back to civilian life; a large number, when they found they could not get over to France, in some cases even offered to go as privates and being refused, returned to Canada. Other officers went immediately off the pay-eheet; they paid their own way back to Canada and have gone back to civil life rather than loaf around. There are other officers who, after being employed temporarily, are being sent back gradually.. Take the officers of the Fifth Division. At the time that division was up to full strength, and after the artillery of that division was taken away, there were some 330 officers released to be disposed of. There are something like_ 2,300 officers employed in administration, and a large percentage, I am informed, employed in these administrative services, are unfit to return to France. In the reserve battalions, I have not the actual figures, but I may say that these officers are being very rapidly returned to Canada, and where they cannot be absorbed here-we cannot give employment to everybody-they are very rapidly returned to civil life. Those to whom we 'have given preference and priority, having regard to efficiency, are the officers who have served actually at the front and who have been wounded and are not fit to return to the front. I am afraid I cannot give the actual number of officers now in England now unemployed, but my information is that there are very- few -and they are returning rapidly by every ship.

The principle of taking officers from the ranks dates from the 38i
beginning of the war. On one occasion, long before the overseas minister was appointed, we had the honour of taking over two hundred and fifty men in one day from the ranks of the non-commissioned "officers and promoting them to be officers. Let me give in detail the plan. The First Division passed over. I can not recall a solitary instance in the First Division, where officers were put on from outside sources, the promotions were always from within. Then the Second Division went, taking over very few officers outside of those who had been engaged' in raising and training the battalions composing that division. The officers who were qualified in that division were retained. Some we had to replace, but in replacing them, as far as we could) we selected officers who had already served in the First Division. In the same way, the new officers held their battalions as far as qualified, which was perfectly right, and each man had to go through a very rigid test to prove whether or not he was qualified to take his position in the battalion. In other words, we did not impose on any division that had already been in the fighting, but we did take the ground that new divisions going in, or new brigades, should as far as possible, retain the officers they had been trained under, provided they were qualified. In cases where an officer had to be replaced, he stepped down and out willingly, but he was always courteously treated, not thrown out like a buccaneer, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Bal-lantyne) was when he went over with his battalion. When we organized the Second, Third, Fourth and Fifth Divisions, in large numbers by battalions, every officer was given to understand that unless he measured up, and unless his unit measured up, he must give place to the corps already in the field, and his unit must be broken up. That was distinctly understood by ninety-nine out of every hundred, and if it was not understood' it was contrary to orders. They -were to go over taking their chances, and if by their efficiency they could merit recognition, they were to be maintained together as far as possible as reserve battalions. There never was any intention I can assure hon. gentlemen but that officers who had given their time and money, as they had done in the years 1915 and 1916-I may say here that there was never anything to equal that system in the history of this or any other country-were entitled to absolutely fair treatment.
It was only when the overseas minister was appointed that these men had their

battalions taken from them and they were thrown out. I never in my life saw anything like the way they were treated. Noncommissioned officers would sometimes take the battalions away from the colonels who had brought them over. In my time they were treated with the utmost courtesy in every solitary instance. It was all right enough to break the battalions up. That could not be avoided, except in some cases where there was favouritism shown, and men were put over the heads of better men, and others were treated discourteously and given no consideration at all.
On whose recommendation were these men put over the head of the others?
I have not the records. The hon. member will have to get that from the records. It did not. occur in my time.
In your time? On whose recommendation were these inferior men put over the heads of the others?

There were no
inferior men, no junior men, put over the head of the senior, unless the senior were absolutely unqualified, in my time. But later on there were many instances where men were put over excellent officers, their betters in every way, and these had no chance whatever, but were passed over, and then, of course, there was a good deal of trouble. The whole trouble could have been avoided if these men had been courteously relieved of their battalions instead of their being ruthlessly taken from them. Perhaps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries can explain why he was thrown out.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot altogether concur in the last observation of my good friend the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes). I certainly was not, as he puts it, thrown out in England. I endeavoured to raise an overseas battalion of infantry, the 245th Battalion Canadian Grenadier Guards, and with the loyal and enthusiastic assistance of the officers associated with me, and at the expenditure of a respectable sum of money, I succeeded, after great effort, in Tecruiting a considerable number of men with a splendid organization, but I could not bring my battalion up to strength. The (reason fox this was that the voluntary system of recruiting had broken down, and notwithstanding the fact that there were plenty of available men in the good city of Montreal, I found it quite impossible to

induce them to join up for overseas service. Before I left with my battalion for overseas I was perfectly well aware that it would be broken up shortly after our arrival in England. I knew that my men would be drafted into one of the reserve battalions there, and later, after they had completed their training, sent forward to France. When I arrived in England wi,th my unit I was allowed to Tetain command for about ten days in Shoxeham ca'mp, and then I received orders to turn my unit over to the 23rd Reserve Battalion. I was then ordered by the General Officer Commanding, Shore-ham Camp, to report at London. I offered my services to General Turner in any capacity that he considered I could best serve in either in England or in France, but he informed me that my services could not be accepted, for two reasons: First, that qnly junior officers would be allowed to go to England, men not over 35 years of age, ,and inasmuch -as I was fifty years of age, tI could not be permitted to revert to the rank of lieutenant. The second reason was that there was a large number of junior officers in the various camps in England, *some fully trained and others training, waiting an opportunity to go to France. I found no fault with the policy prevailing in England, that overseas units arriving there of necessity had to be broken up to maintain up to strength the four divisions of Canadian infantry in France.
That was in May, 1917?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I admit that there was a large number of Canadian officers in the various camps in England at that time, but that was not surprising. Notwithstanding the training officers and non-oammissioned officers and men receive *in Canada before they leave for overseas, they have to take a long course of additional training in England. At the present time there are not nearly so many Canadian officers in England as there were when I was there, because owing to the heavy casualties at the front they are being sent over more quickly. I will admit that, like all other commanding officers whose battalions are broken up on arrival in England, I was disappointed. I knew full well, however, before I left that this system would prevail, and I can find no fault with the treatment accorded me.
The hon. gentleman, on his return from overseas, was one of the most wrathy men I ever met.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Disappointed.
The remarks of the exMinister of Militia (>Sir Sam Hughes) maybe very interesting, tout I would ask him to speak a little louder, so that we all may get the benefit of them.

I was saying that'the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), on his return from England was-J will not say the maddest man, but one of the most intensely disappointed men that it has ever been my privilege to meet. I told all whom I met before they left that they must take their chance; that the proficiency or strength of their battalions would be the measure of their chance of being retained in the new divisions. I wish to pay my good friend (Mr. Ballantyne) this tribute: no officer in Canada surpassed him in zeal, in enthusiasm, or in the desire to have a good battalion. For some unaccountable reason-he knows, you know, and others know what the troubles were; I shall not intrude them on the committee now, though I may do so later in the session- recruiting did not measure up as I had hoped. The officers who went over with these battalions knew that it was not possible under the circumstances for every battalion,to go to the front as a unit, but what did hurt me was that officers who had given of their time and money to the raising of their battalions should have them taken from them immediately on their arrival in England. To illustrate-I say it advisedly; the facts are as I state them unless officers have misrepresented them, *and I do not believe that they have-officers have landed in England, marched their battalions into camp, and have never 'been allowed to see them again. One member of this House told1 me that his battalion had been taken from him by a sergeant major and marched off, while he and his officers were left behind. That has been the cause of much dissatisfaction.. Many of these officers-all; I think, who were within the age-were desirous' of going to the fronts At that time there were not, of course, places for all officers. The system of taking non-commissioned officers from the ranks and giving them commissions was>
not new; it had been in vogue from the beginning of the campaign within each battalion, division, and so on. But when a new division went over it was right that the officers who had raised the units and who had given their time and money to the work should, provided they were qualified, command the battalions, companies and platoons in the field.

My hon. friend has told us that many of these battalions
were disposed of rather unceremoniously. He has cited the case of a man whose battalion was marched off by a sergeant-major; was this done at the instance of the Canadian, or of the Imperial, authorities?

The policy had: been to keep the battalions there for a time and let them get settled down, the old officers remaining with them until the units were broken up. Later the policy was inaugurated of breaking up the battalions immediately on their arrival in England. That was done by the Canadian local brigadier and officers in command of the unit to which the battalions were assigned. Certainly I had nothing whatever to do with it.
Did this come from the Overseas Minister of Militia?
I do not know from whom else it would come. I should hope that it did not come from this side.
The same thing was done before an overseas minister was appointed. The commanding officer of the 189th Battalion, a very fine young man named Piuze-
A fine fellow.

He recruited his
regiment with great success and crossed over in 1916.
What month?
In September or October.
October, I think.

An officer was waiting on the wharf at Liverpool, and when the regiment disembarked the officer asked for Colonel Piuze. He then told Colonel Piuze that he had orders to take over the command of his regiment, and that fine officer, who had been the most successful recruiting officer in the province of Quebec and who had been assured that his regiment would go to the front as a unit, had not the glory -if it be called a glory-of commanding his own unit on British soil. He had to act as a sort of visitor at the camp for some months. Colonel Piuze, who is a very well qualified officer, is to-day commanding the depot battalion at Quebec. That is what happened in England; I was there at the time, and I know what I am talking about. All the officers of the unit were very angry, and took opportunity to yentilate itbeir grievances. Colonel Piuze 'himself did not complain.

The other day one of the_ members inquired regarding an article in the papers about the treatment received by the soldiers returning from overseas. The Minister of Militia and Defence replied that the matter rested with the overseas minister. I must say that I know very little about this overseas minister, and I am anxious to kno w more. We have in this House a Minister of Militia who is,responsible to Parliament for everything that is done in bis department, and we are here to criticise him if we have occasion to find fault. But things are done by the Overseas Minister of Militia for which the Minister of Militia who sits in this House is responsible. We cannot criticise those things because we do not know what is going on overseas in regard to them. The question that comes to the ordinary mufti-dressed man is: Why should there be two. departments in one, and why should one man, if I may use the expression, wear the harness, draw the cart, be exposed here to all the criticism, and yet have no- control over the pther man? il do not believe, unless they have private information, there are many members of this House, except those who have been overseas who know what is being done there. I do not know what is being done nor who is performing what duties. When I look over the statutes and read the authority of the Minister of Militia and Defence, I know exactly what his authority is and what constitutes his department; I know exactly what powers Parliament has vested in him. But when 1 speak about the Overseas Ministry of Militia, why, I do not even know by what authority it exists, unless it he by Order in Council. I do not know what are the powers of the Overseas Minister of Militia, what duties he is performing overseas or what is under his control. There is no doubt he must be spending a great deal of money in England. If I understand aright the position as it is now, the authorities in England are spending money on our behalf and we are spending money on theirs, but the balance must *be drawn some day. If they are equipping and paying for our men, if we on this side are paying for ships or wheat or other commodities, when the day of reckoning comes there is a balance to be drawn.
[iMr. E. Lapointe. 1
Who has the supervision of that expenditure on the other side? I do not know. Are we to have any control over it? Are we going to be allowed to criticise the way in which the money is expended? Certainly not, according to the way in which things are being done now. I do not, of course, want to be understood as fault-finding, all I want to know is what control or authority the Overseas Minister of Militia has with reference to the Canadian Forces, and how it is that you can have two or perhaps three departments in one? Does the Overseas Minister of Militia control the expenditure of Canadian moneys or the administration of Canadian forces in France? That is what I should like to. have light upon in order to he able to put questions so .as to ascertain what condition we are in and what we may expect from this duplicate or triplicate administration of the Department of Militia and Defence. It is most unfair -that one man should shoulder in this House the whole burden, and be in this unenviable position of sometimes being unable to give information when that is absolutely not his fault. I do not want the minister to understand that I desire to criticise him. I know he cannot do any better than he is doing. If T had two* 'branches of my business one being in Montreal, and I could not go to Montreal, nobody could blame me for not knowing anything about my deeds and abstracts there, but the system could be blamed, and people could accuse me of ignorance, or neglect, or recklessness*, for which I would be answerable if I were at the head of that office and had the administration of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I shall endeavour to relieve, as far as I can, the darkness which, according to my hon. friend, is overspreading him. If he would extend his researches into the statutory law a little further and examine the statutes that were passed last session, he would find there a statue which defines the powers, duties and jurisdiction of the Minister of the Overseas Service. That can be stated in a very few words. The Minister of the Overseas Service is to have, and does have, the isame jurisdiction and powers and duties in resipect of the troops in Great Britain and France that the Minister of Militia and Defence has in respect of the troops that are raised here before they embark for overseas. So far as the payments overseas are concerned, I have already explained to the committee-I do not know whether my hon. friend was

present or not-that they are under the direct supervision of the Auditor General, who, after consultation with the Government about eighteen months ago, detailed officers of his department for the purpose of examining the system of checking accounts overseas. Officers have gone to England for that purpose and have made any necessary examination. Further than that, my hon. friend does not seem to be aware that the major portion of the expenditure overseas is regulated by statute; that is to say, the pay and allowances of the troops who are serving in Great Britain and in France. That is provided by law'; it is not subject to the discretion of any minister or officer. In respect of transport and in respect of the provision of food, expenditures have to be made, and are made in the ordinary way. The maintenance of the troops in France is undertaken by the British Government, and a fixed amount per day for each man serving in France has been agreed upon between the Government of this country and the Government of the United Kingdom. Those are matters of accounting -which will be adjusted afterwards.
Can the Prime Minister tell us how much the amount is per man per day?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have already stated that this afternoon. I shall state it again. The amount per man in France, as regulated in the first instance, was six shillings, which covered not only the maintenance of the man there, but ammunition for the rifles, shells for the guns, everything that was to be done in France.
But not the pay of the men.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But not the pay of the men. I thought, of course, I had made that plain already. It is for the maintenance of the men and not for the pay of the men, so that there is very little left to the discretion or regulation of the overseas minister, but whatever is left has been under the direct supervision of the Auditor General and has been carefully checked by him from time to time. I spoke to the Auditor General to-day before coming into the House, and so far as I could1 gather from him, the arrangements made in the public interest to superintend those expenditures are entirely to hi-s satisfaction.
My right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) tells me, as one of the explanations- to make sunshine in my darkness, that that expenditure is authorized by statute.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The greater part.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry if
my efforts were so unavailing. I will repeat-
I understand what you said; yon need not repeat.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: I suggest that the expenditures should be controlled here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They are controlled here in the same way as other expenditures, by the Auditor General. They are controlled, in the first place, by the fact that they are, for the most part, fixed expenditures. No man can pay anything in

excess' of the amount fixed by law to any officer, non-commissioned officer or man who serves at the front. They are controlled, in the next place, by the supervision of the Auditor General through himself and his officers here as well as -by officers whom he sends overseas.
I presume the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) does not wish to give the wrong impression that the Auditor General brought about any reforms when he went over there?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that,
On the contrary, he was compelled to report-I do not know whether willingly or against his will-that he found everything correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think that is correct.

I might point out, to show what the conditions were in England for a while, that when the troops went over there at first they were regarded, not as Canadians, but as British soldiers-. I had the honour of going over in 1914, arriving at the same time as the troops, and while speaking with the Acting High Commissioner, Mr. Perley, now Sir George Perley, he said to me: " You do not pretend to have any control of the soldiers here?" I said: " Why not?" " They are British soldiers," he said. I said that I was not aware that I was called u-pon to offer any explanation, but that I felt, as I was bound to feel, that I was standing by the law. I later on- met the Secretary of State for War, who used almost identical language. On the strength of the remarks of the Acting High Commissioner, Nie said that these troops were British soldiers, and added: " You do not pretend to have any claim upon them?" I said " I make no pretense to anything, but I merely claim what the Army Act allows." Section 177 of the Army Act, to my mind, clearly gives Canada absolute control of her troops except as to military directions in the field. Tbry are subject to the Com-rnander-in-Chiei of the British army in the field. That is the line I took. That is the ground I stand on to-day and that is the ground, I' am pleased to have to observe, is taken by the Government, although I had a long up-hill fight before I carried my point. A little later I received a message from Canada asking if the Canadians were in action. I replied " No." A cable came back asking if So-and-8o had been killed in action, saying

that his wife had been, notified by the .British War Office that her husband had been killed in Belgium. I made inquiries and I found that a man had been killed in Belgium two weeks before and it did not require a great astuteness to see that there was something wrong. Some one had drawn .pay for that man who had been dead for two weeks.	I found that the
*pay of a great many absentees without leave had been drawn by somebody. I presume that the officers did not check the matter up very closely in some cases. I immediately set to work to rectify this and I found that the Pay Department, by somebody's instructions, was under the direction of the British War Office and that ,we were not supposed to interfere. I let it pass for the time being but I instructed the officers to keep a careful eye on this aspect of the matter. Later on I found out that in order to have anything like a proper control of payments there must be a different system, and after consultation with General Carson, I placed in charge of that department, and made responsible for the correct auditing of the accounts, a very capable officer whose name I forget at the mloment. He did willing service and in a short time he reduced the system to a proper basis. We then introduced the system of paying by passbook and carried it out so that we had it down in a short time to as perfect a system as could be established anywhere. Still wishing to strengthen the system, II selected Colonel Ross, of the Royal Highlanders, Montreal, and sent him over with instructions to see that everything was done in an absolutely correct manner. Then the Auditor General, after he had been well worked up by the hon. the .Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), in a fit of epilepsy thought things might be going wrong over there and he went over himself. When he got to England he gratefully acknowledged that he found everything in absolute ship-shape. I want to narrate the condition of affairs .to the House, to show that every avenue .and every loophole for the possibility of *fraud, looseness or carelessness had been closed before the Auditor General and his .assistants were sent over by the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and the Finance Minister. Perhaps the present *Minister of Militia might explain-although I do not charge him for being responsible for anything that has gone wrong-whether .the Auditor General has been active in seeing that accounts for separation allowance and assigned pay are kept in proper condition in Canada, or whether there have been any slips and any money lost.
Major-General MEWBURN: I understand the Auditor General has been and is auditing the accounts regularly.

And that everything is all right?
Major-General MEWBURN: I have no statement from him, but I know that, as a matter of fact, there are a large number of accounts for separation allowance and assigned pay where over-payment has been .made, and I think in the early stages of the war, in the years 1914 and 1915 particularly, mistakes were made when the separation allowance and assigned pay were being paid out by military districts, instead of by Headquarters. In many cases where troops have gone overseas there has been over-payment in connection with the separation allowance. Every endeavour, I understand, has been made to recover those payments in some instances, and I imagine .quite a number; but I do not think those amounts can be or should be recovered. They are at present, I understand, written off or put in suspense account, and will .have to be dealt with by the House at a .later date, when they are finally ascertained, but they chiefly were cases where .married women received over-payment in connection with separation allowance, and where they have endeavoured to keep up their little homes and families. I think it would be an extreme hardship if they were .asked to refund $50 or $100. It was through no fault of theirs that they were overpaid. I am speaking generally, and am not in a position to give figures.
And is there on this side of the ocean any office or any representative of the overseas Department of Militia and Defence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Minister of the Overseas Service sends regular reports to the Prime Minister and copies' 9 p.m. of them, to the Minister of Militia and Defence. In that way touch between the department and the department here is continually kept up.
Is the Overseas Minister of Militia and Defence under the control in any shape or form of the Minister of Militia and Defence on this side, or of the Militia Council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The minister
overseas is in the same position as any other minister of the Grown He is a member of the Cabinet, responsible for the administration of the department which has *been confided to him.
He has not, as yet, laid upon *the table of the House any report of his department overseas, has he?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The report of
his department was 'comprised in statements made upon this appropriation last year. At the commencement of last year the present Minister of the Overseas Service had been in office only a very short time.

I want to ash the Minister
of Militia and Defence what system exists in so far as purchasing of war material is concerned? Is the war material purchased for the expeditionary force on this side of the ocean', or in England? I wish to refer specially to general service wagons, for instance water wagons, munition wagons, and also to arms, clothing, equipment and munitions.
Major-General MEWBURN: As far as the Amy Service Corps wagons or kitchens, or any equipment of that kind is concerned, none has been purchased in Canada in the last year or two. With regard to arms, the answer is, no. The arms that onr force is using at the front are supplied, I understand, by the Imperial army-the same weapon as they use. As regards the clothing, that is contracted for and purchased in Canada, and those purchases are made through the War Purchasing Commission on demand from the Department of Militia and Defence here.

For the soldiers at the front?
Major-General MEWBURN: All the uniforms are sent from here for the troops overseas.

Even for those at the front?
Major-General MEWBURN: Yes, certainly-made here in Canada.

Since when?
Major-General MEWBURN: I am advised that system is carried on at the present time. They are shipping a certain number of uniforms over regularly.

For troops in England?
Major-General MEWBURN:	And the
boots for our troops in Canada have been manufactured in Canada, issued to the troops in Canada, and each man going overseas takes two pairs of boots with him.

I do net know what the latest order is, but I might place the facts before the House. In regard to the

troops in England, the statement is correct. For the troops going over to France, they take the uniforms on their back, and do not change before they go. They keep the boots on their feet.
What about the uniforms?

When the uniform was supplied the rule was-and I fought against it-that the troops in France and Belgium should be supplied with a British outfit.
Major-General MEWBURN: Those were replacements, I understand.

No; they are supplied to our troops, and the Prime Minister will remember that when the arrangement was made and submitted to me loj approval, I drew his attention to the fact that if these uniforms were to be taken from the British stores, the British Government should give to the Canadian manufacturers orders for a similar number of uniforms to those supplied to our troops in France and Belgium from the British store. The hon. Prime Minister will remember that. -I understand that has not been done, although we still take uniforms from the British store, but I understand the British Government is not buying from Canadian manufacturers an equivalent amount.
Is a scale of prices arranged for with the British Government, in so far as the equipment arms, and clothing is concerned? Who has control of them?

The minister has just
mentioned one fact-
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to obtain an answer? I put a question and the minister will answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will be patient, he will get hie answer.	.
Would the hon. the minister answer my question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will give the
hon. gentleman the answer as far as possible. In the first place, the men go over with their uniforms from here, and with a certain additional supply, with extra boots, for example; and when they leave England for France they are fully equippea with uniforms, boots and every lining else which has been supplied to them before they leave this country. It is impossible, of course, to keep up separate depots for the Canadian force in. France. That force is part of a very large army, and it is necessary to have depots, commissariat arrangements, and everything of that kind provided for the army as a whole; it is entirely impossible to have separate arrangements foT 150,000 men out of perhaps two millions. So, in France, the replacements of uniforms, as I understand it, are made out of the British stores. I am not sure at the moment
whether or not any exact arrangement has been made as to the amount which shall he charged for these replacements. If no such arrangement has Ibeen made, it, will be suibject to adjustment at a later date. We have never found any disposition on the part of the British authorities to endeavour to exact from this country a higher price than that which would be just and reasonable for all such supplier.

Yes. _ But probably the difficulty would arise when the war is over and the readjustment takes place. Would it not toe 'better-and I suggest it with no political intention-that some arrangement should Ibe made right away so that-regard should Ibe had to prevailing prices, and no advantage taken-of perhaps higher prices at a later date when the readjustment takes place?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When the readjustment takes place, of course, it must be on the basis of the prices at the time the articles were furnished. J do not at all anticipate any such difficulty as my hon. friend suggests. However, inquiry will be made with regard to the matter if he considers it important. There are a good many subjects which will come up for adjustment between the two governments when this war is ended, and, of course, on both sides a complete record is kept of such matters for the purpose of the proposed eventual adjustment.

I would draw the Prime Minister's attention to the point I raised some time ago. It may seem a small matter, but I know that the British Government is willing to deal fairly in the premises-they told me so personally, and I think the Prime Minister took the matter up also. The manufacture of clothing for 150,000 to 200,000 men is quite a little item. It is of primary importance that our factories should be kept going and employment -given to our workers. I drew the Prime Minister's attention, at the time the conference with the British Government was arranged, to the desirability of purchases being made directly through this Government from our manufacturers, or that a quantity of uniforms corresponding to the number which the British Government have supplied to our troops at the front should be replaced from here. In that way the manufacturers would receive orders and the labouring people get employment in the same manner as they would if we were ourselves supplying our own troops with uniforms.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am bearing the hon. gentleman's point in mind. I impressed that consideration upon the British authorities not only by correspondence, but also orally; it formed the subject of some discussion about a year ago. The British Government are desirous of doing anything in that regard that may be practicable, but, of course, we have to take into consideration the difficulties of transport, which are very considerable. They are able to point out to us, as they have pointed out, that if we may be a little short in the supply of uniforms or equipment of any kind, we are very much ahead in the supply of shells, munitions of war and a great many other articles which have been produced in enormous quantities in this country, in very great excess of the requirements of the Canadian troops at the front. So on the whole I think we hare not anything to complain of, although we would be very glad, indeed, if an arrangement could be made by which some of the uniforms for the British troops could be purchased in this country.

The principle which has been enunciated by the Government with regard to the appointment of two cabinet ministers for one position is something which we on this side of th_e House cannot understand. It is to us subversive of all principles of ministerial responsibility and parliamentary practice. There are other countries at war just now as well as Canada, but I have yet to find that in any of the other governments they have considered it necessary to have two ministers of war. They are satisfied to have one minister on the parliamentary benches, and to have officers who are properly qualified for the position in the trenches. But to have ministers in the trenches and on the benches at the same time is something that does not appeal to' us at all. Now the-'United iStates are allies of ours, and I have yet to learn that they have two cabinet ministers attending to the War Department, although there would be much more reason for them to have two ministers than ourselves, because their administrative system is entirely different from ours. In the United States there is no ministerial responsibility, the cabinet is in no way responsible to the House; and if a member of the United States cabinet wishes to take a jaunt across the Atlantic to see how matters are going on at the front, the business of the country can go on just the same. I see by the newspapers that Mr. Baker is conferring with the Allies on the other side, but no Additional minister, as I understand it, is taking
fSir Sam Hughes.]
his place even Under the American system. The only reason I can suggest why there should be two ministers for Canada-one on the other side of the Atlantic and one on this-is that they should not quarrel, and therefore it is well to have the Atlantic ocean between them. Or, it may be, that the right hon. the Prime Minister, in his desire to see that both parties were properly represented in the Union Government, thought fit to provide that the Conservative Minister of Militia should be on the other sde of the Atlantic, and the Liberal Minister of Militia on this side.
- Mr. ERNEST LAPOINTE (KamOuraska): Fifty-fifty.	[DOT]

This system of providing positions in order to make room for every person, in order to see that every person is happy during these strenuous times, is further exemplified in the division of the functions of the Minister of the Interior. That position has also been divided, and now we have a Minister of the Interior, looking after the Department of the Interior I suppose, and we have a Minister of Immigration and Colonization. At no time in the history of Canada did we less require a Minister of Immigration than at this time when there is not a single immigrant coming into the country, and as for colonization the matter is not to be thought of until after the war is over. And yet it was considered necessary to create a new portfolio only a few months ago, and $7,000 of the people's money accordingly goes to the up-keep of a Minister of Immigration and Colonization.
Then we have also the Ministry of Finance divided, and we find a Conservative Minister of Finance in California three thousand miles away, and at the same time we have a Liberal Minister of Finance in Ottawa, so that every one is satisfied.
So far as I can understand, Mr. Chairman, the position which the Overseas Minister of Militia occupies just now is nothing more or less than that of a glorified paymaster. That is all he is, because we cannot hold him responsible for anything he does. The session will have prorogued before we are able to see the classic lineaments of this gentleman on this side of the Atlantic, This business could be done just as well by a deputy minister, and not by a full-fledged Minister of Militia and Defence, whose duty is to ibe right here at this particular time to answer all questions that are being put to him. The House had an opportunity the other day of seeing how a minister refused to accept responsibility for

certain acts committed in Quebec. When'the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) referred to one department, that gentleman stood from.under and put it on the other minister, and then that .gentleman tried to absolve himself from responsibility. That is what is going to happen in this case. The Minister of Militia and Defence will say: I have nothing to do with that; the other minister is attending to that. We have no means of checking him up, and in that way the party responsible can escape because of the duplication of the position. It is an endeavour to make some person responsible for the acts of some other person. That is what is being done by the creation of this new position. It may be that I cannot see this matter as well as some hon. gentlemen in the House, but I have always been 'brought up to believe in personal, individual responsibility, not vicarious sacrifice, and that is probably why it is that I rise to ask some further explanation from the right hon. Prime Minister, or the Government, as to why this position was duplicated at this particular juncture.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid that my hon. friend has not pursued his studies into cabinet responsibility very far, otherwise he would have learned that the Government as, a whole is responsible for the acts of every minister. There is not any such individual responsibility as he alleges, apart from the collective responsibility of the whole Cabinet. The minister has his responsibility in the first instance, but the Cabinet as a whole is responsible for the administration of every minister of the Crown. My hon. friend has not pursued his studies far enough, or he would have known what has taken place in Great Britain. One of the first things done in the first six months of the war was to divide up the War Department in Great Britain. Has the hon. member never heard of the Minister of Munitions?
Is that gentleman who has been created an additional member of the Cabinet following the camp in the same way as our present minister, or is he in London?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He is in London, and it would be rather idle-to establish a Minister of Overseas Service and have him here when hi-s duties require him to be overseas. My hon. friend seems to think [DOT]that we have divided up departments for the sake of making positions.
Of duplicating positions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Let me say that Sir Edward Kemp was not desirous of assuming the duties of Minister of Militia -overseas, and it was at my urgent request that he accepted; he is endeavoring to discharge his duties to the best of his ability, and he is discharging them with great ability and diligence:	But with regard to
the illustration which I gave to my right hon. friend, of the division of department with which he found so much fault
Might I interpose a question? Has the Minister of Munitions in Great Britain 'a seat in the House of Commons? I think he has.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, he has a seat in the House of Commons, and so has Sir Edward Kemp a seat in this House.
It is unoccupied.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does my hon. friend imagine that every minister of the Crown must be present in this House all the time?
Sometimes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Doe3 he not
know that both in Great Britain and here there are ministers of the Crown who are members of the other House, and their colleagues have to answer fox them? And we .shall endeavour to answer for the Minister of Militia Overseas. But I can give you hon. friend some more illustrations to indicate to him how imperfectly he has followed u.p this question in the United Kingdom. After itihe outbreak of the war, I think about a year and a half after, .a Minister of Blockade was established in Great Britain, who undertook duties which formerly were performed by other departments of the Government, and later on ia Minister of Shipping was appointed, who undertook certain duties which theretofore had been discharged by the Admiralty. I read a statement in the British Hansard not long ago to the effect that there ate ait the present time something over ninety members in the British Government, taking ministers, parliamentary secretaries and every one else. So I think that, on the whole, considering that we are alt wax-and I hope my hon. friend will not forget that,-
I helped to vote 8500,000,000 this afternoon, eo I have not forgotten it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1 thought in the course of his observations that he had forgotten it for a moment; I am glad it is always in his mind. We are at war, and there

are very serious duties devolving upon those who sit on the Treasury benches, much more serious and arduous duties than have ever before been placed on any Government in this country. It has been necessary somewhat to enlarge the Governaient, but not in anything like the same measure as has 'been found necessary in the United Kingdom. We have established a Ministry of Militia Overseas, and have put a man on t'he spot, with the idea that he could supervise over there and keep in continual communication with the Minister of Militia here, each one of them having definite and specified duties, and we have also-
Mr. JAjOOBS :	Why could not a deputy
minister do that work instead of torturing the Constitution in this way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will pardon me, I do not propose going over all that debate which took place last session-
I was not here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -when a statute was passed which established the Ministry of Militia Overseas. I repeat that, so far as the Minister of Militia Overseas i:s concerned, we, his colleagues here, will answer for him. In the very nature of things he cannot be here to answer for himself. We shall give all the information with regard to this expenditure that he could supply, and if anything is asked for which the information is not available, we will telegraph for it.
Mr. Chairman-
Mr. Chairman-
I caught the eye of the Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I told the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) a few minutes ago that I would see him next.

I do not wish to revive a corpse, hut I would like to ask the Minister of Militia what became of the Ross rifles which were discarded?
Major-General MEWBURN: My information is that very few of them were dis-

carded, but I am not positive. I understand they were disposed of to great advantage in the United Kingdom.

Were they transformed?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I cannot
answer that. The hon. ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) can probably give more information than I can.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question, and I may say, incidentally, that I do not propose entering into a discussion. I am trying to remember that we are at war-although there are ninety members of the British Government, the British are not meeting with any great success at the front at the present time; and bearing that in mind, I shall not enter into a discussion of what is fully in my heart, which might not be just as advisable to discuss at the present time as we might like. I may point out here that the United States Government, having in view the fact that the Canadian Government has multiplied its officers to a very large number, and in view of the fact that the British Government had increased its membership-though I did not know it had reached the number of ninety; God pity the country if they have ninety-refused point blank to have a committee appointed by either branch of the Congress of the United States to advise and consult with either the Secretary for War or for the Navy on matters connected with the war. If I may express an opinion, they did absolutely right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In the United States they have appointed a great many boards and commissions.
All under the Secretary of War.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Each board or commission is under a chairman who is in some association-I do not know precisely the nature of it-with ia department of Government. For example, they have a War Industries Board, a War Trade Board, an Ordnance Board, and a great many such bodies. I was informed1 to-day, though I do not say it authoritatively, that very important additions have been made to the War Department quite recently.
Under the Secretary for War?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes,

The member for Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) made an inquiry regarding Separ ation allowance and Assigned Pay, and

I understood the minister to say that in future, in cases where the refund asked for could not he made by the person whp had been overpaid, the amount would be written off the books and a report made to the House. I suggest that when the minister makes his report on this subject, he ask Parliament also to vote an appropriation to reimburse the poor women who have already made such payments, and who in many cases have had to borrow money in order to do so.
Why not treat all alike, and give it also to those who were not overpaid?	.

The cases would not be identical. The ex-minister suffers from the same disease as the Prime Minister, who gives an example of the subdividing of departments. I do not object to the subdividing of departments, but I do object to the duplicating of departments and the creating of concurrent jurisdiction. The Minister of Militia Overseas has the same power as the Minister of Militia in Canada. I know that there is solidarity among the ministers, but what I do not know is what the other gentleman is doing overseas. I should like to see him in his seat, the same as the Minister of Militia for Canada, so that we could quiz him when we wanted to find anything out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have no doubt that he would like to be here and enjoy the privilege of being quizzed by my hon. friend or by any other hon. gentleman, but in default of his presence, my hon. friend is at liberty to quiz us.
Why the concurrent jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I pointed out the statute to my hon. friend; it is chapter 35 of the statutes of 1917. He will see that his assertion that these ministers have the same duties is entirely unfounded. Ministers of various departments have to act in conjunction with each other. For example, if any member of the Government desires additional acdommodation for his department, say, the erection of a new building, the minister who desires the building erected gets in touch with the Minister of Public Works, under whose direction and by whose officer the construction of the proposed building is carried out. There is nothing very difficult about the situation as regards the Minister of Militia and Defence and the Minister Overseas. One deals with the raising, provision for and equipment of troops here
in Canada until they embark for overseas, . and when they reach England they come under the immediate jurisdiction of the Minister of Overseas Service.

In regard to the Separation Allowance, there were many cases of hardship where overpayments on both separation allowance and assigned pay had been made. The officers in charge of the department, asked, and rightly so, for refunds where these overpayments had been made. In cases where the refund would cause hardship, however, the amounts were left in what we call the suspense account, consideration having first been given to the matter by the Auditor General. I had intended, when the adjustments were made, to come to the House and ask permission to write the amounts, off. I do not see how we could very well make the provision retroactive, because, as the member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) suggests, we might have to pay every one the additional amount.
It is known that these overpayments amount to several hundred thousand dollars?
I could not give the amount.
Is the minister prepared to admit that they amount to over $100,000?
I would say that the amount does exceed $100,000, though I could not say by how much.

A great many of our boys -transferred from the -Canadian Expeditionary Force to the Royal- Flying Corps, and in doing so they reverted in rank and were required to take less pay, and there was a great deal of complaint. Has anything been done in this matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If I am not mistaken, an Order in Council was passed some time ago by which -it provided that Canadian officers entering the Flying Corp6 and thereby receiving smaller pay than that of their rank in the Canadian Expeditionary Force should have the difference made -good to them. I think that is the case today.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Chairman

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I promised the member for -Oharlevoix-Montmorency (Mr. Cas-grain) that I would -see him next. I will recognize the hon. gentleman (Mr. Glass) as soon as the member for -Charlevoix has finished.
(508

Reverting to the matter of overpayment in assigned pay and separation allowance, I just wanted to ask the minister whether, under the auditing system which is in force now, there is likely to be any recurrence of those errors. I presume not. In the early stages of the war, several cases of that nature came to my attention in my own district, and I knew of several cases in which it was positively impossible for those who had' been recipients of overpay to return the money. It would be a great hardship for them to have to do so. I agree entirely with the hon. members who have stated that the action the minister purposes taking in that matter will meet with the approval of the House. It would be uncharitable to attempt to enforce payment from those unfortunate beneficiaries who have been overpaid through the error of the Government. I have not had my attention personally drawn to any cas-es of the kind during the last two years, and I presume the system of accounting will prevent the recurrence of the mistakes made at the beginning of the war.
Major-General MEWBURN:	I think 1
can honestly and safely say that there have been no mistakes of that nature under the present system of accounting. In the early stages of the war those accounts were all paid out by military districts where the troops were raised. There was no oversight,

and that is how the mistakes occurred. Many mistakes were made during the first two months of the war.

I think all hon. members understand the requirements of our men overseas, but my opinion is that the men who are required at the front are trained *men, and as soon as the men are trained, we are as willing and ready as the Minister of Militia and Defence to send them overseas. But while we have the food here for them, we would not like to send them overseas until they are fully trained. Why should we send them to England to he trained, when we can look after them better than they can be looked after on the other eide iwhere there is such a scarcity of food! Last week, I was asked this question by a gentleman who has a son a prisoner in Germany:	" Is the (Minister of Militia
aware that the fathers of prisoners in Germany are sending overseas equipment, boots and everything else they require? Are we supposed to leave those .men there without any equipment whatever or are we supposed to look after them?"
(Major-General MEWBURN:	I do not
know wheither the hon. gentleman was in the .House this afternoon or not, but I shall endeavour to make myself very clear in regard to the training of troops. In the first place, I believe I am supported in my view by everybody who is vitally interested in this war and who realizes the urgent need of reinforcements. The fact of having our men in England even untrained is a great source of relief and comfort to our troops in France, because they feel thiat those men are only a hundred miles away from the firing line instead ot three thousand miles. Our men going to England now are being given what is known as intensified training in all branches. An individual soldier can, with fourteen weeks of a syllabus of intensifieu training, he fitted for service in France, and no man who goes over to England is allowed to cross over to France until he has gone through that course.
As regards prisoners in Germany, I think I am right in saying that every possible measure has been and is being taken to see that our men get the proper and necessary supplies and money there through the various missions. I know whereof I speak because one of my cousins has been a prisoner in Germany since the battle of St. Julien in June, 1915, and I understand they are geltting everything that . is necessary.
Sir W1LLFRJD LAURJER: I understand 'the policy of the Minister of Militia is to use as little as possible the camps that have been built in this country, such as Camp Borden, Valoartier and Petawawa, and to send the men as soon as possible to Europe?
Major-General MEWBURN:	It would
give me the greatest amount of satisfaction and pleasure if we could use Valoartier and some of those . other large camps. As far as Camp Borden is concerned, that camp will be utilized, I think, to the full extent, by the Royal Flying Corps. I am in hopes that we will be able to get sufficient men under the Military Seryice Act this spring to enable us to have troops for training at, Valoartier and at some of the camps in the West. I had hoped that we could have forwarded overseas reinforcements at the rate of about ten thousand per month and always hold sufficient in hand for our training here. But our flow began to drop off and it would not he possible to open some of the camps unless we got an increased number of men.

The minister will only be able to send a certain number overseas because he has not the ships available to send too many. Undoubtedly there will be such a rush to camp in the spring, and with the impetus given by the Union Government, and all that sort of thing, that our camps will be more than filled and we will not have room enough for the thirty or forty thousand men in the camps all over the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Let us hope so.

The minister says that it gives courage to the boys in the trenches to see the other fellows beside them. But I do pot see .any reason why . the minister should speak in a loud voice or accuse us of ignoring that there is a war on, or treat us with suspicion when we ask honest questions. When it is suggested that the scarcity of food on the other side might be regarded as a ground for training some of our men here, consuming the food here and dispensing with the necessity of finding transportation for it, that is no reason rvhy the minister should impute motives to gentlemen on this side of the House. If the minister is going to get angry when we ask a question we will not get any farther. He will not scare us by talking in a loud voice-I do not intend to have any motives imputed to me, and I do not propose to refrain from .asking questions because the minister gets impatient. He had better remain



patient and give us answers to the questions we ask without imputing motives.
Major-General MEWBURN:	The hon.
gentleman has misunderstood my motives. If I talk in a loud voice it is probably my misfortune and not my fault. I did not intend to convey any idea of resentment. Probably I may be feeling very deeply and very sincerely in my desire to get troops overseas. If the hon. gentleman had seen some of the cables that have come into my possession in the last three months, and if he had known how necessary it was to get troops over there, he would probably have felt as keenly as I do. But I want to assure my hon. friend, and every hon. member on the other side of the House, that I had no thought of answering anybody in the way my hon. friend has suggested.

The men have to be trained on this side of the water or on the other side, and my hon. friend from .Char-levoix-Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) asked a very pertinent question and even made the suggestion that it would be better to have them trained in this country where there is a sufficient provision of food, rather than in England. My hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence in answer to that, said the men should be in England as soon as possible, because we were at war, and .the troops got comfort and courage because they saw these men beside them. That may be true, but the question was one that was perhaps not answered as it should have been.
, Major-General MEWBURN: I shall endeavour to make myself a little clearer. My first object was to rush quite a number over to England as quickly as possible, if we could get the ships to take them over. It all came down to a question of ships. Secondly, they have various training schools at which these men are trained. A cable we received last week spoke of some of the men who had gone over under the Military .Service Act, and said that they had made marvellous progress and had become expert in various lines of training. This cable also spoke of the great effect upon the morale .of our troops which had been caused by the fact that these men had gone over.

Might I suggest, as one who has been over there and has known the conditions, that there are such things as emergencies in war. We do know that the casualties in battle in any army, even the Canadian army, can count up very rapidly, even in the space of a few hours, and that the reserves which I believe were 	'
available for trench warfare in England a few weeks ago would hardly last any time .at all. I think every man who knows anything about conditions, who knows the crisis that is existing to-day, who knows how low the Canadian reserves have been, must congratulate the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence on the methods he has taken to get men across the Atlantic. I was over there in the days before conscription was introduced into England. My regiment often was down to two hundred, two hundred and fifty or three hundred men in place of a thousand.

Do you mean a Canadian regiment?
, Mr. McGIBBON: No, I was in the Imperials. Many a time we got recruits over from England with only three or four weeks' training. We were glad to get them. We found them very useful, because after all, the best training you can get in this war is the training the boys get in actual work in the trenches.
Progress reported.

. On motion of Sir Robert Borden, Bill No. 12, respecting the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin <in the Chair.
On section 1-Short title:

So that there may not be the same misunderstanding as there was in regard to the last measure before the House, I desire to get an explanation. I observe this Bill is in the name of the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I ehould like to know
what department will be -shorn of any of its prerogatives by the creation of the new department of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Bill speaks for itself as to the duties imposed upon the minister, and as to his powers.
How are they being performed, and by whom? Or is this measure just for future emergencies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The House has already been informed of the change that is made in remitting to the Department of Militia and Defence certain duties that heretofore have been performed by .the Mili-

tary Hospitals Com mission. The line of demarcation, I think, is perfectly clear. Until the soldier is discharged his care, whether in hospitals or otherwise, is to remain with the Department of Militia and Defence. If, after returning here from overseas, he requires further treatment in the hospital, he will receive that treatment in a hospital which is under the direction and control of the Department of Militia and Defence, and will remain there until he is discharged. If, on the other hand, he requires no treatment in a hospital he is to he returned to a depot home in the militia district.

There was one point this afternoon which ,1 did not understand. As long as a man is sick, he is under the Department of Militia, but the hon. (Minister of Militia stated a case of a man who, for instance, had tuberculosis or a disease which would make him unfit for. future wmrk. T did not understand what they were going to do with such a man-the man with articular rheumatism or something that makes him absolutely unfit for future occupation.

The explanations which have just been given by the Prime Minister and Minister of Militia and Defence do not seem to fit. The object soughtt Major General MEWBURN: I was explaining what would happen to a tubercular man.

We are here dealing with the creation of a department of government-the Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment. The explanations given by the Prime Minister and the hon. Minister of Militia dlo not agree with the object of the Bill, which is stated in clause 5.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was interrupted by a question as I was about to give an explanation.
I asked a question which had no reference to this Bill.	-
The right hon. gentleman might state the object of the Bill.
It is my fault; I plead guilty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was merely explaining as a preliminary matter that a clear line of demarcation had been fixed between the work of the Department of Militia and Defence in connection with the soldiers returned from the front, and the work of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. The Department of Militia and Defence has complete control and direction of the men until they are discharged, and if it is necessary that the men receive treatment in hospitals before they are discharged, they receive that treatment in hospitals under the control and direction of the Department of Militia and Defence. While they are in those hospitals, however, they may receive instruction, vocational training and help of that kind, by arrangement between the Department of Militia and Defence and Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment.
That would only be regarding instructors. 'They would be loaned?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think they would be loaned. They would be permitted to go to the hospitals, and give instruction and vocational training to men before they had been discharged. That training would be given under the direction of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. The Minister of Militia and Defence has pointed out that men suffering from diseases on account of which they should be discharged immediately for prolonged treatment, will be discharged, and provision made for their treatment by the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Department and by the Invalided Soldiers' Commission which is attached to that department in sanatoria and in convalescent homes. But that is only a portion of the work of the department which we are now seeking to establish. In regard to men who do not require hospital treatment when they return to Canada, and who are discharged immediately, the Department of Soldiers' Re-establishment will assume the duty of seeing that those men are provided with any- training and any re-education required to fit them for taking up once more their duties in civil life. And further than that the department will have the duty in connection with the authorities of the provinces, in connection with the commissions for that purpose which have been established in every province in Canada, to find employment and means of activity in the life of this country for men who have been so returned from the front. The w'ork of this department is intimately connected with the question of demobilization. If this war should end tomorrow we would have three hundred thousand men or more to be returned to Canada. It would be quite a task to see to it that those men are provided with the opportunity in this country of earning their livelihood, or receiving training or re-education which would better fit them for that purpose.	.
The Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment is charged with the duty of solving that problem as best it may. It takes over the soldier who requires' treatment in sanatoria, or convalescent homes, or asylums, takes him over and provides for him re-education or vocational training when he is able to receive it. It also takes over all those who do not receive any special care and treatment so far as their physical condition is concerned. And finally, this department, in connection with the commis-

sions which have been established in the various provinces of Canada, is charged with the duty of re-establishing these men once more, of absorbing them into the general activities of the country and bringing about once more the conditions which prevailed before we entered upon this war.
What control will this department have over the men,-I will not say soldiers because once they come back they cease to be soldiers-or what means of asserting discipline?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no control in the sense of military control.
That is the point I have reference to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no such control. They are absolutely free from all military discipline. So long as they are in hospitals I suppose there must be some control, but I do not know precisely how that will be worked out. But the department, the general commission that has been established, the Invalided Soldiers' Commission, and the various commissions in the several provinces of Canada, will be at the service of any man who desires vocational training or re-education, or who. desires the assistance of any of these commissions in seeking such employment as he may consider himself fitted for. The department, in short, is charged with the general problem of assisting these men in re-establishing themselves once more in civil activities.

If I might make the suggestion, it would be well to avoid the fault that was committed at the time of the creation of the Military Hospitals Commission, and which resulted in. an overlapping of authority, which was largely responsible for its failure.
