speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I think so.

My right
hon. friend will pardon me for saying that, in my judgment at all events, and I think the judgment of most of those who sat around me, the explanations which he has given are rather hazy. It is not so much my right hon. friend's fault as it is the fault of the Bill being either ill-digested or not digested at all. If the Bill means anything it means that the Government have created a department to assist men in getting re-established in civiil life. It is not proposed that the men who have fought shall always remain in military life; on the contrary, we hope that as soon as possible

they -will ibe returned to civil life, and the object of the Bill, we gather, is that a department is created for the purpose, of assisting those men who return from war to take their places once more in civil life. Let me read the section of the Bill which bears upon the point:
The minister shall have the management and control of all matters relating to the reestablishment in civil life and activities of all persons who have served' in the naval or military forces of His Majesty, or any of His Majesty's Allies during the present war, and the dependents of such persons, and the administration of any statutes or of any regulations or orders enacted or made by the Governor in Council for such purpose.
What are the matters here referred to?_ My right hon. friend has stated that they will relate to the looking after of men who have returned diseased from the war and have to go to a hospital or a sanitorium. That has nothing to do with the establishment of a man in civil life, it is a matter of caring for the man who is diseased, or has been crippled and cannot engage in civil work at all, and who must he a charge upon the country. When I first took the Bill in hand I thought what it was proposed to do was, for example, to seek to help a man who wanted to go into farming, or something of that kind. The object of the Bill may be all right, what is intended may be good, but it seems to me we should have before us a concrete plan of what this department intends to carry out. The whole thing is very hazy, we are left in the dark, and the explanations are very meagre and cannot be otherwise unti-l the Government has arrived at a well considered plan as to what it proposes to do in order to restore the returned soldier to civil life. Perhaps the returned soldier may be without any occupation, or, perhaps, he cannot return to the occupation he formerly followed for some reason or another. In that case the Government should have ready a concrete plan under which they could say: We propose to do this or do that to assist the man into this or that occupation. Certainly there is nothing in the explanations which have been given, or in the Bill itself, which indicates what the Government are going to do. It may be that the department itself should initiate some plan, but at the present time, it seems to me-I speak with all due deference, and not in critical terms, because the object contemplated may be a very good one-we should have more information than we have at the present time to justify the creation of such a department. After the American Civil War in 1865, nearly one million men, perhaps over that number, went
back into civil life without any effort at all. Those who were disabled were given a pension, and those who were able to earn their own living with brain or brawn were simply discharged and absorbed in a very short time into civil life. Perhaps it is advisable that the men here should be aided in returning into civil life, but I warn my Tight hon. friend, and not in any carping manner, that if this Bill establishes a department to assist returned men to go back again into civil life he is preparing for himself a crop of applications which will, perhaps, be very embarrassing. I would rather trust the manhood of the man, if he comes back sound in limb and body, to find his own way into civil life, than depend for that upon the assistance of apaternalgovernment. I would urge my right hon. friend, if he will permit me to say so, to think very seriously before he undertakes to hold out hopes of that kind to the men who come back_ but rather to trust to their manhood as far as possible. If they are crippled or disabled then, of course, the country must take care of them, but if they come back sound in 'body and limb, we had better leave them to their own exertions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There might be some force in what my right hon. friend has observed if these men were coming back sound in limb and body, and, further than that, possessing the capacity for continuous work which they had before they went overseas. But I may tell my right hon. friend-and I think he will realize it -that this is not such a war as ever was in the world before, and even when men. do come back apparently sound in body and in limb in every way, I venture to believe that they will require some aid and guidance before they can once more take up their work in the civil life of this country as they had taken it up before they went overseas. I know of what I am speaking from absolute experience among some of these men. No one of us can realize the effect upon a man's temperament and nervous system of two years in that awful warfare at the front. It has a very serious effect sometimes. But>
apart from all that, there are thousands and tens of thousands who will no,t come back sound in body and limb. Some of them .are coming back, unfortunately, blinded, some maimed with the loss of an arm or of a leg, or the loss of both arms or both legs. Is it not desirable that we should give these men some assistance so that they can continue, after they return to Canada, to have an interest in

life and to feel that they are performing some honourable service in the ordinary life of the country? I venture to think that we would be derelict to our duty if we did not make some provision, for them. The problem is a great one which has been studied in the United Kingdom during the past year very attentively, and we have given consideration to it here. I spoke to my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence about this, and he agreed that it would be a cruel thing if we brought these men back and dismissed them from the army and told them to shift for themselves. We could not do it.
That is what is happening to lots of them already.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not happening so far as I am aware. At all events, I do know that the Military Hospitals Commission and the various commissions which have been established! in the several provinces, have been doing a very creditable work in that regard, and I have been trying to keep in very close touch with it. It is valuable and wise work. It may be that, in some cases, men have been overlooked. If so, I am sorry for it. This new department has been created with the general problem placed before it, and one of the duties of the minister at the head of that department will be to consider and to submit to the Government the methods (by which he will proceed to carry out what I venture to believe will be regarded by the people of this country as a proper and a necessary purpose. We have not the concrete proposals to submit to the House this evening because the minister has not yet been able to give that study and attention to the general problem which will be absolutely necessary before any matured scheme could be submitted to the Government or presented to Parliament. So we are asking the authority of Parliament for the constitution of this department, realizing, as we do, that a very serious task is imposed upon it and that it will have great scope for usefulness in the immediate future. For these men are coming back in considerable numbers now, and when the war is over we shall have the problem immediately placed upon this department of undertaking work of this character for three or four hundred thousand men as rapidly as they can be returned from overseas.

When the Liberal party came into power in 1896, times were not good in 'Canada. I may be pardoned for bringing in the name of a gentleman

to whom I attribute the good times which followed. It was the Hon. Sir Clifford Sifton who foresaw the opening up of the Northwest and the bringing in of settlers from the United States. That made good times in this country. And without entering into that discussion any further, I have observed that fact very closely, having been engaged in the development of the Northwest two years before the Liberal party came into power, and having been instrumental in directing the attention of that gentleman and his Government to the prospects in the Northwest. In short, the opening up of the Northwest made Canada prosperous for many years after 18%.

And it made Sifton rich.
Sir SAM HUGHES': I was speaking to the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) a few minutes ago-and let me suggest here, that, from my point of view, that department can utilize from two hundred and fifty to three hundred thousand men directly and indirectly as soon as they return from the war and millions more who may choose to come in afterwards. That department is required and there is work for it to do now. I think the money we are voting for it will be well spent money. Some one objected to it, but the appropriation shbuld be made. I am satisfied that the whole Northwest of Canada should be surveyed from the viewpoint of drainage, for the provision of main arteries of wagon roads and of railroads. New territories are there only awaiting development, waiting for settlers to come in, and many of these settlers will come from the United States; others with a little money will come from other places, and they will start their homes. They will require furniture, hardware, farming implements, and in order to put up their homes and out-buildings they will require lumber and other building materials. This will bring about a repetition of what occurred from 1896 onwards under the administration of the leader 'of the Opposition, The consequent stimulation of trade will make eastern Canada feel good, and bring about most harmonious relations between the East and the West. I am satisfied that we would not have any trouble at all in absorbing the great bulk of our returned men. iBut I can see that there is still room for the work of a commission of this kind to help those who are not in as independent a position as others, and to assist in opening up for those some new avenue of life. I look with great faith and interest to the new Department of Immigration and Colonization to help to ab-

sorb the soldiers on their return, provided there is preparation made in advance for the work they have to do. Millions of acres could be reclaimed by drainage, and tens of thousands of men could be employed in drainage and road building, as well as in the construction of new railroads; and the Government must, to my mind, see to it in advance that these things are done so that when the boys come back they will find avenues of work.

Has the hon. gentleman any idea, or any warrant for the idea, as to what percentage of the soldiers who return from the front will be suitable foi farmers and what percentage will he likely to go into farming?

I have no conception. I was not thinking of farming alone, for the farmers may come from any place. Any one familiar with the development of the Northwest knows that in every six miles of settled country there are stores, blacksmith shops, employing men, churches requiring ministers,-
And Orange lodges.

Yes, thank goodness, Orange lodges, which give men employment in building them. Often the men work as carpenters or at other trades, and in the evening they attend to their adjoining homesteads. In some cases their wives remain on the farms while they step into the towns to carry on their particular work. Thus one development brings on another; 'the farms and the towns are built up and in that way a development of ithe whole country is brought about.

I look upon this as one of the most important measures that was ever brought before the House. It is only another evidence -that the Government intend to carry out their promise to the boys who went overseas. In the constituency which I represent cases have come under my observation of men who, having returned from the front, have been discharged and allowed to drift about, seeking employment here and there, and in many cases not getting it. Those suffering from tuberculosis; those who are otherwise diseased; those who are unfortunate enough to have to be sent to military asylums; are being provided for in some way, while those who do not come within those categories, but are simply unable to seek employment in regular walks of life, are given three months' pay, and the Militia Department has no further interest in them. I have felt for a long time that the Government should take hold of this matter in a more serious way-and I congratulate the minister on bringing it to the attention of the Committee and giving us an opportunity of expressing our views. We have in Canada to-day a number of training camps, and it is my view that after the war, when the soldiers return from the front, instead of being given three months' pay and set adrift they should be mobilized in these camps under military discipline until they are honourably discharged, or until those who wish to employ them go to the Government and: request their services. I suggest also that employers give the Government some guarantee that the positions they are offering are permanent and will afford sufficient remuneration to the employees at least to enable them to keep the wolf from- the door. The returned soldier should, to say the least, be placed in as good a position as he occupied before enlistment. We owe a debt to these men, and I think we should discharge it to the full. It is not right simply to pay them off when they are unfit for further military service, and leave them on their own resources. We cannot furnish positions to. all these men, hut we should continue their military pay and keep them under military discipline until they are fit for service in their different walks of life.
Is that the intention of this Bill?

The Bill does not go that far, but I would go further than the Bill does. A number of men who have returned from the front are walking the -streets to-day, looking for Government positions. There -are not enough of these positions to go round, and these men are criticizing the Government and the Militia Department. This condition should not exist; those of us who are at home should! be sufficiently interested in the boys* who have fought our battles to see that they are properly looked after.
- Mr. NICKLE: I agree with the member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Wigmore), that this is one of the most important measures that have come before the House this year, and probably quite as important as any that will come before the House. I agree with him also that this Bill has not gone far enough, but I view it from a different angle altogether from that from which ,he regards it. He takes the position that the returned man should be kept in some central depot battalion under military discipline until he is discharged.
I mean at the close of the war, when 300,000 or 400,000 men are brought back.

I misunderstood the hon. gentleman; I thought he meant at the present time. I was going to say that my point of view was diametrically opposed to his. My idea is that this Bill does not go far enough in that it does not make the line of cleavage between the soldier returning to be restored to civil life and the civilian being prepared for the work of a soldier. In my judgment, as soon as a soldier is brought hack to Canada, all our energies should be directed to getting him away from what we call military discipline. There should be a cessation of accentuation of his position as a soldier, and. accentuation of his duty as a citizen. I agree with the object of the Bill in making the demarcation, but when the man returns to Canada, it being reasonably clear that he never again can be a soldier, he should be taken from under military discipline and put under civil discipline. I believe no man in this House has given closer attention to the problem of the returned soldier than I have. No problem is going to be of greater difficulty of solution, or is apt to cause more heart-burning and sorrow than the position of the returned soldier in the community in the years that are to come. In speaking of the mental position of the returned soldier, I refer to the man who has been to the front; who has been under fire; who has suffered more or less from the nerve strain incidental to actual warfare. His nerve is not altogether broken; his nerves are not altogether gone. I do not know that I can describe his condition any better than a surgeon in Kingston, in one of our military hospitals, described it, when he said that the man was " susceptible to his environment." To-day we are bringing the men back to Canada, we are dividing them, if I understood the Prime Minister correctly, into two classes. One of these classes, such as the tubercular, we are turning over to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. But the ordinary man who comes back wounded, and is not tubercular or affected with a disease that makes it clear that he never again will be useful in any capacity as a military man, is put in one of the large military hospitals and there kept under military discipline. The result is that instead (O f developing individual initiative in your returned man and accentuating ihe duties of self-restraint, you continue to emphasize the military system. flMr. Nickle.]
The man ie not taught self-restraint; he is not taught personal responsibility; but it is impressed upon him, as it has been impressed upon him for months, that duty and obedience is something he owes to the man who occupies a higher rank than he does. Instead of stimulating, as I termed it a moment ago, individual initiative, you stamp still further upon him an apathy towards self-responsibility and towards the attitude of mind that makes a man realize that he is going to pay the penalty of his own mistakes, not because some superior authority iis going to punish him, but because the inevitable trend of events will be to make his future action unsuccessful. It seems to me the military authorities are carrying this idea of military discipline towards the returned men to ridiculous lengths. I have never been in a military uniform; I have never had to respect what is called superior rank in the army. But when a man issues an order to men in military hospitals that they must salute a military officer, and if their physical condition is such that they are unable to give a salute in the ordinary way, they must turn their heads in the direction of such authority, I say, as a Canadian citizen, that is ridiculous. Such an order was issued a short time ago.
Where?
It came.to Kingston.
Do you know the officer?
Yes.
Why did you not report him?

I am reporting it now. That order came through the Army Medical Service, and I think came through General Fotheringham, at least, he and I discussed it vigorously at one time. The order was that men who had returned from the front had to salute their superior officers, and if they could not give the salute in the ordinary way they had to turn their head in the direction of the officer.
On their pillows?

I am not saying that because I dto not.know, but I assume that it is so, (because it was a hospital order. All the nurses in the Army Medical Service hospitals are lieutenants. That makes every nurse in those hospitals the superior officer of the private and the non-commissioned officer, and that carries with it that the nurse must be respected 'because she is

a superior officer and not 'because she is a nurse. If you think that is going to develop individual initiative, I do not believe it is going to do anything of the sort. Those hospitals for returned men should all be civilian. We should impress upon the returned men: You owe a duty to yourself to behave yourself. If you behave yourself you will be treated as you will be in any other hospital. A man in that way would be taught that good conduct brought good results, and that bad conduct brought bad results, not because, as I say, some superior authority impressed that on him, but as the actual reward of every day life on his own conduct.
I. want to go into another matter. I feel pretty strongly on this returned soldier problem. I do not think any board of doctors who have to determine what a man's pension shall be should be superior in military rank to the man making application for a pension, and they should not he in uniform. A private or non-commissioned officer goes before a medical board to be examined as to his disability. That board has the power of determining to a very large extent what that man's financial status shall be during the rest of his life. Some of them do not approach that man as doctors to decide on his case. I am only speaking, of some doctors, and in a ease like that we must speak oi the case of the man who cannot be heard and who is going to suffer. Some doctors approach his case as a lawyer might cross-examine a witness. They approach him from the point of view that there is an antagonism between the State and the man and not from the point of view that he is a man who has done something for his country and for whom his country wants to do all to which he is entitled. I have been told by men who have gone before these medical boards for pensions that they were asked to tell their condition, how they felt and this, that and the other thing about themselves and that when they had done so, the medical officers who were their superiors in rank said: "That is not so; we do not believe it; that is subjective." When a doctor used the word "subjective," he means: That is your point of view as to your disability, but it is not the true point of view. These men could not contradict the doctors because, according to military etiquette, they cannot contradict a superior officer. When a soldier comes before a medical board to apply foT a pension, the soldier should ibe in mufti and the doctors should be in mufti. It should Ibe a consultation between a medical man who is there to protect the state
and a soldier who has done his duty to the state. The soldier should be absolutely at liberty to state his condition and position, but there should be no suppression of the facts and no browbeating of the man by superior authority. Their rights should be equal. That is my view.
(In regard to .what has been done for the returned soldier, I do not know what has been done in the other provinces, but in Ontario we are doing quite a little as the Soldiers' Aid Commission is assisting in a branch of what was the Military Hospitals work. The provincial legislature, by statute, constituted the Soldiers' Aid Commission for the express purpose of aiding and assisting the returned soldier. The central office is in the city of Toronto where there is an inspector. There is a western inspector in London and an eastern inspector at ^Kingston. Each of those inspectors has a subordinate officer whose duty it is to make an industrial survey of that part of the country in which they are working, so as to make themselves thoroughly conversant with the positions open in industrial work, and offices have been opened both at Kingston and at London to which the returned soldier may make application for work. The returned soldier goes there and the man in charge will learn from him what work he can do. He then tells the soldier if there is any industrial occupation open to him and he tries to bring employer and employee together. In that way very much good has been done. This is one of the problems that is going to meet us. The returned man particularly the man who has had to undergo the rigours of active service in the front line trenches, while he may appear all right, while in ordinary cases one would say he is a normal man, be really is not, he is affected in his nerves or as I put it a few moments ago, he is " susceptible." You send him to a factory and the very roar of the machinery breaks that man down and he cannot continue. Within the last year while I had the power of recommendation of those who should assist in the care of the convicts in Kingston penitentiary I suggested to the warden the names of nine or ten men who had been overseas, to act as nightkeepers in that institution. The warden co-operated most loyally with me in trying to give the men work. Of the ten men sent there there was only one man I think who lasted twto months. Some of them told me they could not stand the mental strain of knowing that the clock was coming round to the hour at which they had to begin their work. All they had to do was to walk

around the grounds and buildings and see that things were all right. Some told me their nervous condition was such that they could not stand the strain and they gave up the job. What are you going to do with such a man? His brain is clear; his eye is bright, but the ordinary man does not understand his real condition. The country has to be taught to understand him and we have to devise ways and means by which the country may he taught to understand him.
I should like to advert to one point which the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) brought up. He asked how many men were going to go back on the farms. My inquiries lead me to believe that very few will go hack. I doubt very much if you will get ten per cent. You may get five per cent who will take up farming and stick to it. These men have had all the outdoor life-the camp life-they want. They want to go hack to the cities and enjoy * the comforts of everyday life. I think what we have to plan for is to see that industrial openings are as far ae possible made for these men, and in working along that line I would urge on the Government that_ while this is a move in the right direction, they give careful consideration to the fact that they have to go farther than the Bill has gone and take every man, when he returns to Canada and whom the militia authorities admit cannot again be a combatant, into a hospital manner) by civil doctors and nursed by women in ordinary nurses' uniform, and endeavour to stimulate the sense of personal responsibility and to develop individual initiative.
Mr. WiIGMORE:	I am afraid that my
hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nicltle) misunderstood me. I meant to say that when the war is over and the troops come home they should be kept in these camps for a while instead of being turned loose. If you took two hundred thousand or three hundred thousand men and turned them loose with nothing to do, even if they were all Presbyterians, they would not turn out very well. What I meant was that they should be put in these camps under military discipline eo that they may be looked after until the time arrives when they can get suitable positions throughout the Dominion.

I just wish to say a word in reply to the observations of the hon. member from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) in regard to the treatment and attention given these returned soldiers in military hospitals. Did I understand my hon. friend to

mention the name of General Fotihering-ham?

The hon. ex-Minister of
Militia and Defence asked me who had issued a certain order and I said that I thought it had come from General Fotheringham.

I have been overseas
and I have seen some of the military hoe-pitals; therefore, I may he able to give some reasons for some of the conditions referred to by the hon. member for Kingston. I have the very greatest respect for that hon. gentleman because nobody is in a better position to speak on this subject than he. I remember that during the progress of the battle of Vimy Ridge it was my duty and privilege to dress the wound of the son of the hon. member for Kingston in order that he might return to the firing line and continue the fight, which he did, displaying such gallantry and courage as to win the Military Gross. In some of the remarks which my hon. friend addressed to the committee he was not quite correct. For instance, he spoke of the discipline in military .lospitals. I have had a good deal of experience in military hospitals and one of the difficult things to do in a military hospital where soldiers are being handled is to deal with them in such a v-ay as to maintain discipline. I am saying this most respectfully to the soldier because nobody has a greater admiration for the Canadian soldiers than I have. But a certain amount of discipline is necessary in a military hospital or you will find the soldiers over-running all your orders and imposing upon you. The point that my hon. friend made in regard to soldiers being irritable is absolutely correct. A man coming back from the front, after he has been in the firing line for from seven to ten months, is exceedingly irritable although perhaps he is not conscious of it. His nervous system has been subjected to a shock that has upset him. The reason I asked about General Fotheringham was this: I happened to know General Fotheringham very well. I was a student of his fifteen or sixteen years ago in Toronto and he was then, as he is now, my friend. I knew him at the front when he was A.D.M.S. to the Second Canadian Division at the front, and I have had some dealings with him in Canada. I think that the remarks of my hon. friend were an implied charge against Dr. Fotheringham and therefore I wish to say that there is no officer whether he be in the medical service or in the ordinary military force, who is more conscientious.

more honest, more upright or disinterested in eve'y sense of the word than is General Fotheimgham.

If you can discipline a hundred and fifty or two hundred soldiers suffering from tuberculosis in a civilian hospital as the Prime Minister proposes, why cannot you discipline the same number of other men without military discipline in another hospital?

I am not suggesting that military discipline should be carried to the extreme. The point I am making is that a certain amount of military discipline is necessary to get the best results in handling patients in the hospital. I am speaking from personal knowledge. I remember being in a British hospital for some time and it was in charge of a colonel who was a very lax disciplinarian. The result was that the patients were allowed to ignore the officers and it was almost impossible to handle the patients. I think every real military man-not an honorary one such as I am myself-will back me up in saying that no man, including a patient, is expected to salute any superior officer more than once in any one day. If he salutes him once that is sufficient and he does not have to turn his head and salute him the second time. That rule applies in hospitals as well as elsewhere.

In order to have discipline in military life it is necessary. A man who has never been in touch with military affairs does not realize the necessity for discipline. If you did not have discipline and if you did not have saluting in the army, you would never succeed in getting your men to go over the top and suffer the trials and dangers that are necessary. As I mentioned, yesterday was the anniversay of the battle of Vimy Ridge. The Canadians would celebrate it at the front. I did not hear it mentioned in the House by anybody; I presume it was forgotten. In fact, I had forgotten it myself.
There are no soldiers who have ever gone to the front who have shown themselves to be superior to the Canadian -soldiers, and I do not think we can do anything too good to the Canadian soldier on his return from overseas. There is nothing that we can possibly do, no money, no position that we can give him, that will remunerate him for the sacrifice that he has made. Every consideration must be given him. I just offer these suggestions in justice to General Fotheringham. I would like to impress upon the committee the necessity of everybody remembering that the men, when they come back from the front, whether they belong to the ranks, or whether they are officers or noncommissioned officers, are in an irritable condition and must be given special consideration not only by this House, -but by the people of the country. I would beg the House to give every consideration to these men.
Major-General MEWBURN: I entirely disagree with the remarks of the hon. member from Kingston (Mr. Nickle), and I entirely agree with the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Manion). There is no desire on the part of the military authorities to keep these men under military discipline or control for a moment longer than is absolutely necessary. If the hon. member for Kingston had ever taken an interest in military matters, or if he had ever been in uniform and in personal touch with military affairs, he would probably look at the matter through different spectacles and have a different kind of vision.
I think I am quite safe in saying that every European nation, and partioular y England, France, and the Allies in the United States, for many years past, have gone into this thing very carefully, and if has been proved beyond the shadow of a doubt that a soldier should be under a certain amount or military control until he :s discharged from the army. This question of saluting and looking up to superior officers, and everything of that kind, to me is all nonsense. You would think from the remarks of the hon. member for Kingston that the officers and nursing sisters were putting themselves on a pedestal away above the soldier. I do not believe that to be the case. Saluting is not a question of paying any particular respect to the individual officer or nurse. It is the amount of respect that is shown throughout the army, not only from the man to the officer, but from the officer to the man. This matter has been -very carefully considered. If my hon. friend says you should immediately get the soldier back to civil life, then why should1 my good civilian friends, who are sincerely and honestly, I believe, endeavouring to help in this matter, wait until the soldiers come back to Canada? Why not go to No Man's Land, and, when the soldier comes from a casualty on the battlefield, take charge of him there? Why wait until he returns to Canada? Why not look

after him from that point before he is discharged from the army?

Do you think that would be practicable?
Major-General MEWBUEN: No, and I do not think the other proposition would be practicable.
' Sir SAM HUGHES: It is a question of pay. As long as he is under pay of the Militia Department, that department has the right to control him.
Major-General MEWBURN: The man is brought to England and taken to the hospital, then taken from the hospital, and brought back to Canada. All we desire to do-and it is no particular desire, I believe it is our duty and responsibility-is to look after that man up to a certain stage. If that is our duty, we must assume it and live up to it. Why bring in those various classes of men? MV hon. friend was speaking of the different classes of men requiring medical treatment, who will go into a military hospital and undergo
11	p.m. the treatment required. Working in conjunction with that hospital is the other department where the vocational training may continue as long as the man requires further medical treatment. He is under military pay. He is drawing his pay, and allowances up to the time the medical profession say he should be evacuated from that hospital, where 'he can no longer do himself any good. He is only taking up room that may be required for another invalid soldier. He evacuates the hospital, and then goes out on to a pension or is paid up in full as a soldier. He goes out of the hospital at the earliest possible moment, as he will not require further military treament. Then he passes into your new department, and if that man is not fit for further work in the civilian line, and requires further treatment, he will then be taken care of as a civilian. I think probably the Bill does not go far enough. I hope in future further attention will be given to this, but I am thoroughly convinced-and I speak not only from my own observation, but from the experience of Great Britain, Italy, France and the United States-that it is a mistake to make some other change, and probably make more mistakes. With reference to General Fother-inghaih I appreciate the remarks made by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Mahion). General Fotheringham' has had long experience in his profession, and long military experience, and has served with great credit to him-
[Major-General Mewburn.]
self with the Second Division at the front. I do not wish to doubt the statement of the hon. member for Kingston, but I cannot conceive any orders that may have been issued for any man to keep on saluting his superior officers and nursing sisters. If a soldier is in a hospital under discipline he will pay respect to those in charge as any other good soldier will do, and I think I am safe in saying that the majority of these men who have returned from the front would prefer to ;be under military care up to the time they are discharged from the army.

I do not want the hon. Minister of Militia to put. words in my mouth, and I will not let him, if I can prevent it. I do not know that I said he should keep on saluting. I used no such language. I simply said that, in my opinion, an order issued that a man in a hospital must turn his head in the direction of a superior officer, provided he was not physically able to salute in the ordinary way, was in my judgment ridiculous, and it would not make the slightest difference to me whether the ex-Minister of Militia and the present Minister of Militia thought differently, I still would think it ridiculous. I stick to my ground on that point. Those hon. members are soldiers; I am not. As the Minister of Militia says, if I had taken an active part in militia affairs, I probably would see eye to eye with them. Probably I would, because I have noticed, from the little experience I have had, that there is a singular contagion in military etiquette in regard to the exercise of authority. I made no reflection on the good intention of General Fotheringham. I made no reflection on his capacity or his medical knowledge. The ex-Minister of Militia asked me from whom that order came. I told him from whom I thought it came. Dr. Fotheringham may be right. He approaches the matter from the point of view of the soldier. When a member is asked a question in this House as to who gave a certain order and he names the man, it cannot be implied that there is anything improper in his motive. I simply say that he issued an order that, in my judgment, was not a wise order. Dr. Fotheringham thinks differently. He is responsible for the administration of the Army Medical Service, and I am responsible to my constituents. He is doing what he thinks is right; I am doing what I think is right, and we will leave the matter there.

No man in Canada, passing along the street and meeting a very

charming lady, takes off his hat with greater grace than the hon. member for Kingston.
"Mr. NICKLE: Not because I must.
Yes, because the hon. gentleman must. Common courtesy would rise in rebellion in the heart of the hon. gentleman if he did not do that.
Because it is the weaker sex.
What is a mud major?
I do not know what he ie and do not care.

I asked, what is a mud
major. .

A bum major. If
the soldier knew his business, all he has to do is to write a report, reporting this officer for misconduct, and I am satisfied when the matter came before the proper authorities the officer would be the one who would get the wigging, not the poor soldier. It ie not generally understood that the officer owee a salute to the soldier just as much as the soldier owes it to the officer, and as to the question of a soldier lying in his bed and turning his head to an officer as he comes along, it is perfect nonsense. No medical officer ever heard of it being done. The soldier lies there and the officer comes along and always has a kind word for him.
That order was issued.
Then the officer had no business to issue it.
We agree there.

Yes, the proper
spirit to have in all these things is to shut one's eyes to these little delinquencies. I have had men walk up to me and say "Hello, Sam, how are you, I want to have a talk with you."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will have to ask the hon. gentleman to come nearer to the subject matter.

And I was only too pleased to acquiesce in his request and have a good talk with him. I may say, Mr. Chairman, I am merely following the lines laid down, and I think it is very important, if we are going to get along with this Bill, that a proper understanding of discipline in this matter should be reached.
I have n<o hesitation in saying that the man who is going round all the time insisting upon the observance of little points of etiquette and discipline, and wanting himself to be regarded as somebody, is unfit for his job; he should treat these wounded soldiers with every courtesy and consideration. Personally, I have never . met many soldiers who would not be inclined in matters of this kind to meet their officers more than half way.

Whether a soldier is an inmate of a soldiers' hospital, .or whether a man is a civilian and an inmate of a hospital, the moment he goes within the doors of that institution he comes under discipline, and he must do so for his own good. I am very strongly of the opinion that no officer who had seen active service at the front would think of insisting on a wounded private-a man who was wearing blue badges on his sleeve to indicate that he had been wounded- saluting him. Ilf any officer has so far forgotten himself as to insist upon a wounded soldier giving him a salute, I venture to say that officer is a man who .perhaps three and a half or four years ago was in civilian life, but who upon the outbreak of the war was given a lieutenancy, and then with only a few days' interval between each stage was jumped up successively to the office of captain, major, and colonel. If you want to get persons who are in sympathy with the returned soldier to determine pensions, or promote his welfare in any other respect, by all means secure the co-operation of men who have been overseas. The man who has never been outside of Military District No. fi, or for that matter any other military district-the man who has never left the shores of Canada, no matter how kindly natured he may be-is in my judgment

absolutely unfit to deal with the question of pensions, or to sit on a medical board in connection with questions of discipline. Because, no matter how genial he may be by inclination I do not think he can have that proper sympathy for the returned soldier that an officer would have who has seen service overseas.
I believe there are plenty of offices in this .country occupied by men who have never been oustide of Canada, although they are wearing uniform, men who have jumped .very rapidly from one rank to the other. Such men should be relegated back to civil .life and their places taken by men from .overseas. If that were done, it would be most advantageous all round. I am conversant with the case of one young man .who enlisted five days after war was declared, went overseas with the First Contingent and served twenty-six months in France. He had graduated at the Toronto Veterinary College and did good work in .France, but came back a broken man and .unfitted for further overseas service. His case came 'before a medical board, not one of whose members had ever been overseas, .and they decided that he was unfit to return to the front. On the seventh day of a certain month-mark the day-he received notice that he was only fit for home service if anything could be found for him to do, and on the eighth day of the same month he was notified that no employment could be found for him and that he would be given his discharge. That decision had been .arrived at between the seventh and the eighth day of the month, so that there was not very much time spent in ascertaining whether there was anything available for this poor fellow or not. Let me tell' the Committee that in Military District No. 3 there are to-day two men acting as .veterinary officers. One has been overseas, I believe, but the other was never outside of Military District No. 3. Yet both men are drawing colonel's pay. What, in the name of Heaven, the officer who was never out of the district did to entitle him to be .promoted to the rank of colonel, I do not ,know; it certainly was not the blood that he spilt overseas. I have it on pretty good authority that there was only one sick horse .to attend to last winter, out of all the horses that came under the charge of these officers in Kingston, and a year ago last .winter there were only three. Yet, for such slight services we have two men drawing colonel's pay, and the man to whom I have referred, and who had served twenty-six months in France, was discharged because

.there was nothing for him to do. Mr. .Chairman, I believe there are thousands pf cases. in this country of men ,who were formerly civilians and when .the war started donned their uniform, and secured rapid promotion to the .rank of major and colonel. I am .always glad to hear of the promotion of any man who has gone overseas, whether he went as private or as officer, and nobody will envy his promotion after he gets there, but I do think that thousands and tens of thousands of dollars have been improperly paid out in this way; that men have been advanced in rank without sufficient justification. I refer to men who have never been outside of Canada since this war commenced, who were contented before that to strut around for twelve or fourteen days each year in camp, thrusting out their chests and exposing their gold buttons and gold lace, and all that sort of thing, and who would humbly kowtow to those placed above them in rank. Too many of this type of men have been advanced in rank with a corresponding advance in pay, and in Military District No. 3 at Kingston it has simply come to this, in my humble judgment, that we have practically got a little ring there that they say among themselves: "You boost me and I'll boost you."	.
In reference to returned soldiers going back on the land, you would think that with three or four hundred thousand men returning, all you had to do was to send them out on the farms and they would take their places there. A great many of the men who enlisted and went overseas came from cities; they do not know a bit more about farming than the hon. member for South York (Mt. W. F. Maclean), and he would not know which end of a horse to put the halter on if he went on to a farm. These men should not go to the farm, simply .because, that, theoretically, it would be a nice place to put them; they are going to exercise, the same as other people do, the right of selecting	their own	job.	While Iwould	like	to see a	great	many ofthese	men	go on to	farms,	I don'tthink	you are going to	solve	the difficulty which has to be met in that way; these men will hunt their own vocations. *Some of them will go back on the farms, but a great many will' look for positions in the cities and towns.
I would like to add this one word more. Whatever we do, do not be in too great a hurry to get rid of the men, and get them off our hands, when they come from overseas. We might better throw away a few million dollars in overpaying than in underpaying the men who have come back from

the front. There is one thing we cannot afford to have in Canada. When this war is over we cannot afford to have any person pointed out as one who, having served his country is neglected after he returns from overseas.

I agree with nearly
every person who has spoken to-night that this is perhaps the most important Bill which will be brought before the House during this session, unless we are to have other Bills which will more clearly define the policy of the Government in regard to the aiding of men after they have come *back to this country. In looking over the Bill, which purports to establish a department for the re-establiehment in civil life of the returned men, I have no doubt that the exigencies, of the case will make it necessary for regulations to be passed by the Council allowing the minister in charge to carry into effect whatever the. policy of the Government may be. While this discussion may not come within the terms of the Bill I believe that the members of the Government will be very glad to have had this discussion to-night in order that they may gather the views of members of the Commons from various parts of the country. Personally, I have some very strong views with regard to some points. I come from a district in which a great many men have been enlisted for overseas and a district to which a great many men- have returned from the front. Clause 5 of the Bill, setting out the powers of the minister, says:
The minister shall have the management and control of all matters relating to the re-establishment in civil life and activities of all persons who have served in the naval or military forces of His Majesty or any of His Majesty's allies during the present war, and the dependents of sudh persons, and the administration of any statutes or of any regulations or orders enacted or made by the Governor in Council for such purpose.
This clause is broad enough to cover all those who return, and the dependents in this country of those who do not return. The first class which will be considered, no douJbt, will be the dependents of the men who have been killed at the front ot have come back absolutely incapacitated for the performance of any duties in civil life in this country. That class will be dealt with by the Pension Board.
I understand that a special committee is to be appointed for the consideration of the question of pensions. I wish to call attention to one or two facts. Although the Government has made generous increases in the matter of pensions, I still think that further increases can be made. When a man is killed
and leaves his wife and children, the Government makes an allowance of only eight dollars for the support, maintenance and education of each child. It is beyond belief that under the present conditions any woman can possibly bring up her children as they should be brought up on such an allowance. If there is any class of people who should receive the consideration of this Government, it is the dependent children, because they are the future citizens of this country, and very great consideration should be given to them. Again, when a man is returned invalided, I have known of some pensions which have been payable at the rate of $2,50 per month. I do not believe, under any circumstances, that there can be any justification for a man found to be entitled to a pension from this country receiving so small a pension as $2.50 per month, and I think that the Government should take into consideration the fixing of a minimum pension which shall be paid, or the adoption of the old bonus system.
The next class to which we come is that of men who have been invalided home and have been confined in hospitals. Every possible means should be adopted in order that these men shall be returned to take their part in civil life, and if it is found that they cannot be returned to such a condition of health, then adequate compensation should he given them by way of pension.
The third class includes the men who return to this country and are physically fit and who wish to embark upon civil life. We must realize that the men who left this country in 1914 and in subsequent years are men who have made great sacrifice. The sacrifice which they have made is the sacrifice of opportunity. While they have been absent from their homes and their work for three or four years, others who have remained at home have made that much advance in their civil life, and in the vast majority of cases have been acquiring a competence to live upon. What should be the attitude with regard to these men when they return? The present system is that when they receive their discharge from the army they get a post-service pay of three months, which simply means that a man, after serving at the front, anywhere from four years to the close of the war, has only three months' pay on which to re-establish himself.
We know of no other provision which has been made by the Government other than the provision made by the Land Settlement Act, about which I shall speak later. I believe that if these men are to be successful in their civil life they should be retained, as

has been suggested here, under military service in so far as their pay is concerned, and that they should receive their pay, and their family should receive separation allowance for a reasonable length of time, even if that should be six months or twelve months, in order that the man himself may look around and view the opportunities which lie before him to enter voluntarily upon some civil employment for the rest of his life. You may attempt to carve out a man's future, when he is between fourteen and eighteen years of age. But when you take a man from twenty-five to forty years of age, his life is so shaped that others cannot carve out for him his future course, and I believe that the responsibility rests upon this Gov-which will be the congenial to him. the opportunity of selecting employment which will be congenial to him. In addition to that, I think the Government is to be congratulated upon the system of education which has been established in, connection (with the military hospitals, and it should be expanded so that the men, if they so desire, may further equip themselves upon any particular line which they choose.
Now, in regard to the men going upon the land, we have the Land Settlement Act, passed by the House, I believe, last yea^, But I do not think that Act is in any way a compensation for the soldier. They have the opportunity, if they are farmers, of taking up land and procuring a loan from the Government, but I understand that the man must be a skilled farmer, and must prove himself worthy of the loan, in order to procure it from the Government. In that case we are not doing much more for the soldier than the Federal and provincial governments are doing for civilians. In the provinces of British Columbia Alberta and Saskatchewan, I understand legislation is now in effect whereby they will make loans to any agriculturist cn security of his land and chattels. So that the position of soldiers in the matter of land settlement does not differ materially from that of men who come to this country from any Other part of the British Empire or, perhaps, from any foreign country.
I do not concur in the view expressed by the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) with regard to the matter of aid to returned soldiers. There is no doubt that the responsibility for the care of these men and their dependents after the war is over rests upon the Federal Government, and the Federal Government alone. It is not in keeping with the dignity of this young and

prosperous country that charitable organizations throughout the country should be seeking subscriptions for the purpose of rendering aid to soldiers and their dependents. In the early days of the Patriotic Fund I was an ardent supporter of the voluntary system, but at that time we anticipated that the war would be of short duration and that the enlistments would be small in number. Since then hundreds of thousands of men have gone overseas, and I now believe that all funds of this kind should be financed by the Federal Government and paid out to soldiers and their dependents as a matter of recognition of services rendered, not as a gift from any class of the people. These men enlisted of their own free will; there was no bartering, no trading, no dickering on their part as to what amount they should receive for their services. They left it to the honour of the people at home to see that they were fairly dealt with on their return, and it rests with this Government to make fair and generous provision for these men and their dependents.

I am glad that the Government are taking some steps in the matter of looking after the returned soldier when he becomes incapacitated. At different times during the past three years I have approached departments of the Government in regard to these matters. I have asked the Board of Pension Commissioners that justice be done to the dependents of soldiers who had been wounded or killed overseas, and I was met always with an excuse, courteously expressed, of course, but having the effect of bringing no definite re

suit. During last session I had occasion to approach officials of the Government with a view to getting information regarding pensions which I thought should be paid to twd mothers of soldiers who had been killed at the front. I was told that while it was just and equitable that these pensions should be granted, it was impossible under the regulations to grant them. Soon after the prorogration of Parliament an election came on, and during the progress of the election, early in December, pensions were granted in respect of the two claims which I had previously brought to the attention of the Board of Pension Commissioners. It is evident, therefore, that though the regulations six or nine months previously prevented the granting of pensions in these cases, there was nothing to ( prevent their being granted during the early part of December. If this Bill has the effect oE creating a department that will

honestly investigate all these matters and decide them equitably and thus bring an advantage to soldiers generally and their dependents, it will have my hearty and undivided support, hut it it is the means of bringing about further delay, it will mean a large expenditure with very little resulting good.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Department constituted:
Mr: CANNON: Who is the minister in charge of the new department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Sir James Loug-heed.

This Bill creates a new department and all the machinery and organization necessary for its operation. I realize the importance of this problem, and I have no objection to the Government's taking any step to facilitate the re-establishment of returned soldiers. The member for Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe) suggests to me, however, that it would be well, in this or another section of the Bill, to provide a time when this department and the machinery created for its administration shall cease to operate. My object is to have it stated that there shall be a Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment for the period of time that the condition of the soldier or the war may require, so that when that time comes, whoever is in power, will not have to face a large number of civil servants in that department who will ask him to let them continue in their positions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend must realize it will be quite impossible to fix a definite time at which this department would become unnecessary and its continuance undesirable. I shall, however, recall to his mind that, in an Act which passed this House a few days ago, power was taken for the Governor in Council to amalgamate departments and also to abolish departments. Under t'he power which is vested in the Governor in Council by that Act, this department and other departments which have been constituted by reason of the necessities of the war, can 'be abolished when there is no further occasion for them.

I realize the position,
but I want to point out the difficulty that will confront the Governor in Council as well as Parliament in abolishing a department after it has once been established, while at this particular juncture, when there will be no pressure exercised and no objection offered, we should say:	This Act
shall ibe in force for a period of twelve, or fifteen or twenty years, or longer, after the war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I really think
it would be undesirable to fix a definite period. I would hardly assent to that. The power is vested in the Governor in Council. As I have already declared in this House, that power will be exercised as soon as that Act receives the assent of His Excellency the Governor General, by the amalgamation of the Department of Inland Revenue with the Department of Customs.. In the same way, at the pro.per time, this department will cease to exist under a like order of the Governor in Council regarding it. It will be impossible to define the time at present. This departmeht may have to continue in existence for half a dozen years after the war is over. We cannot foresee the conditions at present. There are in the public service at present many people who cannot be continued in the public service after the necessities of the war have ceased. I appreciate entirely what my hon. friend has said. Those aTe difficulties with which this Government or some 'future Government will have to deal, and they must be dealt with in the very best way possible with due regard for the public interest in dealing with them.

I understand there are
at present twenty-three Cabinet ministers. Am I right?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will tell the
hon. gentleman who they are. There is the Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Railways and Canals, the Minister of Overseas Military Forces, the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, the Secretary if State, the Postmaster General, the Minister of the Interior, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and of the Naval Service, the Minister of Customs, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, the President of the Privy Council, the Minister of Militia and Defence, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Labour. Then, there is Hon. A. K. Maclean, who is Vice-Chairman of the Reconstruction and Development Committee and who is also discharging the duties of Minister of Finance during the absence of Sir Thomas White. There is Hon. Mr. Robertson, who is Chairman of the Labour Committee and Chairman also of the Registration Board. Both those gentlemen are quite as actively occupied as any of the



ministers in the duties which devolve upon them. There is also Hon. Mr. Cochrane, who i3 a minister without portfolio.
This list includes twenty-two ministers, if the Hon. Mr. Maclean and the Hon. Mr. Robertson are to be considered as Cabinet ministers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are Cabinet ministers.
But at present they have no special department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They have the duties_to which I have already alluded. One of them is Vice-Chairman of the Reconstruction and Development Committee, and virtually Chairman, because the work devolves altogether upon him. The other is Chairman of the Labour Committee and Chairman of the Registration Board.
Am I to understand that besides those ministers there are also par-parliamentary secretaries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There are two parliamentary secretaries, and the Solicitor General.
Who are they?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The parliamentary secretaries are Mr. McCurdy who is Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and Mr. Hugh Clark, who is Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of External Affairs. The Solicitor General is the Hon. Mr. Guthrie.	. ,,
According to custom in Canada, the Solicitor General is not a member of the Cabinet. Is the Solicitor General under the present ministry, a member of the Cabinet?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Solicitor
General is not a member of the Privy Council, nor is either of the parliamentary secretaries.

Judging by these answers, we have at present 22 ministers, one Solicitor General and two parliamentary secretaries, making in all 25 ministers, and as I might call them, assistant ministers. At a time when we are all speaking of economy, I would suggest that it might be possible for the Government instead of appointing -a minister to administer this department, to pass the work over to another minister whose department is not working as hard on account of the war. I see, for instance, that there is in the Cabinet a Minister of Immigration. Immigration, at present, is ab-

solutely nil. There is a little immigration from the United States, but the work of the department is in no way large enough to occupy the ability and energy of the minister. Why not utilize his energies and abilities in the administration of this new department? We would save money by doing so. The country would not have to pay the -salary of one minister, and I am quite sure the work the Minister of Immigration would do in this department would be satisfactory.	,
Instead of putting the very important question of the civil re-establishment of soldiers in the hands of a -minister who, unfortunately, in most cases is a politician, why not put it into the hands of a commission? The Prime Minister has, I understand, had a special preference for forming commissions since he became Premier of this country. The hour is late. I do not ask the Prime Minister to tell me the number of commissions he has formed since 1911, as the number is very considerable. I would not even ask the Prime Minister why all these commissions have been formed and wrhat they have done. But I think that this is a case where one should be formed instead of entrusting this responsibility to a minister or a department. These soldiers are coming back from the war; I agree with all the remarks which have been made on tooth sides of this House, that they deserve the 'best treatment possible. Is there not a danger that if this civil establishment is left in the hands of a minister and a politician, you will have a certain amount of patronage? When the Union Government was formed it was to have many effects, but it had one effect, and a good effect, if we are to believe the newspapers. That is the effect of abolishing patronage. How long will this Government keep to its attitude as regards patronage? I do not know, but I hope patronage is abolished never to return. But when Union ceases because-after all, Union is net to be eternal-

Why?
*Mr. 'CANNON: If it is to be eternal the ideas of some of our friends on the other side will have to change, because we have been watching since the session opened and we have seen certain signs of a lack of cohesion in the ranks of the Government supporters. But supposing Union ceases, we will have in this country either a Liberal or a Tory Government. If it is a Liberal Government there is nothing to fear as to how the soldiers will be treated. If it is a Tory Government, I hope everything will be

all right, but I am not so sure of it as I would be with a Liberal Government. In either ease we will have patronage and under those circumstances ought a question like this to toe left in the hands of a politician? I say tio.
This same question has been submitted to parliaments before. The question of the civil re-establishment of soldiers has arisen in other countries. If you will refeT to the history of France after Napoleon's wars you will see that the question was up before the Parliament of France. It was a very serious question. What were the French people to do with those soldiers .who had fought for twenty years under the .Emperor in every part of Europe and who had won glory for their country? These soldiers were handled by the Government as the Government thought best, and the consequences were very bad for the country. The soldiers were disbanded too quickly. They had acquired an adventurous spirit and it was hard to get them to return to the habits of civil life. That is a danger that we will have to avoid in Canada. What means will be taken we do not know, the Bill does not mention them. As to the evils of patronage in connection with the civil re-establishment of soldiers, the best example we have is what happened in the United States after the Civil War. Any man that would support a Republican thought he was entitled to a pension and he sometimes got it even though he had not fought at all in the war. After the Civil War had been finished for over forty years the number of people who were receiving pensions from the government was far greater than the number of soldiers who actually fought in the war. Is this going to happen in Canada? If it is what am'ount of money will be spent? Where will we stop? What guarantee have we as long as a politician is administering affairs in connection with the civil re-establishment of soldiers?
The hon. gentleman calls them politicians; the members of the Union Government are statesmen.

I suppose that if we have statesmen everything will be all right, but how long will it last? I submit that this Bill, the principle >of which is very good, the principle of which I approve of, ought to be amended in such a way that instead of establishing a new department, we shall have a commission composed, of independent men, composed, for instance, of soldiers *who have gone to the front, composed of business men, composed Of men who can
g've justice without any regard to the .political preferences of the people who apply to them for justice.. What has happened since the war started? Soldiers who have gone to the front, soldiers who have done their duty, because they did not belong to the right side of politics, have been unable to obtain justice from the Government in some cases. I understand that since the Government has changed and has teen improved by the fact that some Liberals have entered it, conditions have altered. But, we have no guarantee for the future.
I heard the Prime Minister say that this Bill was introduced because the Government realized that we were at war and that ,we had to do something for the returned soldiers. We all agree, but how it is that it took the Government four years to realize. this? We have been at war since 1914, we are now in the year 1918, and it took four years for the Government to realize this. I believe the real reason is that some friends of the Government needed portfolios, that they had to be given portfolios on the fifty-fifty basis which the papers mention, with the result that instead of having a commission of impartial men in whom the people would have full confidence we have now a department the portfolio of which will be given to some politician, either Liberal or Tory Unionist. Mr. Chairman, before finishing these remarks, .1 wish to say that I am willing to give every support possible to the Government in helping the returned soldiers but I sincerely hope that politics will have nothing to do with the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have listened .with a great deal of interest to the observations of my hon. friend (Mr. Cannon). He seems to think that the late Government, myself particularly, appointed too many commissions during the past six and ,a half years, and yet he desires me to heap .another sin on my head by appointing .another commission. The observations of my hon. friend do not seem very logical in that respect. .1 leave it at that. As far as the duties of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization are concerned, I can only say to my hon. friend-if he will permit me to say it with all respect-if he were discharging the duties and carrying on the work which the minister is carrying on at the present time, he would find himself very much busier than ever he has been during his entire life. As far as the appointment of .a politician is concerned, we ha,ve taken that matter into account and we have appointed a gentleman who is not a politi-

cian. My hon. friend has not been long enough in parliament to realize that in the pure and serene and happy atmosphere of the Senate there are no politicians at all, and it was for that reason that we selected Sir James Lougheed, who has 'been a minister without portfolio for six years before he assumed this post and who, during that time has given, without salary or remuneration, very effective and valuable service to the people of this country in many ways. My hon. friend also observed that we had waited for four years. We have not waited four years, because it is less than three years since the soldiers commenced to come back from the front-probably not much more than two years. They have not been coming back in great numbers until recently, but now they will- be coming back in much larger numbers, and it seems desirable that this department should be established, in order that desirable safeguards and measures that are eminently necessary might be adopted and carried out.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-Duties.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I desire to mo.ve ' that clause five of the Bill be amended by adding thereto the following proviso:
"Provided, however, that nothing in this Act 6hall be deemed in any way to affect the powers or duties of the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada."
I do not think there is anything in the Act which would affect these powers and duties, but that hoard was appointed under the report of the special committee, approved by Parliament and afterwards carried into effect by Order in Council. It is desirable that the independent
12	p.m. status should he maintained. It is probable that the board will report to the Minister of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. Hitherto, it has reported wherever there was occasion to report, to the Minister of Finance who has desired more than once to be relieved from giving attention to such matters for the reason that his other duties and responsibilities are sufficiently onerous.

I notice on reading
Clause 5, the following:
The minister shall have the management and >
control of all matters relating to the re-establishment in civil life and activities of all persons who have served in the naval or military forces of His Majesty or any of His Majesty's allies during the present war.
Would it not he preferable to limit it to those who resided in Canada before the war?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I understand
the point my hon. friend mentions, but it was thought it should apply to any soldiers who served in the Allied armies and came to this country, and that we should endeavour to assist them with vocational training and re-education and otherwise, so that they might be assisted, so far as they needed assistance, to take their part in the ordinary activities of our national life. That is assuming they came here to take up permanent residence.
IMr. LEM1IEUX:	I was a member of the
Returned Soldiers Committee last year. I listened to the evidence which was presented to that committee and took part in the framing of the resolution which was adopted, and that principle was consecrated. Soldiers belonging to another nationality, hut fighting with the allied nations should be treated on a footing of equality with our own men. The safe principle was embodied in the resolution introduced last year by the Minister of the Interior as regards the land in the West. It seems to me the principle is a good one.

I have the honour to come from a province which, I believe, contributed by voluntary enlistment about one-tenth of the entire population. A very large number of those men, I am not prepared to say how many, are from the rank of what we call in British Columbia small farmers. They were on what we call ranches. A great many of those who are returning are looking forward to resuming civil life on some such plan as existed when they left, and I venture to suggest to the Government the advisability of making some special provision for them which, if I understand the Land Settlement Act correctly, is not made in that Act. We have in the province of British Columbia a great many thousand acres of the richest land in Canada, which is at present practically unoccupied. While theoreticallj and absolutely held by the Dominion Government, or held by some of the natives of that country, the land is wasted, has never been used, and in all probability never will be used. It might be well at this juncture, if consideration were given to the advisability of satisfying the Indian claims, and so arranging matters that these men could be placed upon small holdings of say 10 or 20 acres, so that they could resume the occupation which they left upon entering military service. I am safe in saying that if consideration could be given to a plan of this kind, which I have only barely outlined, it would meet with the approval of a
