Hon. C. C. BALLANTYNE (Minister of Naval Service) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 49, respecting the Naval Discipline (Dominion Naval Forces) Act, 1911.
Motion agreed to.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The object
of this Bill is to provide that the discipline on the ships of the Canadian Navy -shall be similar to- that of the Imperial Navy and the Australian or New Zealand Navies.
In 1911 when the Canadian and Australian Navies were being farmed the Imperial Parliament passed' the Naval Discipline (Dominion Naval Forces) Act, 1911.
. The Act declares that any dominion having adopted the Naval Discipline Act, references therein to H. M. Navy and H. M. Ships are to have effect ae including the naval forces and- ships raised by the Dominion,
The Act is intended to give effect to the agreement arrived at by the Imperial Conference with respect to the government and discipline of the naval forces of the selfgoverning dominions and their relations to the Royal Navy and to one another, namely, that there .should be power by mutual agreement between the Home Government and the Dominion Government, and between- one dominion government and another, to provide that the fleets and ships of' the Royal Navy and of the dominion navy, and of one dominion navy and another dominion navy, when co-operating together, should be treated, so far as discipline is concerned, as belonging to the

same service, so that an officer of one such force could he treated as a superior officer in relation to an officer of another such-.force and could assume command over the ships (belonging to such other force, and that for the purposes of court-martial officers could >be taken indiscriminately from both- or all such forces. The Act, however, provided that its provisions should not come into force with regard to- the naval forces of any dominion until that dominion had adopted the Act by legislaion.
The Act was applied to Australia on the 12th-August, 1913, and to New Zealand on the 16th July, 1914.
The Canadian Naval Forces having, since the outbreak of war, greatly grown, it becomes increasingly difficult to provide the necessary disciplinary measures.
It is almost impossible to form a court martial for the trial of offenders under the Naval Discipline Act, owing to the lack of Canadian officers of sufficient seniority. On the other hand, Imperial officers cannot sit on a Canadian court martial, as the above mentioned Act has not been adopted by Canada.
The passage of the Bill, a copy of which is attached, will place the Imperial and Canadian navies on an equal footing as regards disciplinary measures, and will have the effect of making officers and men inter-, changeable in the two navies. It will also provide that officers of both services will use a common form of commission, which is not the case at present. I shall be very glad to give further details when we are in Committee of the Whole.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to enter into any controversy, but would my hon. friend state if, when he speaks of the Imperial Conference, he has reference to the Imperial Conference of 1911?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My remarks do refer to the Conference of 1911.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.	_

speechtext:
I think my hon. friend's question

Ottawa, April 4, 191S. Hon. T. W. Crothers,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,
I hereby resign as your commissioner and examiner, under Order in Council re cost of living, of November, 1916. The resignation takes effect immediately. My reason is that I have failed to secure from you that support in the administration of the duties committed to me, to which support I have conceived myself entitled, and without which I cannot possibly further carry out with effect, such duties.
I thank you for unfailing support until this oocasion. If I did not deem the situation one which demands the action which I am taking,
I would remiember such unfailing support as a reason for overlooking your one failure, but I know that if the course upon which you have entered is persisted in, and if insubordinate employees may go over my head to yours, there will be an end to all discipline, and all effective work, so I respectfully retire from under.
Yours very respectfully, (Sgd) W. F. O'Connor.
To which I replied the next day as follows:
Ottawa, April 5, 1918.
Dear Mr. O'Connor,
I have your resignation of the position you had in the Cost of Living branch in the Department of Labour-'to take effect immediately'- together with the reason assigned for the course you have taken. Your attitude in the. matter does not commend itself to me. and if such is necessary, I at once relieve you from further duty in the Department.
The facts are few and simple. A little friction having arisen in that branch, involving a few clerks, one of them asked me to look into the matter, which I promised to do. Having apparently heard of that promise-
I recollect now that I spoke to Mr. O'Cbnnor about it myself. (Heading):
-you wrote me advising among other things, that I should not trouble myself respecting the matter. The next morning I had a talk with you about It, when it appeared that you had no personal knowledge concerning it. I then saw your assistant, who also stated that he tvas not personally familiar with the circumstances causing the friction, but had learnt them from the officer immediately in charge of the clerk in question. I then asked him to request her to come to see me, but instead of her coming, in a few minutes you came in to see me, considerably excited, when you said, in substance, that if I pursued the inquiry further, you and they would resign, to which I replied that you were at perfect liberty to do so.
The simple question is whether a minister at the dictation of a superior officer of his department, is to refuse to make a personal inquiry at the request of a clerk who alleges unfair treatment. I have never refused, nor shall I refuse, to hear the humblest clerk in the
6.54

department who feels that he or she (in this case a young woman apparently exemplary in conduct and character) has been unfairly treated. However, you have chosen your course, which you had a right to take, and to which I have no right to object. *
Yours faithfully,

The House again, in ^committee on Bill No. 3, to confer the electoral franchise upon women, Mr. Boivin. in. the Chair.
On .section 1-Women, to be entitled to vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Bill has already been read, amended and reprinted. It was distributed last Monday as reprinted.

I presume it is now in order for me to discuss the merits of this Bill. This Bill, with respect to woman suffrage, which is now under our consideration, is only one of the forms of feminism which are now spreading throughout the world. The question may be' asked whether all the laws which have opened the liberal professions to women and which have conferred upon them the right to vote, or to be elected to Parliament, have had any beneficial results on the progress of civilization, or have advanced the happiness of humanity. It is our urgent duty as law-makers to examine this Bill with the greatest care, and not to accept as necessary a radical reform, the advantages of which have not been clearly demonstrated. I for one say that it will be a great error if, on the pretext of giving a transitory liberty to a class, we should bring down women from their throne at the fireside, where natural law has placed them to fulfil a divine mission. If the consequences of this movement to take women

from the home and to lead them into the public arena where men are disputing great questions, are good, it is evident that we must vote in favour of this Bill; but if, on the other hand, it can be proved that those consequences would be evil for the country and regrettable for the home, it is our duty to vote against it.
For my part, I deplore this movement. The work of woman, her true realm, is nowhere but in the home, and this I say'" not only for the woman who- already possesses a home, for the mother of a family, but for the woman who has no home.
Mr. BURNHlAMi: Does the hon. member consider that he has a right to speak for women?

Certainly; the Prime
Minister said that we could discuss the merits of this question when the Bill was in committee. A woman who has no home will always be able to exert heT energies for the betterment of those who suffer, and we all know that there are not lacking homes where distress and desolation reign supreme. I know of more than one home which is thus visited by good women who spend their leisure hours in helping their afflicted sisters. These good women really have a civilizing influence in these homes of misery. They are not satisfied with healing the wounds of the heart and of the soul, but by the.ir example they raise the moral level of these fallen homes. It is therefore in the home, in that which she has found herself, to which she has brought consolation and enlightment, that woman accomplishes with a royal majesty the work which Providence has designed for heT.	.
Natural law confides to men and to women a mission where the efforts of both are. required towards the accomplishment of a great work. The work itself is varied, and each consort has a particular part to play in relation to the other. Nothing but confusion would follow if one did that part of the	work	which
is allotted to the other, or both were to do the same work. Let me illustrate by the case of a woman who is forced by circumstances to earn the living for her familly which should he provided by the husband. The first unhappy consequence of this pretended freedom, or liberty, of the woman is that the industrial work in factories being ill-spirted to her physical characteristics, she may become sterile or perhaps give birth t-o unhealthy or undeveloped children. This is not all, for moralists have
shown the demoralizing effect offactory work, with its promiscuous and dangerous associations. Only too often the absence of the mother from the home during the greater part of the day is the ruin of family life; in fact, in some cases the children have to be sent to the orphan homes. This is one of the evils which factory work brings to the labourers' home, when the woman leaves her natural sphere and does the work of man.
Let us now pass to women in political life. Woman, naturally so goodi and beautiful, and so easily mastered by outside impressions, will naturally put her whole soul into this fascinating life, and will bring into every home from the most humble to the highest the same cause of ruin. Who can think for a moment that this right to vote, which is to be conferred on women, will be restricted to the depositing of her ballot in the box on election day? If a woman is to vote in an intelligent manner, will it not be her duty to get all possible information concerning political affairs, and to take part in the agitation which precedes the election? This- means that she would have to attend political meetings side by side with men of all classes, or else organize such meetings amongst women. Many of them will make a personal canvass, or take part in the campaign through lectures, newspapers, and literature generally. Election campaigns in this country are usually long, and when one is ended it is almost time for another to begin. There are campaigns of many different kinds, for instance, municipal elections, election of school trustees, provincial and federal elections, the referendum and the plebiscite, which follow each other in almost uninterrupted succession. It seems evident that the question of political life must necessarily draw woman from her true sphere in the home, into the discussions of the forum and of the street, i'f she is to use her right of voting in an intelligent way.
No, Sir, this is not the conception we have of the important part to be played in the world by women. She must remain crowned with the halo of our deep respect and of our love. The work and activities of a man are not srflted to her. We wish to see her in the home, surrounded by the unspeakable affection of her husband and children, and always deserving of the sweet appelation, "Mother of the living." This is the woman who instils life into a new generation, and this is the woman to whom, go my praise and my admiration.

Mr. PAMPHTlLE REAL Du TREMBLAY (Laurier-Outremont): I am glad the Government have brought down this measure this session, although I think it should have been brought down last session. This Bill renders justice to women to .some extent. At the last session of Parliament, the Government saw fit to enact a law giving the right to vote to a certain number of women in this country. The women of this country, of certain provinces at least, are desirous of having the vote to-day. In my constituency the women are very keen to vote. Let me give an example: Two days before the last election I was informed that only 2,400 women were on the list in my county, but on the day of election we w'ere surprised to learn that about 3,400 had actually made application to vote. They tell me that certain women from certain parts of Ontario were so anxious to vote that they came to my county because they could not vote in Ontario according to law, but in my county they could do so. So that we can judge from this fact that the women of this country, to a certain extent at all events, are to-day prepared and anxious to cast their vote, when an election takes place. Now, the question is, do - I favour the principle of this Bill? I say yes, but I want to submit the following observation : I think it is fair to say that all theN women in all the provinces are not desirous of voting, and I think, in what I am about to say, I voice the opinidn of the majority of the women of my province. I think it is a question of education and. of sentiment, and when I speak of education I mean the direction in which education has been given to women. In France, for instance, the women do not intend, and have not the slightest desire to vote, and you will admit that the women of France in all respects are learned and patriotic women, that they desire to advance the interests and welfare of their sex, and take a great interest in the welfare of their country. Then we have, on the other hand, across the channel, the English women. Hon. gentlemen are aware that for some years the women in England desired to vote, and started a widespread campaign with the object of obtaining the right to vote. At first the statesmen in England refused them this right. Fine speeches have been delivered in the House of Commons and before the public, and speeches have been made by the women; I understand that the Government has decided that they will give them this right, so eagerly sought for many years. So that there is no doubt, Mr. Chairman, that this is a question of education, and this depends on the direction in which education and sentiment have been [Mr. Fortier. 1
directed. Therefore, I think, that this being taken as a fundamental truth, wre should leave the question in the hands of each province to decide for itself. In Canada we have a law regarding the franchise for men. It has been in force since 1898; by this franchise each province established a franchise for men within their respective limits. It was enacted by the Liberal Government of that day, and I think we are satisfied with it. In the United States, I understand, ian amendment to the existing law was submitted to Congress, and has since been adopted. The amendment reads:
The right of citizens ot the United States to vote shall not be denied or abrogated by the United States or by any state on account of sex.
This means that everybody in the United States of 21 years and over, by this amendment, shall have the right to vote. Now, what is the law? This amendment, after being sanctioned by the Senate, is to be submitted to the various states for ratification, and in order to become effective, three-fourths of the states must approve of it. There are 48 states in the Union, and, therefore, the approval of 36 states will be necessary ~ to carry the amendment. Twelve states have already granted women suffrage. In the United States,, by this amendment and by this law, they have approved of the principle that'I have laid down. Why has this law been enacted by the Congress? Just for the reason that I have pointed out, that they understand that this question is one of sentiment, domestic necessity and of education, as was we'll explained to this House at the last session by the right hon. leader of the Opposition. In the United "States the women are well advanced and well educated, this question has been before the people for years, books have been written on the subject and a commission has been appointed to study the subject, and this legislation is a result. In this country we are, to a certain extent, in the same position as the United States. We have different zones, and we have a large country. From the Atlantic to the Pacific different people speak different languages. Therefore, I say, if this law is wise for the United States it is wise for this country. If adapted in one province, it will not deprive any one of any right in the other provinces at all. Why force the women of the different provinces to vote if they do not wish to do so? Let this Parliament pass a law providing that each province shall have a referendum on the question. Let every woman over twenty-one years of age have an opportunity of going to the poll and saying whether she is in favour of voting or not. If I am con-

suited I will say to the women of my province to ta<ke advantage of the opportunity that presents itself and declare themselves in favour of voting in future elections. I *believe that the enfranchisement of women will have the effect of elevating out political life to a higher moral level. This is an advanced measure, but I am not afraid of it, because I believe that the women of our country have arrived at the stage where they can render valuable help to the men in carrying on the public 'business.
But, while I am on this subject, let me say that the franchise of a country is an important and a sacred thing. It should not be disturbed often and it should be touched with caution because it is the very basis o.f the liberty of the country. It assures popular liberty and security, and if the rules of this House permitted me to offer an amendment to the constitution it would be that the Franchise Act should not be changed by a simple majority of Parliament at the instance of the Government to carry out their own aims, or for any other purpose, before an election. The constitution should be so amended as to provide that before the Franchise Act can be touched by an unscrupulous Government at least two-thirds of the members of the House of Commons should concur in. the change. We may be some day, as we have *been in the past, at the mercy of an unscrupulous Government. This manipulation of the franchise is what has caused many of the troubles in countries to the south of ua. The troubles which have distracted the Republic of Mexico for the past fifty years have been caused by the fact that political tyrants, in order to retain power, have, before the elections, disfranchised a part of the people. In this way they have sought to ensure victory at the elections. Therefore, we, the representatives of the people, in the interests of the people and of popular liberty, should declare that the Franchise Act must not in the future be changed unless with the concurrence of tiwo-thirds of the members of the House.
In conclusion, I would ask that it be left to each of the provinces to decide whether it is in favour of the enfranchisement of women or not. In that way justice would be done to the women of this country. I hope that some day the women will not only vote but that they will come and sit in this House, and by their presence, add charm to the public life of the country.

Mr. Speaker, this House contemplates the idea of granting the
women of Canada the right to vote in all federal elections, on the same grounds as men. Concurrently with that right, comes (naturally the right and privilege to 'become candidates for, and members of, the House of Commons. My right hon. friend, the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), in proposing this Bill stated that it was not prompted solely by the new conditions created by the state of war, but as a reward due to the high merits of all the mothers, wives and daughters of this Dominion.
With all the reverence and respect due to the word of the Prime Minister, I think that the reward he proposes to grdnt them could be classed in the same category as the gift which Nessus gave to Hercules^ wife. The reward offered the women of Canada bji the Prime Minister will become the instrument of their torture and the cause of their downfall.
Are we not too much in favour of all the ideas coming from the old world; are we not too easily attracted by the whims, fancies and freaks promoted in countries whose people do not know how to exercise their activities? Before granting the women of Canada the right, and imposing upon them the duty, to vote, before' throwing them into the turmoil of political campaigns* before deciding that we shall abolish all and every distinction between man and woman, we must consider, and seriously consider, the ultimate consequence of that action.
With the Prime Minister, I pay a tribute of admiration and gratitude to the marvellous work of all the Canadian women in this dire crisis of the war. With him I acknowledge that they have deserved well of the country, and I would be in favour of granting them the highest privileges possible in so far as it would not be contrary to the best interests of the women and of the country.
A country cannot, without paying the full price, act contrarily to the laws of God and of nature. There is an essential distinction between man and woman. Although they have been moulded in the same clay, although they have received the same divine gift which we call intelligence, although they feel, think, speak and act alike, in almost every walk of life, there is an essential difference which ordains that a man shall always be a man, and a woman a woman, and all the laws of man shall not change that. The immediate passing of this measure will create no commotion in this country; the people will go along living in the same old way, but who shall foretell the result in a few decades from now? Shall

there not be conflicts between men and women? Shall there not be causes of dissatisfaction in the home or elsewhere? Or shall there even be any homes? We cannot take up a daily paper or a periodical without reading that the birth-rate is decreasing every year at an alarming rate. Will the granting of a franchise like this increase the birthrate? People may sneer at this petty preoccupation; people may consider it as a joke, but the future of a young nation like ours rests entirely upon the birthrate. And to keep up the birthrate of Canada we must keep our women within their sphere; we must attract them towards the accomplishment of the duties of their sex, duties specified by the unchangeable laws of nature.
A nation is not a collection of individuals; it is a collection of families,- To judge of the prosperity of a nation you have to look at the condition of its family ties. If the parental authority is respected, if the parents are not afraid of the hardships and difficulties inherent in the bringing up of a family, you may say without any danger of misconception that this nation is strong, because its fundamental element, the family, is sound and healthy. On the contrary, if the family ties are vanishing, if parental authority is a myth, it is a sign of weakness. This Franchise Bill, in my humble opinion, tends towards the disruption of family ties and the destruction of parental authority.
This Bill is not only disastrous from a national standpoint, it is deplorable if we consider the sole interests of the women. It is useless tb review the state of subjection in which women were before the Christian era. They were mere slaves in the hands of men; they still are mere slaves in all the countries where Christian civilization has not brought its light. Christianity has brought women to the position for which the Creator made her; it has made her the companion of man. The wonderful qualities of woman have been utilized by Christianity to complete the work of man. In all matters where men could not exercise all the needed beneficial influence, women have accomplished it. And it is in the Christian home that the all-powerful influence of woman has been felt. For all that she has done in that direction she has been surrounded with respect and love. There is not a man who does not look upon his mother as the sweetest creature on earth. There is not a manly man who does not surround his wife and daughters with respect. Will the passing of this Bill increase that respect? I think it tends to destroy it. This sort of feminism tends to

place women on the same footing as men. They will no longer 'be considered the companions of men; they will become their rivals. I have a great deal of respect for the women who are most desirous of obtaining the suffrage, but my respect is for the purity and beauty of their characters and lives, not for their political judgment. The ideal woman of man is not a politician. I readily, agree that women should be fully guarded by law in all rights of property and labour, but as they have been the guardian and the wellspring of the world's faith, morality and tenderness, I say that if they are degraded to a commonplace level with men this fine essential quality will be impaired, and their weakness will have to beg and follow where it now guides and controls. .
It will be a nice condition of affairs with our women in politics. Imagine at a convention multiplying the tongue whangers, without increasing the minds capable of initiating legislation. It will injure women physically. Who shall say that at all times they will be equal to the excitements of caucus rows, campaign slanders, briberies, inflammable speeches, torch parades, and balloting on stormy days? How will the poor workman's wife go to the polls? It is the sediment, not the wave of a sex. It is the antithesis of that highest and sweetest mystery, conviction by submission, conquest by sacrifice. I want no contest with women, Mr. Chairman.
Oh, oh.

They are higher, purer, nobler, smaller, meaner, more faithful, more frail, gentler, more envious, more merciful, far more merciful, than men are. Those of them who' are Catholics are better Catholics than their husbands and sons; those that are Protestants are better Christians than their menfolk. Women have all the necessary qualities to make good men, but they must give their attention to it while men are boys. If the rich ones do not do so, they will have to hand their work over to the poor ones.
This win-the-war Government is the sponsor of compulsion. If was elected by means of a policy of force, but it should employ its force towards other problems of national needs, paying heed to the call of the Motherland for production, and not to the forcing through of legislation such as the grading of hay and straw, playing with the clock, and forcing women into the foul vapours of politics.

Mr. Chairman, I believe it is only seemly that, when a Bill of such prime importance

as the one now before this House is being discussed, I should pay my homage to woman in 'the beautiful French language.
For more reasons than one the question of woman suffrage is among the most important matters that could be submitted to the law-makers of any Parliament. In the first place, we must remember that we are living in a democratic country, blessed with a constitutional government, and that any law which has to do, either proximately or remotely, with the representatives of the people becomes, by virtue of that very fact, a matter of the highest importance. The representatives of the people, sitting in this House, are here in answer to the popular will, and when it is sought to change the law which governs our elections, whether in war-time or out of it, this, in all justice, should be gone about with the greatest circumspection, for our laws are the voice of Parliament and this voice may be influenced both by the manner in which the vote is taken and by the preparation of the voters' lists.
I believe that the women of the community are entitled to absolutely equal rights with the men.
If the woman of to-day, if the woman of our century, if the woman of our civilization, is not the equal of man in several respects, it is a question of education and training, which are encompassed not by one year but by the work of centuries.
Were I to indite a list of the men who have shone in the arts, in politics, on the speakers' platform, in Parliament, everywhere, and confront it with the names of those women who have acquired a certain fame, there is no doubt but that list of men would be much more imposing-
If we consider the comparative brain capacity we find that man's brain is more developed than that of woman; but this again is a matter of training and of civilization.
With regard to the physical aspect, wor man is man's inferior. This is still a matter of civilization and of training, taking into account the nature of the work that she has had to accomplish for generations as also the nature of the work performed by man.
It is certain, nevertheless, that we. must take things as they are and enact legislation which will keep abreast with the progress of our present-day civilization.
So true is it that womeu.could develop, and should develop, in the same manner as men, that all through the history of civilization you can keep track of civilization's progress amongst the different races by considering the measure of freedom which they granted to their women. It is for ue to guide woman and to educate her; and, having shown her her duty, to grant her all her rights; and I believe that, once sufficiently enlightened, women should enjoy all the rights of men.
Let us take the situation, as we find it. My colleague from Laurier-Outremont (Mr. Du Tremblay) was saying a moment ago that the women of France are not asking for the vote. That is true; but you cannot deny that the Anglo-Saxon women most decidedly do want to vote.
All of us remember the struggles, at times hysterical, which were carried on in England for the cause of woman suffrage; and it is only the recognition of women's tremendous generosity and patriotism during the war that has prevailed upon the Government there to grant them the vote; I do not know as they would have ever got it otherwise.
But, in a general way, if you glance at the map of the United States, it is certain that the Anglo-Saxon womlan does want the vote.. The French women do not desire to vote because their education was not conducted along those lines, whereas the education of women in Anglo-Saxon countries was precisely along those very lines, and these women want the ballot.
lNow, what should our position be? What attitude must I adopt? What attitude shall I adopt?
In theory, as I showed a moment ago, I am in favour of conferring on. woman al'l possible rights, and I believe that these rights should be equal to those of man. When all is said, beyond the theory, there is the practical side of the question; and I do not believe that the time has come to put such a law on our statute books. Let me tell you the reason Vlhy.
Mr. Chairman, how will the voters' lists be prepared? On the one hand, the western provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia and in the east, Ontario, have given women the vote, so we hear, and have found it to their .advantage, on the other hand, in the province of Quebec and the Maritime Provinces women are as yet denied admittance to the voting-booth.
So far, the Federal Government had always accepted the voters' lists prepared by the different provinces for their own elections and I do not see how these lists will be compiled hereafter. The Dominion Government grants a certain right; hence,

its duty to prepare its own electoral lists. This was previously done by the provinces and the plan worked out to the general satisfaction. Do you ask for instances to shtow that the provinces, and the Federal Government as well, were fully satisfied with the system of preparing these lists, in vogue till now? In 1867-86 the Federal Government, which was Conservative, took upon itself to name revisers who were intended to prepare the voters' lists for the following election. What were the consequences? A clamour of indignation against the proposed system arose from the Liberal ranks, and in 1893 the Liberal party adopted as the first plank of their platform the suppression of these revisers, and gave their word that they would take the preparation of the voters' lists out of the hands of the central authorities entirely. When the Conservative party came into power in 1911 they accepted ithe reforms brought about by the Liberal! party, as also the lists prepared by the provinces.
We have another example of the danger of allowing these lasts to be prepared by the Federal 'authorities. Does any one believe, for instance, that we on this side of the House are at all satisfied with the manner in which the lists were prepared for the last election; this thing is not even approved by all the members of the Government and it cannot be satisfactory to those who believe' that an election should be carried on honestly and lawfully.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, .that the Bill we are discussing is not sufficiently clear. It makes no mention of the way in which the voters' lists will be prepared; for instance, as regards the province of Quebec, there is not a word about the way these lists will be obtained. Evidently, the provincial lists will not avail, since women in Quebec are denied the right to vote. The Government can allow women thervote but can they force the women to register? What I say of Quebec province is equally applicable to the Maritime Provinces, since conditions are the same; there, as in Quebec, how will these lists be prepared?
No, Mr. Chairman, 'twere better to allow this idea of woman suffrage to mature; we should let. it grow by itself, make its way unaided in the public mind; let us allow the slow advance of the social education I was speaking of a moment ago. We should wait until this reform has sufficiently matured in the public mind; we should respect the privilege granted the provinces by the central power; let us leave ito the provinces the preparation of the voters'
[Mr. Gerva.is.1
lists, as in the past; in this way we will avoid a new cause of misunderstanding between the western provinces which have given the vote to women and the eastern provinces still withold this right from them.

Does this Act
suspend the provincial lists? For instance, in Manitoba the provincial list is adopted as the federal list; if we pass this Act, will Manitoba be obliged to accept it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, it does not affect the lists for the provinces. Upon the provincial lists there might foe some not entitled to vote at federal elections. Lists would' have to be made up if the elections took place under the War-time Elections Act in the manner provided by that statute. If, on the other hand, an election should be held under the Dominion Elections Act as it existed in the past, it would be necessary to have additional machinery by which women could be put on the lists in provinces where they are not entitled to vote at present. Moreover, in the provinces where women have the right to vote, the lists would have to be brought in accordance with the principles which are embodied in this statute.

I think it- is important that an educational test should be applied under this Act. In 1890 when Mr., now Sir Hugh John, Macdonald was premier of Manitoba, he introduced into the legislature an Act providing that, an educational test should be applied to all electors. In the West we have a very heterogeneous population, including many foreigners, and the view of the then Premier that there should be an educational test was generally accepted in the West. Let me give an illustration to strengthen my point. In the municipal election held in Manitoba not many years ago, they were voting on a by-law as well as for reeve and councillors A number of electors were brought to the poll, and when requested, improperly, of course, to state for whom they were going to vote, in a number of cases they said: we want to vote for Mr. By-law.
The committee will see that if there .are many electors so ignorant-and there are- it is well that an educational test be provided in an Act of this kind. The educational te6t by Mr. Macdonald when he was Premier of Manitoba was that every elector should be able to read and interpret the Manitoba Act. Perhaps it was a rather severe test, but I believe that no person, male or female, should be given the franchise, unless he or she is able to explain

&41
the idea of voting or has some knowledge of the constitution of the country. It was our judgment at the time that the test proposed by Mr. Macdonald was not too strong.
I believe that this country has been all too tardy in rendering justice to the women in the matter of the franchise. The women have demonstrated in past years, and particularly in recent years, their ability, their intelligence and their right to exercise the franchise. Although during the recent election the vote was extended only to women who were relatives of soldiers, I am glad to say that the women of the West generally took a deep interest in the election and worked faithfully and well a month prior to the polling as well as at the time of polling. I have no sympathy with the view held by the gentleman who spoke in the French language (iMr. Ger-vais), or of my distinguished looking friend with the white hair (Mr. Fournier); I do not think that the birth rate would be materially affected if the women were given the franchise. As a newspaper man of long standing I have found the women in favour of moral reforms, always ready to take a hand in promoting such an issue as prohibition or any measure designed to benefit the people. I have great pleasure, therefore in recording my earnest support of the extension of the franchise to women; I believe it will prove to be a good thing for the Dominion of Canada. In Manitoba the women have been given the franchise, and, I think, in 'Saskatchewan as well.

When the Prime Minister moved the second reading of this Bill, he spoke as follows-I quote from page 95 of Unrevised Hansard:
I do not depend for this upon, the considerations which I have placed before the House as to the condition of provincial legislation on the subject. X do not even base it on the wonderful and' conspicuous service and sacrifice which women have rendered to the national cause in the war. Apart from all these, I can see that women are entitled to the franchise on their merits, and it is upon that basis that this Bill is presented to Parliament for its consideration.
Not being very familiar with the English language, I thought it wise to consult Webster's dictionary as to the meaning of the word "merit" when employed in this connection; and this is the definition I found:
The quality or relation of deserving well or ill.
From this definition of the word which the Prime Minister used we find that this Bill is presented for the acceptance of the House on the principle that it is based on
conditions stable and permanent. A Bill presented on its merits is a Bill based on principles which are supposed to the true now, which -were supposed to toe true yesterday, and which will be true in time to come. I would contrast a Bill presented on its merits to what I would call-I wish to be corrected if I am mistaken-an emergency Bill. The question of woman suffrage is not a new one in this House. Last year, there was presented to this House a Bill to give a certain class of women the right to vote. This year, a new Woman Suffrage Bill is submitted for our consideration. I have found it hard to believe that the two Bills do not conflict. Although it may seem rather strange to some hon. members, I would go so far as to say that the ideas contained in the Bill of last year and in the Bill of this year appear to me to be opposed to each other. That may seem paradoxical, but nevertheless I am convinced that the merits of one Bill defeats the merits of the other. Let me explain what I mean. The principle of a Bill presented on its merits was true yesterday, it is true, to-day, and it will be true in the future. Consequently, if last year it was true, on its merits, that woman deserved the right to vote, why is it that last year only a certain class of women were given the right to vote? The merits of the case were the same last year. If it is true and correct to say that on the merits of the case women are entitled to vote, how is it that last year the right to vote was not given to all the women of this country? Is it to be supposed that the admiration or condescension of, the Government towards the whole class was only in its infancy last year, while this year it has attained to its full growth and maturity. If last year we ignored what is this year the merits of the case, it must have been because there was a reason. What is the reason? I cannot find any other reason than this-
To win the war.

It is because last year we wanted to give the right to vote to a certain class of persons who were expected to help this Government to win the elections? This year I suppose compunction has come to the hearts of my hon. friends on the other side, and they want to repair the injustice which they did last year to a large majority of the women of this country by depriving them of the right to vote. This year, therefore, the Government is presenting to this House a Bill on its merits which will give the right to vote to all the women of this



country. If the Bill were presented last year for the sole reason I have mentioned, I congratulate hon. members on the other side on the sinister success they achieved. They certainly made no mistake last year if they gave the right to vote to a certain class of persons with the sole intent of winning the elections. If I may be allowed to use an expression which I have often heard in the speeches of the Prime Minister, I might say that this Bill of last year, drafted as it was, was certainly "fully adequate." It was adequate because it fulfilled the purpose for which it was drafted.
Let us examine the merits of this question. The question is a very wide one and one on which a great deal may be said. Th.e few remarks which I intend to make to the committee will, I am sure, be very incomplete. If we refer to sacred history, as far back as we can go, if we read the first chapter of Genesis, we find that woman was given only as an aid and consolation to man. We find that all through the Holy Scriptures that woman has no other part. She does not govern. She does not command. She has her place in no council except in that of the family. Profane history in antiquity does not show woman in any other role than as an aid and consolation to man, or else in an inferior role. The highest philosophy of antiquity has not conceived any other function for woman than that of companion to man. We all know that a companion is not a principal. A companion is a person whose object it is to follow and assist a principal, but not a person who is supposed herself to be a principal. In all domains of life, from childhood through middle age into old age, whether in science, literature, philosophy or religion, we do not find that woman has shown any superiority. Perhaps, as the hon. member for Berthier (iMr. Gervais) has said, that was because woman was not given an opportunity to develop her mind and her talents. At all events, as it is now, we must admit that woman has shown no real superiority except in so far as sentiment or imagination is concerned.
The physiology of woman, the anatomy of woman, reveals that she is in this world for the purpose of love and motherhood and not for the purpose of political strife. If the father has to he away from the home, it is the part of the mother to remain at home. I do not mean to say that .she should be confined to the house, nor that her mind should be closed to all intellectual subjects; but one of the two has to remain in the home, and if it is not the

mother, it will have to be the father, to take care of the children, so long as there are to be children in this world. From that point of view, I say if the father is not to remain in the home, then the mother should. If we give the right to vote to woman, we must as a consequence give her the right to attend political meetings, .because what is the use of giving her the right to vote, if she is not to be well informed in regard to politics? Women must know for whom they are voting and why they are voting. Consequently, it is a matter not only of marking a ballot, but of studying the politics of one's country, which of course entails the necessity for women attending and assisting at political meetings.
Why not?

If it is my hon. friend's
dpinion that they should, I respect it, but *I hold that it is preferable for the sake of the family that the woman should remain in the home instead of taking part in political strife at political meetings', and at times, hearing the hard words which	we	are often accustomed to hear at such gatherings. Conjugal harmony is almost impossible between a husband and wife holding different political views. It would ibe all right if they held the same views on politics, hut when the husband holds one view and the wife a different one, as will happen very often, conjugal harmony will be impaired. This law, while not especially designed for that purpose, will, it seems to me, lead to a husband being arrayed against his wife in certain instances.
Have the women of this country asked for the right to vote? Some say they have this right already, which is not so true as some people believe. But if it is true that they have an undeniable right to vote, how is it that in England, the United States and other great democracies they have been so long denied that right? Consequently, we must conclude that it is very difficult to decide whether women have or have not the right to vote. But assuming they have that right, are the women asking to be allowed to exercise it? There are many rights which we possess which are never exercised, perhaps because we never think of asserting them. We must not forget that happiness is a relative thing. A man who is happy in one condition may be unhappy in another, and so it is with the right of women to vote. If the women of this country wanted the right to vote so keenly that they could not be happy without it, I might go so far as

to say that, though it would be a dangerous tool in their hands, we should give them that right. But they do not ask for it. What did we see in England? Suffragettes there have been going after the Prime Minister day after day, intruding on him in the privacy of his home, but the Prime Minister would not give them the right to vote for a long time; although lately they have been enfranchised. The same is true of the United States. In Canada there has been no demand by women for the vote. If, then, the franchise is a dangerous tool in the hands of women, why should we give it to them when they are not asking for it, and when it might work against the welfare and happiness of the women themselves?
I will take the liberty of quoting the law of the province from which I come on the status of women. Article 174 of the Civil Code of Lower Canada reads:
A husband owes protection to his wife- a wife obedience to her husband:
Has civilization advanced' beyond that? I do not know, but this is taken from the old Roman law which was introduced into the French law, codified by Napolean in 1804, and now the law of the- province of Quebec. The wife owes obedience to her husband. That does not mean that she is a mere cypher in the family, but that there must be a head and the husband is that head.
Article 175 of our Civil Code reads:
A wife is obliged to live witih her husband, and to follow him wherever he thinks fit to reside. The husband is obliged to receive her and to supply her with all the necessaries of life, according to his means and condition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I should like to ask whether my hon. friend suggests, having regard to the law which he has quoted, that the wife should be obliged to vote in the way that her husband directs?'

Not by any means. I am quoting the law, and the intention of the law. is that the husband shall be the head of the family. If we give the wife the same rights as her husband it might separate the family and' array the wife against her husband. We have seen by Article 175 that the wife is obliged to live with her husband and follow him wherever he thinks fit to reside. If we refer to Article 1292 we find the same principle laid down; in fact, we find this principle all through the Civil Code of Quebec. It is a basic principle of our civil law now in existence that the husband shall be the leader, and that the
rights of the wife, or woman, shall be confined to the family council.
Before taking my seat I sihould like to summarize any objections to this Bill. I say that the Holy Scriptures, -theology, ancient philosophy, Christian philosophy, history, anatomy, physiology, political economy, and feminine psychology, all seem to indicate th-at the place of women in this world is not -amid the strife of the political arena, -but in- her home. Let me give one or two facts. In the United States the right- to vote has been granted to women. This -right to vote necessarily entails the right to become a candidate in the elections for Congress or for Parliament. At the last, election in the United States, Miss Jeanette Rankin was elected to Congress from the state of Montana, the first woman ever elected to the Congress of that country. When she first entered the House o-f Representatives -her name was freely mentioned in the newspapers, and -many people had thei-r eyes on her to see what she would do. The first important -measure that cam-e up in Congress after this lady had taken her 6eat was the question of declaring war against Germany. After the question had been discussed at length Miss Rankin was called on to vote, but she would not speak; she was called the second time, and still she would not speak; when called the -third time she wept, and at last she said- in a voice scarcely audible that she -was n-ot willing to throw her country into war, and she voted with the very small minority against the declaration of war. In the opinion of a great number of hon. members in this House, Miss Rankin certainly did not prove that it was a considerable asset to have women in parliament, -nor I do not think it will be an asset to have them in public life. The experiences of Miss Eva Zaintz, in the Russian " Battalion of Death," have been published in this country. Miss Zaintz was a soldier in the ranks of that battalion. Nothing could be more pathetic than the case of these "'omen who enrolled voluntarily to defend their country when the men of Russia would no longer defend it. I will not take up the time of the House to give details. These women have shown to the world, if ever it will be shown, that they were heroes equal to the best that this wonderful war has produced. They had their hair cut. They donned soldiers' uniforms. They went through their training. They swore they Would fight until death for their country, and that if every soldier in Russia ran away from the Huns, they would stand

their ground. And what happened? They fought the exterior enemies of their country and many of them were killed. Then they fought the interior enemies, the Bol-sheviki, and many others of these women were killed, and at the conclusion the premier, Kerensky, was so horrified that he ordered the disbandment of the .Battalion of Death. All those that remained returned to their homes, and Miss Zaintz adds that after that she made her way with her aged father across Siberia and came to America. Her action reminds one of the Trojan hero of yore, fleeing from Troy, carrying his aged father upon his shoulders, to avoid the vengeance of the Greeks. And yet this woman writes to-day that there is a place for men and women, and it was not their place to go and form this Battalion of Death because they were altogether out of their sphere. The case which I am citing to this House might seem to be an exceptional one. I might relate at length facts in regard to it, but I am simply mentioning this to show, that from my point of view, there is a place for man and a place for woman in this world. Consequently, I say it is a social question, a moral question, a question of education, a question of local tendencies, a question or family traditions a question of race traditions, and a question of personal aspirations and feelings. And for all those considerations I think that this central power of Canada should not interfere in this matter, but should leave it to be decided .by each province in Canada. That, Sir, is my conclusion. We do not want to interfere with the rights of the Anglo-Saxon ladies of Ontario or elsewhere, nor to interfere with their aspirations and traditions. We shall be very happy if they find happiness in getting the right to vote. Let every race, let every family and every province-which is, perhaps, to a certain extent, a large family-decide as to their needs and settle this question for themselves. I have every admiration for the fair sex, but I would be very sorry to think that this admiration went to the extent of sacrificing all the traditions that we have known ever since this world has existed. I say very humbly that I have not been convinced that I should give my support to this Bill.

When this Bill first came before the House I asked the same question as was asked by the hon. member for Springfield whether an educational test would be provided in connection with this Bill. The Prime Minister misunderstood my question, or, .perhaps, I did not make myself clear, but the reply was to the effect

that the Naturalization Act provided for an educational test. My question did not refer to the women that were to come into the country after this time, but it related to that class . of women already in the country- and we have thousands of them who are unable to read or write in English, French, or any other language-and 1 asked at that time if the voters would have to comply with any law the province might pass in regard to a test, .before they could become Dominion electors. I think that was the text of my question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As far as the educational test is concerned, I think I did understand pretty well what my hon. friend asked. Perhaps he did not quite understand the answer I gave. In the first place, if we are to have an educational test at all,
I think it should at ply to men as well as women. There is no particular reason why we should establish an educational test to which women should he subjected, and provide no educational test for men. So far as the matter is left by" this Bill, both are in precisely the same situation. That is to say, any person who comes to this country and is naturalized must have a certain educational qualification, which is provided in the Naturalization Act. Any woman who comes to this country, and is not naturalized in her own right, but is naturalized by reason of the naturalization of her husband, or by the naturalization of a parent, must, before she is entitled to vote under this Bill, possess the qualification which would be required if she were making application for naturalization in her own right. That subjects men and women in this country to precisely the same test, so far as their right to vote is concerned. If the House in its wisdom conceives that some additional test is necessary, that ought to be provided by a general law applicable to men and women alike. It has not been undertaken in this Bill.
Was there a Naturalization Act passed by the Dominion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there was an Act passed in 1914 which has a wider effect than the previous Naturalization Act. Those who are to be naturalized require to have .a fair knowledge of either the English or the French language.

Mr. Chairman, if the few observations which I venture to make in, criticism of this Bill oould be construed as a desire on my part to deny to the women of Canada a privilege which they were claiming, I confess that I would promptly

desist from such a course, remembering as I do this obvious truth, that it is never given to men to have the last woid.
This is not nay intention. I fully recognize, Sir, that it may be claimed with a great deal of justification that, as a matter of right, if the women of Canada really desired the privileges of citizenship which are now conferred only on men, these privileges should be granted to them.
Looking at this question from this angle, I readily admit that the women of this country have the necessary qualifications to exercise the franchise. They have both the intelligence and the culture to grasp the issues at stake and to cast their votes with an unbiased mind and a conscience free and unhampered by those selfish interests which too often weaken the judgment of man.
May we not add, Sir, that strong as may have been their claim in the past to have a vote in the management of our public affairs, stronger still is that claim to-day, when we recall the noble part that women have taken in this war? Their title to the vote has grown in proportion to their splendid service to the state and to their never ceasing sacrifices to our men at the front.
Whether in Canada or abroad, they have given their time and their help for a great cause and amidst these scenes of misery and of iwoe they appear to us to-day, more than ever, "as heaven's chosen messengers on earth."
Sir, it is because women have to such a degree elevated themselves that I hesitate to-day to be a party to a measure which, to my mind, will only tend to bring woman down from her lofty position where she is admired, respected and loved. The influence of her example is a great moral asset to the state. That influence is derived in a large measure from her position of "splendid isolation" within the home. Let us not tamper too lightly with this tradition by dragging, women into the turmoil of political strife.
The question which impresses itself upon my mind is not whether we should grant the vote to women, but whether -the women themselves want it. I do not believe that the majority are in favour of it. I know that in many provinces this right of suffrage is already granted. I recall the legislation of last year passed in this House granting to some women a right which was denied to others. This was a grave injustice. It haa no justification in fact. It was done for a special purpose. It achieved the end which its authors had in view and in so far as
this Bill tends to repair a wrong done, to wipe away an unfortunate distinction that was made in the War-time Elections Act, it has the merit at least, though too late, 'of extending equal treatment and equal justice to all the women of Canada.
Speaking for my province, I do not believe that there will be great enthusiasm displayed for this Bill. We do not consider that woman's mission has changed; her kingdom is still her home. We are more concerned about placing a wedding ring on her finger than putting a ballot in her hand. We feel that the larger field of human activity which is offered to women by this Bill will not raise them any higher, but may even degrade them in the youthful eyes of those whose hearts they never cease to lighten and to bless.
Sir, this does not mean that the women of my province do not take an interest in our public affairs. Far from it. They hold hi a large measure what I may call the substance of power. Their influence in the home is dominant. They are consulted in all matters. Their advice, always sought, is usually followed.
But, with that instinct, which women alone possess, they feel that it is wiser and better to leave to others the expression of that power. They have large families which entail heavy domestic duties which they fulfil with care and devotion. These obligations are a barrier to their appearance on a larger stage. I do not believe that it is wise to take the risk of destroying their true, womanly work, their domestic skill, their lovable and endearing qualities, by tempting them to follow us to a polling booth, to a public platform, and, some day, into this very House. For, Sir, we cannot be blind to the fact that we are but entering into the first phase. The others will follow rapidly.
Neither man nor woman can play a double part in life; they have their own spheres of activity. I 'do not believe that this is a time to experiment with a new order of things or to uproot that which has resisted the test of centuries.

Mr. Chairman, am I wrong in believing that two speeches in the French tongue are not over-numerous when we axe dealing with "la dame de nos pensees," the lady of our thoughts, as they used to say in deaT old France?
The Bill before the House just now brings up this question of feminism which has elicited such divergent opinions in this-House, in the press and elsewhere.

I do not believe in being absolute, neither on the one side nor on the other; and I believe that here, as always, it is in the happy medium that truth and justice .abide.
In theory, it is. indisputable that every person who contributes to the resources of the State is entitled to a voice in controlling the administration of the resources of the State. That is just and logical.
In practice, it should be borne in mind that, ever since 1869 the English have given their women the municipal vote which exists if not everywhere, at least in many parts of Canada. There have been no complaints on that score.
The women-voters have shown themselves to be most discreet, mainly devoting their activities and their time in matters political to questions affecting the relief of the poor, and bringing with them (into this .sphere, side by side with a sound administrative control, a little of the spirit of charity and of tenderness, a little of the maternal spirit.
In New Zealand, in Australia, the women have a voice in the election of their representatives, These representatives .are none the worse for th'at. .. neither are the women. I have even heard that public life in those countries had been chastened thereby. That may be.
Even, if that were all.
It is said moreover, and this of England as well as Australia, that the women voters pay great heed to questions of morality, honesty .and respectability, and that they give more weight to the- moral character of a candidate than to his party affiliations.
If this be so, then the experiment is .surely deserving of .a trial in our own .country.
Forcefully anti-feminist in many respects, absolutely convinced that what exists, and what should exist, between woman- and man, is not equality but equivalency, 1 am grieved to see women invading occupations which ,are not the least hit in the world suited to them and which remove them from tlhedr proper sphere, that i.s from the hearth; most of all I regret that our economic methods and the condition of our manners should often induce women to follow that course; I am saddened, too, toy all this childish, silly feminism, by this insane desire to be mannish in ridiculous things, by women who smoke, women who cycle, by women, man-fashion, astride a fiery steed, women who invade professions nowise meant for them, etc., and who neglect their kingdom for all these things.
Nevertheless, I am inclined to approve whatever tends to establish "equality of
[iMr, Prevost]
Tights" and to facilitate "the exercise of these rights." Here I approve, but with the understanding that the exercise of these rights will not go to lengths where woman will be diverted from her function, from her natural and sacred duty.
When you say to me: The woman doctor, the woman lawyer, my features express my disapproval; .because I am sure that one woman lawyer is perhaps not one lawyer more, but it positively is one woman less- and one mother less.
When you say to me: the woman teacher, my face, begins to brighten up because there is nothing to prevent a woman from being at one and the .same time a teacher and the mother of a family.
No doubt, we would rather see-however, let that be.
And, finally, when you say to me: the woman voter, I haven't a bit of objection left. In the first place I am just and logical and in a country where my messenger is a voter I find it rather "tough" that my sister should not enjoy that privilege; in our day, when a woman may be queen, Queen of .Great Britain, Queen of Holland, Queen of Spain, I can see no reason which would make us consider a woman as unworthy of expressing an opinion on political matters. I even see in the right of expressing that opinion the welfare of society.
There are .people who argue against woman suffrage that the exercise of this right will whirl our women into the political vortex. Do those who speak in this vein reflect that, as a matter of plain fact, that in reality, our women are practically living to-day in the atmosphere of politics, that they devote both time and attention to politics, go to the meetings, very often attend the committees organized, even in the most remote country districts, talk over the election with their husbands and with, their neighbours, men and women; that, even, when the country is in the throes of discussion anent a question of the utmost import, the women are not the last to feel the consequences and to be stirred by them?
For in-stance, when military conscription was brought up, when there is talk of prohibition,'when there is any discussion of questions involving the relief of the poor, public health, .sanitary regulations, etc., our women, feeling themselves directly interested, take an active part in the discussion of these questions and .are really in the current of public life; but they have not th6 right to express their opinion by a vote when the day comes to choose a legislator who will make enactments which

the women will have to observe. Women are to a certain extent inferior to men in education and culture, that is, amongst what we have chosen to call the upper [DOT] classes; they are superior to men in intelligence, common sense and natural keenness, in those things which are comparatively inborn to mankind, I mean to say, in those things precisely which are brought to the fore in the almost universal suffrage of our elections. The working girl has a finer sense of the fitness of things and a sharper intellect than the workingman; the peasant woman has 'better insight than her male companion; the latter is well aware of this and always consults her. Hence, our electorate is deprived of the more intellectual influence in its phere.
Women voters will pay more heed to moral questions than to matters of party, they will give more weight to the morals of the candidate than to his platform, his manifesto and his declarations. The more I look into this thing, the more I favour woman suffrage and the less reason I see for opposing it. Its sole effect would be the introduction of calm counsel and of the human element into polities generally. Another point of view; it will persuade man, by ia tangible warning and a permanent demonstration, of a thing in which, amongst a certain class, he does not sufficiently believe, namely: that the woman is his equal; that he is the head and that he must remain the head, but not the master, and that his helpmeet is a person before the State as before God. And so' I come to ithe conclusion that women should have the vote. However, the solution of this problem, for it is a problem, should be loft to the provincial legislatures.
As a matter of fact, this is a question of education and of temperament. In certain countries people willingly admit that women should go to the polls, in others where, nevertheless, the ideals of liberty and progress are in honour, as is France, for instance, this right has not yet been granted to women because it is not consistent with the French temperament. It is the same thing in Canada where ideas differ and education varies from province to province within Confederation. Each provincial legislature is better informed than any other regarding the state of mind and the opinions of that province and it should be left to that Parliament to decide whether or not the women of that province shall vote. Moreover, this interference of the Federal power in the provincial sphere has an uslv look to us. We have reason to
believe and to fear that in thus assuming the role of the legislature and defining the electoral qualifications on a given point, the Government of Ott&w-a is heading towards the old system of Federal voting lists, which was so faulty and so unjust. Prior to 1896 the Federal voting lists were prepared by revisers who were handsomely paid by the Government at Ottawa and who could add or cancel a name, at their own sweet will, so as to make the lists favourable to their masters. Nobody has forgotten the crying injustices which were wrought against so many voters whilst this system was in vogue.
The liberals came into power in the year 1896; and in 1897 they abolished the system of Federal revisers. Since that time the voters' lists have been compiled in each province in accordance with the provincial law. For instance, in the province of Quebec the lists are prepared by the secretary-treasurer of each munincipality and are revised by the municipal councils where every voter has the right to produce his qualifications and get fair treatment. By this law granting the ballot to women all over Canada the Government at Ottawa is encroaching on the system established in 1897, it deprives the provinces of the right-to themselves define the electoral qualifications which shall preside at elections, and seems desirous of setting up once more the very vicious system of olden days. This foreboding is all the more justifiable on our part since at the time of the last Federal elections, in 1917, the Government, hy its ignoble War-time Elections Act, was guilty of the gravest injustice against a huge number of voters in giving over the electoral lists for revision, in the very last days preceding the election, into the hands of a legion of examiners who, in nearly every part of the country, played havoc with the lists; which is one of the reasons behind this Government's success. We meet again, in 1917, the Tory spirit of former times, the spirit which presided at the preparation [DOT] of the voters' lists to the detriment of the voters but all to the advantage of those in power. So I do not look favourably upon the present interference of the Government who, through their law granting women the ballot are beginning to deprive the provinces of the right to prepare, themselves, the -list of voters. That is why, although favourable to the principle of woman suffrage, 1 am opposed to the law which the Government is now asking the House of Commons to sanction. It is the right of the provincial legislature to decide

whether or not their women shall vote. 1 fail to understand the eagerness and the zeal of the Federal Government, which has suddenly become imbued with an excess of politeness towards the ladies, in taking away from the provinces the opportunity of granting or refusing to their women the right to have a say, by means of the ballot, *in the elections of our country.
M. ARTHUR TRAHAN (Nicolet) (translation) :	Mr. Chairman, pray do not be
astonished if I make use of the French tongue in voicing my opposition to this measure. When, under pretense of protecting woman and of elevating her social status, the Government proposes a law which is a slight upon woman and which will fatally result in lowering her, I believe candidly-with the hon. members for Ber-thier and for Terrebonne-that, in championing the dignity and the grandeur .of woman it is only proper to employ the richest, the most 'delicately shaded, the daintiest and the purest of human tongues, which, by reason of these qualities has been acclaimed as the language of diplomacy.
On the second reading of this Bill the right hon. Prime Minister brought up a question of principle. Amongst other things, he said:
I can see that women are entitled to the franchise on their merits, and it is upon that basis that this Bill is presented to Parliament for its consideration. It is our belief that the influence of women exercised in this way will be a good influence in public life. We believe that beneficial results have ensued wherever the franchise has been granted to them ; indeed the principle of granting the franchise to women generally was practically affirmed in the last Parliament.
Let us examine right away, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, the pretext invoked in the last sentence I have just read. Personally, I am not very much inclined to follow the bad examples of the last Parliament; it was guilty of far too many iniquities: witness, the conscription law, a monumental blunder from both an economic and a patriotic standpoint, founded on a principle which is false and unconstitutional, and a law which I would choose to see wiped off our statute books, if the thing were possible; witness, again, the Wartime Elections Act which embodies the most heinous injustice and an absolute breach of faith towards thousands of British subjects, citizens of this country; that law also should be repealed, which repeal moreover has been requested by the Prime Minister of Saskatchewan.
[air. Prevost. ]
I would never be through were I to recite the long list of iniquities perpetrated by the last Parliament. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, we were not elected for the purpose of approving all that had been done by that Parliament. If that were the case, an election would always be superfluous and we ourselves would be mere machines.
This argument of the hon. Prime Minister is not serious and he knows that better than any one else. We are here to study questions on their merits and to decide them according to our conscience and not at all according to what may have been the opinions of the members of the last Parliament.
Read over the hon. Prime Minister's speech and, outside of the pretext just mentioned, you will find nothing but the glittering generality: "Women have the right to vote and their exercise of this right will be an influence for good." Not a single word of argument to prove his contention, so much so, that if we had only his utterances to guide us in forming an opinion upon this question, which is highly important from every point of view, we would be hard put to it to reach a conclusion founded not alone on reason, hut, I say more, on the teachings of experience and of facts.
So I was obliged to look elsewhere and it is a brief synopsis of these explorations that I wish to present to the members of the House. In running through the best authors who have dealt with this subject I have become convinced that the Bill before the House is contrary to the natural order, to the social order, to the economic order and to the moral order. For the sake of argument, I take it for granted that, once this Bill has become law, women will exercise the privilege granted them and will take an active part., in the same way as, and side by side with, the men, in political contests. They will come to the meetings in search of information, they will busy themselves with propaganda and with what we commonly call electioneering; consequently, they will undergo the rude apprenticeship of the brutalities of public life and, sooner or litter, will claim the right to become members of Parliament and to sit in our legislative halls. This, of necessity, will divert, them from their homes and from their usual occupations and will pit their native weakness against all forms of seduction and deceit.
With this admitted, allow me to try and demonstrate the truth of my thesis. First, this Bill is contrary to the natural order which has endowed woman with a different constitution from that of a man; and since

nature has not given woman the same strength, she cannot impart to woman the same tasks, the same duties! and the same rights.	.
"In general," says Auguste Comte, "the true, path of human progress Is this: to render the feminine life more and more domestic and to release it more and more from all outside occupation, the better to insure the accomplishment of its end: mating."
This theory of the Positivist philosopher is confirmed hy a .celebrated practitioner, Doctor Fonesagrivas:	/
"Woman," he teaches in a treatise on the education of girlhood, " is essentially a hidden being, primordially destined to a private life; public life, once it touches her, transforms her into a strange being, a hybrid, a sort of pariah creature."
Further, it is contrary to the social order which demands a guardian over the home, and which in consideration of woman's relative weakness has confined to her everywhere the ministry of the interior.
Woman's place is in the bosom of her family. Everything calls her there, everything holds her there, everything ties, her there.
" The state of the family," writes M. Villey,
" assigns to each his natural task: the man works and produces; the woman administers and takes care of the children; you cannot normally ask her to perform any other task; her own, well accomplished will require all her activity, and it is a great pity that she should engage in outside occupations: this is responsible for the fact that the domestic hearth is broken up and that family ties are loosened and often sundered."
It is also contrary to the economic order and on-this score I will quote no less an authority than M. Paul Leroy-Beaulieu. In his treatise on the theory and practice of political economy, he expounds the following doctrine:
Well-ordered consumption is equivalent, in part, to production, since it causes objects to last without diminishing the pleasure they afford. So, just as we say that the woman constitutes half the fortune of a home, we might add that the qualities of thrift and of caution in its women form half the fortune and welfare of a nation. Hence, the absurdity of trying to foist upon woman the functions of man; it is against the most natural division of work and of tasks; it is striving to destroy wealth. (Page 202, vol. 4.)
And elsewhere:
The question of the condition of women is one of the most delicate and the most complex that exists. We tried to deal with it in one of our first works. No doubt, we must grant women more rights, make them mistresses of their earnings and of their savings, make their lot happier.
