But we must not fail to realize that the " Feminist Movement " such as promoted hy a number of propagandists and favoured by
several of the lesser States, constitutes, from any point of view, a serious menace to civilization. By making the home less desirable, and motherhood more troublesome, more formidable, the masculinisation of woman must gradually strike at the birth-rate which, already, in most civilized countries, has too great a tendency towards falling off. So legislation, while making it easier for women to earn their livelihood, should not favour the assimilation of woman to man, neither should it suppress what is consecrated by law, nor interfere with the natural division of the functions -between the sexes. (Page 625, vol. 4.)
The reduction of the ibirth-raite, Mr. *Chairman; is not that the shoal we should avoid, particularly at this sorrowful period of our history? The birth-rate is intimately associated with the question of the int-crease of our population, which is one of the hardest problems to solve, when you consider the tremendous number among us who will have fallen victims to this disastrous war. The Government has given its . attention to this problem. In order to solve it, partially at least, they have evolved the problem of giving more importance to immigration by placing it under the special direction of a minister who will have charge of both immigration and colonization. But they should not, it seems to me, render fruitless the efforts of this minister towards increasing our population, as they are doing in a law like this which will inevitably result in gradually decreasing our population.
I wish to draw your attention to a further drawback from both an administrative and economical standpoint; is not it to be feared Mr. Chairman, that when women have the vote they will demand their share of the election spoils? Then the plague of patronage will be intensified. As a consequence, the expenses of civil government will constantly tend to increase, for I doubt very much if the ministers-no matter what Government may be in .power-will be able to resist the prayers and supplications, not to say the orders, of the women voters who will demand their reward for services rendered. Why preach economy when the Government by this Bill is deliberately laying itself open to greater expense and greater waste.
Finally, it is contrary to the moral order which suffers greatly from promiscuity be<-tween the sexes, and from the desertion of the domestic hearth. The women are exposing themselves to- serious dangers in taking an active part in our political contests which, too often, alas, are carried on without pity, without generosity and without courage; and where the clash of interests, of dislike and of selfishness seek their only outlet in the crushing

of an opponent. Even if they were to escape all these other perils it seems nearly impossible to me that their minds should remain chaste; in the language of Jules Simon "she will inevitably suffer in her virtues." Woman cannot fail to be the enormous loser when, in the social relations brutal constraint, material force, "the yoke of numbers and that of wealth," ineradicable consequences of political contests, take the place of persuasion, of reason, of sentiment, of intelligence and love. The mite of material .power that, by means of the vote, she might painfully obtain through the sacrifice of her health, her modesty, her motherhood and her happiness, cannot possibly be sufficient compensation. Through mingling in public affairs she will feel the need of, in a way, deserting the home, of becoming interested in others than those who have a natural claim to her love, she will live her life for herself and1 not for her loved ones, she will become dissociated, so to speak. Only part wife, she can be none but an insufficient mother. Her role and, [DOT]consequently, her grandeur will inevitably wane.
On the contrary, by remaining in the home, which is her sanctuary, woman will wield an influence beyond compare. She will remind all classes of the ''Fundamental preponderance of sentiment over reason and over activity."
What woman needs is to live in the midst of her family, to return to the home. We are here concerned with the future of the nation, with the dignity of woman, with the sanctity of family life and with the welfare of the country.
In a preface written to Mesdames Van Vorst, for their book "The Working-Woman in the United States," ex-President Roosevelt says:
A people whose men are not prepared to labour in every way, not ready to fight with all their might and who have not in their hearts a yearning after fatherhood; a people whose women are not convinced that there is for them nothing grander than to be a good wife and a good mother; well, such a people has serious reasons to be alarmed about its future.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, this Bill to my mind is a deplorable yielding to a wretched sort of feminism and bids fair to cause the social disintegration of what remains of the family, to the injury of the true woman: wife, mother and queen of the household. As a result, all the world of feminine parasites-blue-stockings and "society women"- will unfold. And that is only the beginning. To complete the disintegration, there is

thought, it seems, of submitting a Bill to facilitate the granting of divorce. What profound' aberration!
Those are, Mr. Chairman, some of my .reasons for opposing the present Bill, which is not called for by the majority of women, but solely by a few emancipated creatures, a few suffragettes, crazy for a crumb of petty glory.
If I take this stand, if I maintain that women should be exempt from all political responsibility, it is not, I pray you to believe, with a view to lowering her social rank and limiting her influence. Far from that. It is so as to consecrate woman with more splendor to the eminent role which nature has assigned her and which she alone can fulfil; it is to prevent the dispersal of the family, to labour towards the resurrection and, at the same time, the reconstitution of a solidly organized society, which will make suffering much more bearable and will avoid1 an incalculable amount of harm; it is because I respect and love woman that I do not wish to see her abandon her rank, and I intend to remain worthy of her and of her teachings; finally, it is to safeguard, in its entirety,, her moral sovereignty which, till now, has been the whole charm of our civilization.

I have the honour to represent the constituency of Welland, which I represented in the local House for ten years, and during all that time no woman in my county ever asked me to vote for women's franchise. To-day, the cry is apparently "women's franchise." I am free to admit that the women of this country should have a vote; they are far more intelligent than the majority of the men. But I want to say right here and now that in the county of Welland the women are not looking for the franchise, but they are looking for help to be sent to their fathers, husbands and sons overseas. Why should we waste time? We have wasted one day discussing titles; we are wasting another day over votes which the women do not want, and we are not dealing with matters which will support our men at the front. Why do we not get down to business, forget these side lines, and try to help the boys who are helping us? These matters of titles and votes for women are mere camouflage; let us forget them and turn our energies towards the means of sending help to the boys at the front.

This is not the first attempt which has been made in Canada to put upon the statute book a uniform Franchise Act. Government has been deemed a practical thing made for the happiness of mankind and1 not to furnish a spectacle of uniformity to justify the scheme of visionary politicians.

,1 also defer to British practice on this question. We have had no general agitation throughout the country in favour of the adoption of a federal measure of woman suffrage. We have had in a restricted degree an agitation for woman suffrage in some of the provinces; I do not object to the granting of the franchise to women in such cases. But no petition in favour of Dominion-wide franchise for women has heen sent to this Parliament, and I do not see why at this moment, under the flimsy pretext of giving votes to women throughout the Dominion, we should ignore the first cardinal principles of our constitution. I am willing to give the women of my province the franchise if they ask for it and if the majority votes for it. Living in Ontario, I should have no objection to woman franchise if it is the will of the majority. It would be a provincial franchise, and that is thei only franchise which constitutionally elects the members of this Parliament.

The hon. gentleman says that if the women of the province of Quebec asked for the franchise he would be willing to grant it to them. Will he tell me whether the women of his province have ever had an opportunity of expressing themselves on this subject?

There has been in all the provinces-mostly throughout the West- some agitation in favour of woman suffrage. In the province of Quebec we have women of the highest intelligence, some of whom are leaders in social works, yet there has been no concerted action on their part in favour of woman, suffrage. I think I am right when I say that the majority of the women in the province of Quebec to-day are safe in the hands of the men, and do not care to exercise the franchise.

I desire to congratulate the Prime Minister on having brought forward this very advanced and progressive measure.

I believe a strong sentiment prevailed throughout the Dominion that the franchise should be extended to women.
My experience in the West has been that there is that general feeling, and if there is the general feeling that the franchise should be given to women after this thorough test of whether they are the equal of the men-and 1 say they are the equal of the men-it is our duty to extend the franchise to the women in appreciation of the great work they have done. Do you not think there will he great rejoicing among the four hundred thousand of our boys overseas when they hear that this Bill has passed this House and that their mothers and sisters and other female relatives who have been working morning, noon, and night to help them, are to be given the right to vote? I appreciate very much the Premier's action in bringing this measure forward. It is a Dominion measure, not a provincial measure. It has been suggested 'by several members on the other side of the House that this is a question for the provinces to deal with; I do not agree. The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) has spoken of some of the western provinces, and he thinks it quite right that [DOT]the women in those provinces should have the franchise. Well, if he is consistent, why should not the women of all the provinces have the franchise? He should he consistent and say: Give it to the women of this whole Dominion; they are as well qualified to vote as are the women in the western provinces.	_
Mr. E. D'ANJOU (Rimouski) (translation) : Before confiding to the House the few remarks I wish to make on the important question which forms the subject of this debate, I would like to cite an instance to the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) which will prove that his statement is not true when he claims that the province of Quebec always gives proof of narrowmindedness. I shall cite an instance which has to do particularly with the county which I have the honour of representing here. I wish to inform him, should he not know it, that on the suggestion of the great Lafontaine, Robert Baldwin, beaten in his own province, was elected in the county of Rimouski, the most beautiful county of the province of Quebec. I cite this incident 
[DOT]to show that it is not always right to arouse popular passions and prejudices, and on all occasions to strike at the back of Quebec in an effort to prove that we are behind the times and that we are shortsighted people.
The hon. member for Peterborough said also, in the,course of his speech,that we, of the Opposition, we, the members from Quebec province, had no mission from our women, nor from the women of the country generally, to come here and oppose this legislation.
I might say the same thing to him and ask him if delegations of women came to him begging that he would champion this measure.
Mr. Chairman, for my part, il would believe myself guilty of a serious lapse of duty 'towards the voters who did me the honour of electing me as their representative, if I were not to submit to the House the reasons which prompt my opposition to the present Bill.
I am entirely aware of the sentiments of my constituents towards woman suffrage, and I know perfectly well that the women of my county haven't the least desire to vote at Federal elections.
Mr. Chairman, I shall not beat around the bush. I am opposed to this legislation, on principle, because I believe it to be radical and inopportune. By obliging woman to take part in our political contests and quarrels you are forcing her out of her own noble role. Woman's place is not at political rallies, on election committees or in the polling-booth.
The ideal spot for woman is the family fireside. Isn't she, in all truth, the angel of the hearth, which she has helped to establish and of which she is the most beautiful ornament?
The application of the law of woman suffrage will necessarily contribute to the destruction of family unity and to the decrease of that respect which man must have towards woman. What quarrels we will witness, and how many interminable disputes; all of which will be the result of our own deeds, if we adopt this Bill which gives to the women, of this country the right to vote.
I am surprised, I find it strange, Mr. Chairman, that a Government which calls itself a Union Government should bring up this legislation which is foreordained to cause disunion in most of our Canadian homes. And I wonder what respect men will have for the woman voter, the woman organizer, who lend themselves to all sorts of low machinations so as to favour such and such a candidate or such and such a political party.

If we wish to safeguard for woman that respect from man which is her right, let us not, by granting her the franchise, deprive her of that dignity and daintiness which make of her the most delightful and most exquisite of creatures.
In my humble opinion, I believe I can assert that woman suffrage is immoral and that it Will, of necessity, result in regrettable and irreparable disasters.
-So, let us leave our women beneath their own roof with their husbands and their children. There they will fulfil their true function, that of rearing noble and valiant defenders for their Canadian fatherland.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of those who have spoken, especially to those I was able to understand. One gentleman, whose name or constituency I do not know but from somewhere in the East, stated principles with which I most heartily agree, and I wish to take him at his word at that particular point where he said he would advocate a policy of education, of enlightenment, of instruction, study and research, or words to that effect. I think that is right, and permit me to say that for a generation at least that very policy has been in operation among the women of this country, to such an extent and with such a result that from the spot where we now stand to the Pacific ocean there is not a foot of ground which is not hallowed with the presence of a political atmosphere that recognizes no distinction of sex. The women of the West have given a great deal of study and attention, to this question, and so have the men, with the consequent result that, in the provinces west of the Ottawa river, without exception, the women have equal privileges with the men. We have in each of the two extreme western provinces a woman sitting in the local legislature. And why should not women sit there? In one of those provinces, from which I have the honour to come, there is a woman in the local legislature. Her husband was formerly -an ornament in that legislature, and was a member of the provincial cabinet. If 'I mistake no-ti she has given three or four sons for the defence of her country, and at the voice of her fellow-citizens she accepted a nomination, and obtained a majority of some 3,000 over her male icompetitorsf. '-She was iaecorded a most hearty welcome in the provincial House, which House she graced -as an ornament, not merely because she is a woman, but because of her capacity to discuss provincial and other questions. And why
should this not he so? I have listened with a great deal of interest to the arguments and statements of the members of the Opposition on this question. Why should there be a distinction between man and woman in the sole item of franchise? Men and women equally recognize the law and obey the law; there is not -a law prohibiting certain crimes which -applies -only to man and exempts women. But, when we come to the door of the -polling booth, in the -past women have -been prohibited from entering because of their -sex, although in mental capacity -and general ability they are fully the equal of men. Why should they be debarred from the expression of their convictions at the polls? They have -a right to express themselves because of their services to society and their contribution to the intellectual -and -moral wealth of the community and of the State.
I have listened also to the address of the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) who has spoken of himself as one of the deans of the House. I had listened to his remarks up to this stage with a very great deal of interest, but I confess that to-night I was disappointed, lit may be because of my parliamentary youth. Why, Sir, I believe this is the year 1918; we are not in the last century. If reference be- made to the action of celebrated -British statesmen and their deliverances in the latter half of the last century, why not go back a little farther? For, if we do we shall find equally celebrated British statesmen unwilling to grant the franchise to men. It is only in comparatively late years that a practical manhood suffrage law has been in force in England. They have grown. But why go back to that date in English history when to-day we find that in England the franchise has been extended to women? They have grown, they have widened, they have seen the obligation resting upon them as citizens and they have granted what the women in England have asked for and what the most advanced conviction of English manhood believe to he their right to enjoy.	,
One other argument advanced by the hon. gentleman was that women were unfitted for military service. I felt like hanging my head when that statement was uttered. Look at the state of affairs in England to-day. Look at the countless thousands of women who are working their full time and every day for the defence of the realm. Look at the women who are taking the places of men in, as far as I know, every avenue of life, every avenue of manual labour-working on the farms,

driving motor cars, acting as conductors on tramways, taking their places in the munition factories by the tens of thousands. Is any one justified in saying that these women are unfitted for military service? Does military service simply mean taking your position on the firing line? Hon. gentlemen on the other side have been telling us that there were men in their provinces who were engaged in agriculture and that that was a form of military service. I grant it. But is it not a form of military service to supply the men at the front with the munitions and the materials of war? Surely military service is not confined to pointing a gun?	-
The records of the past will show that in all forms of active national service in the history of mankind woman has taken her place and done her full share. There is no question in regard ta that. Military service is such a broad term that I take it that every man and woman who does his utmost for the Empire, for the protection of society and for the great principle for which we are all striving is deserving of the qualification of being fitted for military service.
Another point spoken of by my hon. friend -and I hesitate to state it here at this hour -^was the necessity of preserving our chivalry towards women. I endorse that most heartily. But, Mr. 'Chairman, let us remember that we cannot preserve our chivalry while we allow women to remain under this injustice. We cannot have them retain our respect, and we cannot secure and hold' their respect, if we are unwilling to do the right thing 'by them. It is certainly at this hour in the world's history, the right thing to recognize their equality in the realm of active life, and the only way to secure and preserve their respect and confidence is to grant them the privileges which we as citizens enjoy and not condemn them to inferiority because of the accident of sex.
My hon. friend to whom I first referred showed his true manhood, I think, in his closing words. His remarks seemed to me to suggest a political argument. He argued against woman suffrage, but I noticed that when he came to the conclusion his bigness of heart shone forth and his manhood expressed itself when he said that he hoped soon to see women in the position in which this Bill seeks to place them. If I understood him correctly, that was his concluding remark. That is characteristic, I 'believe, of men all over. Many talked against this reform, and I would fain think that if there are men on the other side of the House who talk against it it is because they are in Par-

liament. They feel that to grant women the franchise is the right thing to do and when it comes to the vote, and to the decision I trust they will not act against their better convictions.

Mr. Chairman, it is somewhat late in the evening to attempt to say anything new about this very important Bill. But there are, perhaps,-some observations which can be made on it with regard to features which have not been touched upon before. There are two objections to this Bill generally. There is a great deal in favour of the Bill, but I will first mention two general considerations against woman suffrage. The first general objection is that it may possibly create a certain amount of friction at election time if the husband belongs to one political party and the wife to another. I think that is an objection which should be considered, although I do not believe it is strong enough-to offset the good features of the Bill, The main objection to the measure is that which John Bright found to a proposal for woman suffrage towards the end of the last quarter of the nineteenth century. Woman suffrage is not a new proposal in British countries'. It was about 1873, if I mistake not, that John Stuart Mill introduced into the British House of Commons a Woman Suffrage Bill, and it was defeated, but received a surprisingly strong support at that time. John Bright on that occasion voted in favour of the Bill; but subsequently, he voted against the Bill, and the reason he gave for so doing was that it would enormously increase the power of the church in politics both in Great Britain and in Ireland. Now, we are all, I take it, anti-clericals. None of us want to have the church trench on the state; none of us want to have either priest or minister suggest, dictate or exhort from the pulpit what attitude his flock should take on a political question. And there is no question but that at the beginning of woman suffrage it may increase the power either of the priest or the minister of religion. We Liberals in the province of Quebec have for years and years stood out against clerical interference in politics. There is an interesting case in the law reports of our province where an election was set aside because a parish priest had unduly endeavoured to influence his flock to vote for one candidate rather than another. We have set our faces against that. For forty years and more the Liberal party in Quebec fought against that attitude of mind on the part of the church, and we stopped it. And, Mr. Chairman, gentlemen

in other provinces, as well as in Quebec, have got a work to do along these lines in regard to the ministers of other churches, because in the last election we had a very sad condition arise. We found that ministers" of the Gospel did not confine themselves to advocating principles, but they stood up on the Sunday before election day and told their floeks for which party they were to cast their votes. Now, I am no enemy to the Christian church; I hope I am a humble member of that body. I remember on the Sunday morning before election day that in a church in the county in which I was running a certain circular letter-a mandement we would call it if it came from a bishop in our province-came from a certain committee on social and moral reform of a very great church in this country, and those ministers who read it exhorted their flock to vote for one political party rather than another. That happened on the Sabbath morning. I did not go to church that morning; I thought there was going to be something like that, and I thought I would rather not hear it or he tempted to walk out, as a number did do on that morning. In the evening I went to church, and there the minister prayed the Lord for guidance for the people that they should vote in the way that their conscience and mind dictated, and you could not tell from his sermon whether he was going to vote for me or for my adversary, land I do not know which way he voted. That was the proper attitude for a clergyman to take. This question of clerical interference in politics touches very closely the subject we are now discussing, for women are more religious animals than men are, and are more likely to be affected by either the priest or the minister. Now, I trust that we shall have no more of this in Canadian elections. I trust that the ministers and the priests of all churches will see to it that they render unto Caesar the things that.are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's.
Now these are two points against woman's suffrage on the surface; I do not think they go down to the foot of the matter. I am in favour of the principle of this Bill. The husband and wife may disagree even if one of them has not got the vote. The fact that both of them have the vote may lead the husband to endeavour to convert the wife. It will he worth while, for she will have a vote. And the wife, of course, will not cease her efforts to convert the husband. The unbelieving husband may be saved by the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife
may be saved by the believing husband. And, as regards clerical domination, it is just as well foy women to have the vote, because that will raise them in their own self-respect and it will make them in time less prone to take political direction from their husbands, or their ministers, or anybody else.
What are the arguments that can be, and have been, brought forward against giving women the vote? There is the argument that woman is queen of the home. I often think she is more really queen of the dish-pan or of the washtub. The idea that a woman sits regally enthroned by the fireside is very pretty, but it is not according to facts, because, as a rule, women have to work longer hours, go through greater drudgery, and enjoy fewer holidays than men do. The idea that women are going to be in any way lowered by mixing in politics does no credit to the political atmosphere of this country. If our political atmosphere is low we must endeavour to raise it to make it worthy of the women we are admitting to our ranks to-night. It has been suggested that women will have to go to political meetings. Of course they will. I will say that they go to political meetings already; (they ,certainly do in the county which I have the honour to represent. So far as the children are concerned, I have seen a grandmother come along with a daughter, accompanying the father and with a tiny baby who was placed on the schoolhouse desk and who slept peacefully all through the meeing.

Mr. MdMAiSTER:	Small families, my
hon. friend says. Political meetings do not come 'along at all times. Most women do their own work, and are very busy, but most are able sometimes to get out to church even in the country districts. They are able to attend social functions at times, and there is no reason why they should not attend political meetings when i'hey wiant to. lit is for us to see that political .meetings are conducted with isuch fairness and decorum that it will be an honour for women to attend them. I believe that their presence always tends to make debate more moderate. And let me say this, Mr. Chairman, politics will not become less hitter when the ladies come into it. -We saw that very plainly in the last election. The ladies are often prone to bring a personal element into a discussion which men do not. But that is possibly due to their training; possibly after they have

been vo'ting for some time they may tend to view matters from not .s>uoh a close personal point of view.
Now, I would not like hon. gentlemen opposite to think that because certain of us from the province of Quebec are not in favour of woman suffrage we are any less gallant than the rest of the country, because that is not so. The reason for it is that in the province of Quebec the woman in the family occupies as high a position and is as much looked up to-more looked up to-than anywhere else in the Dominion.

Mr. MbMASTER:	I will say as much;
we won't make any invidious distinctions. What I mean is 'this: I believe that the inhabitant of the province of Quebec is as prone to consult his wife, and to he guided by her opinion on every important transaction in life as people are anywhere else in the Dominion of Canada. I think that perhaps one reason why there has been no demand among the vast majority of the women of Quebec for the vote-and that is absolutely true, there has been no great demand from the women of the province for the vote-is because they have had a very large influence in politics and in social life through the simple fact of their position as wife and mother. There is no place in the wide world where family ties are stronger, where father and mother receive more affection and more respect, than in the province of Quebec. The .law of that province creates' a partnership between, man and wife. All the movable property-the personality, as you would say in the Englieh-law provinces-which either of the consorts, owned at the time iof marriage goes into the partnership fund. All real estate which they acquire during .the marriage falls into the community property; that is, generally speaking, there are exceptions.. During the marriage the .husband controls that community property, tout when he dies, he can. only will half of it away; the wife who survives the hus-toand becomes immediately the owner of half the joint acquisitions which have been .made during the lifetime of the husband, the theory of the law being that the wife toy her work in the house and by her prudence and, economy does just as much to build up the family fortunes as the man does by his work. There is a statement of law in the province of Quebec that the husband is the "seigneur et maitre," that is, lord, and master, of the community. .But, as our professors told us in college,

that is only a legal fiction; the husband is not lord and master of the community; he <is the 'joint partner-the senior partner perhaps only in name, because he has to consult the junior partner all the time. I make this explanation because I do not want hon. gentlemen from other parts of the country to have the impression that we of the province of Quebec wish to keep the women in a place inferior to ourselves. Those gentlemen, who have spoken out against the Bill are interpreting in a large measure the views, of the women of the province of Quebec who are not anxious [DOT]for the vote. But m.y contention is that there are women in the .province of Quebec who wish to have the vote, and even if the majority do not want to- have it, that is no reason for keeping the vote away from those who- want it-and there is no law to compel people to vote who do not want to dO' so. (I am, therefore, in favour of the principle of the Bill.
. But I wish to direct the attention of the committee to section. 2 of the Bill, which reads as follows:
2. This Act shall be construed! as one with the Dominion Elections Act, chapter six of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, and The War-time Elections Act, chapter thirty-nine of the statutes of 1917, and in each of the said Acts the expression "person'' or "male person," or any similar expression, shall include a female .person, unless a different meaning' is required by the context or by the terms of this Act.
It was with deep regret that I observed this clause in the Bill, because it seems to indicate that the Government propose to keep on the statute book an Act which I consider to be a blot on the fair name of Canada, that is, the War-time Elections Act. This Act was described by the member for North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) thfe other evening as having been passed for certain purposes. I read as follows from his remarks, found on page 404 of Hansard:
As I say, we lhad to face-
"We" apparently was the last Borden Administration, as distinguished from the present Union Government.
As I say, we had' to face an adverse vote in Quebec and in the West, and men like myself realized that if the Government had gone to the country without first adopting the War-time Elections Act, the control of the country would have .been lost to anti-British-
With that statement, of course, I do not agree in any way; there are no anti-British people in this country. We all desire the success of the Allies; we all have affection and respect for the Motherland, and al-

though we may differ as to the best means to a given endi, that dioest not give hon. gentlemen opposite the right to infer that we are anti-British or anything of that kind. (Reading):
Oh, oh.
The control of this country would have been lost by the iBritsh element and handed over to the anti-British element for the next twenty-five years.
I rise to a point of order. The hon, gentleman is quoting from another debate^ which is not allowed by the rules of the House.

If I am not allowed
to quote further from the debate, I certainly will not do so.

speechtext:

quote from a previous debate during the same session but reference to a previous debate by way of illustration only, would be considered in order.

'That is to say, I may rely on my memory, but not on the written words. Well, my memory is that the member for North Simeoe stated in very emphatic terms that this Government owed its election to the War-time Elections Act; that without it, this Government would have been defeated. Moreover, the hon. member justified the War-time Elections Act on the ground that without it the country would have passed into the control of anti-British people. That is what he said- I do not agree with him. What I would not hopefully, hut very respectfully and very earnestly, ask the Government to do is to strike out from this Bill any reference to the War-time Elections Act. Why should a woman from Switzerland or some other part of Europe whose language is German, but who is a true Canadian woman, not have the right to vote? Under the WaT-time Elections Act a man who came from a country at peace with us, hut whose native language was German, lost his vote. I do not wish to go into this matter at length, hut I know that other gentlemen sitting opposite think with me that the War-time Elections Act is a blot on the fair name of Canada, and should be removed. We do not wish to see the conferring of the franchise on women tarnished by the restrictions on their voting which are imposed by the War-time Elections Act. The other day Mr. 'Asquith addressing his constituents at Cupar, Scotland, said that he felt sure of the success of the Allies in this war because the great spiritual forces of .righteousness were fighting for us. The
War-time Elections Act was morally wrong; it took away from people who were as loyal to Canada as any of us the right to vote just because they happened to come years ago from countries with which we are now at war. Bohemians, Ruthenians, people who had no sympathy at all with our enemies, were deprived of the right to- vote. It was not right; it may have been expedient, but I belong to the school of political thought which believes that honour, justice and righteousness are stronger than expediency.
I believe that we .shall be on the side of the great spiritual forces fighting for righteousness if we, the common people, in Parliament assembled, see to it that ' in granting the franchise to women, we take away the stain from the Canadian shield and escutcheon by wiping off the War-time Elections Act.

In rising to say a few words in this debate, I do not presume that I shall he able, at this late hour, to contribute any new thought or add to the arguments in favour of granting the franchise to women. But if I did not place myself on record as being in favour of woman suffrage, I feel I should not be doing my duty to the noble women of the district which I represent, who have rendered such splendid service to the nation during these four years of war. I have listened with some interest to my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster), and, for a moment, I was hardly able to understand whither he was drifting. He gave two outstanding objections to granting the franchise to women, first, that it would create friction at election time, and, secondly, that it would enormously increase the power of the church. If his opinion in that respect were correct, I am at a loss to understand why he drifted to the other angle later on. I am reminded of >a homely story which, while it may be an old one, is very apropos. A couple of tramps travelling through the country arrived at the gate of a farm where a large collie dog, in his happy, or, as it might have been, unhappy way, was wagging his tail, and at the same time growling and showing his teeth. These men wished to go to the farmer's house so that they might get something to eat. Henry was a little in advance, and Pat was a little in the rear. Pat said to Henry, "Go on, he will not bite you; he is a good-natured old fellow; can't you see he is a-waggin' of his tail." "But," said Henry, "he is also a showing of his teeth, and blest if I know which end to believe."

During a period of many years women have been more or less engaged in election contests in the province of Ontario, and 1 cannot agree with my hon. friend that the granting of the Dominion franchise to them is liable to cause family friction. I would respect and honour my wife quite as much even if her opinion differed from mine. My hon. friend refers to the pgssibility of the wife trying to convert the husband and the husband trying to convert the wife. I suppose, under such circumstances, if they were pulling apart and were settled in their views, neither one could be converted. I am reminded of an incident of a public man, a politician, who was on one occasion accosted by a suffragette and asked for his opinion on woman suffrage. He was very ready to answer her question. He said, "Yes, my dear lady, I go further than believing in woman suffrage; I maintain that men and women are equal in every respect." The lady's reply was, "Now, Professor, are you not bragging?"
I have found, in the activities of our women during recent years, that woman has measured up in her powers and capacity for assuming responsibility in every respect equal to man. Let me give an illustration to show the quality of intellect and the capacity of women even amongst the girls of our schools. I hold in my hand a pamphlet issued by the .Greater Resources Committee of the province of Ontario, in which it is attempted to show how the boys and the girls in that province assisted in the great work of production last year. In connection with that work a competition was held amongst the schools in the different counties. In each school where the competition took place there were offered first, second and third prizes. The object of the competition was to have the boys and girls write an essay showing the best way in which greater production could be assisted by the co-operation of boys and girls. I find that in one competition, out of the three prizes given, a girl won the first and a girl won the third. I was interested enough to look into the pamphlet further, and I found that in the schools of the province in which the competitions were held, of the first prizes won, 96 went to the girls and 50 to the boys, and out of the total number of prizes, first, second and third, 206 went to girls and 180 to the boys. Some time ago the Canadian Municipal World bad an article written by Miss Agnes Chesley, in which she was answering the arguments of Dr. James Murray, who, amongst other points of opposition to 
woman suffrage, brought forward the following: First, that when the franchise had been extended to women they had not shown an interest in the work; second, that they had not recorded their votes in the proportion that was expected of them. Miss Chesley went on to show that this argument was not borne out by facts. She said:
In New Zealand', according' to the latest returns, 82 per cent of the women voted as against 84 of the men. In Australia 57 per cent of the women voted as against 68 of the men. Practically all the women registered, and the percentage of women voters was higher in the settled districts and1 lower in the unsettled; as might he expected'. It is not difficult to understand, in places where the voters have to travel, that it is easier for the men to go than for the women.
She stated further:
In Wyoming, SC to 9<0 per cent of the women vote; in Colorado 15' to 8'5 per cent vote; in Utah, 8'5 to 90 per cent. In Washington 85 to 95 per cent; in California, a splendid' percentage, 90 to 9'9, and so on through the list. Statistics show conclusively thiat where women have the vote they do use it.
Mias Chesley at that time undertook to make a report as to the conditions in the province of Quebec, to which my hon. friend has referred. She said that at the civic election held at Montreal previous to the writing of the article-that is, at the last election-the Montreal Local Council of Women undertook to get out the women's vote. She continues:
So successfully did they accomplish their big undertaking that the percentage voting was very high, in one ward reaching 90 per cent. I wonder if any ward would show such a high percentage of men voting! At one civil election in a ward of this city, 25 per cent of the men voted. Talk about the apathy of the women! The women of Montreal are vastly more interested in municipal affairs than the men.	*
If women in that part of the province have manifested such an interest in municipal affairs, it is only natural to conclude that they will manifest a similar degree of interest in the larger sphere of provincial and Dominion affairs. There will be all the more reason as the years go by for the influence of the women in our public affairs, because many of the things on which the provinces will have to legislate go very closely home to. the people. The article goes on:
Suppose we now examine a few more of Mr. Murray's preposterous statements and see if they are also based on ignorance. "Even in matters affecting- the lives of women and children, the women voters1 have shown little interest," he says. This is the apotheosis of ignorant dogmatism. The very smallest enquiry into facts would have stopped any pen

from making such a statement. I can go over country after country where women have the vote, and the unanimous testimony of the wisest and best is that the women's vote has invariably been used for his very thing:-the betterment of the conditions under which women and children live. Judge Lindsay writes, "We have in Colorado the most advanced laws of any state in the union for the care and protection of the home and1 the children, the very foundations of the Republic. We owe this more to Woman Suffrage than to any other one cause." Turning to our own British Empire, Sir John Cockburn writes, after an experience of nearly twenty years in Australia: "It may be safely affirmed1 that the inclusion of women in the electorate has greatly facilitated the passage of laws safeguarding the welfare of children and women and removing temptations from the path of men."
It is not necessary to quote such statements, because we have other evidence. No statesmen dare say on the floor of the legislature in those provinces where the franchise has been extended to women that it was a mistake. I believe that giving women the vote will raise politics to a higher plane-to a plane which as my right hon. friend has said, w'ould justify women taking a more, active interest in public affairs. If our country is growing better, and we think it is growing better from day to day, every move that has been made for a higher civilization and better ideals of citizenship has been due, to a large extent, to the influence of the women behind it. The moral laws, the laws of right, the'laws which provide for better care and protection of the home and for better citizenship, have been largely the result of women's influence.
I congratulate the Prime 'Minister on introducing this Bill at this time. Some hon. gentlemen think this an inappropriate time, but in view of what woman has done for the state in this crisis, in view of her activities and the real serviceable work which she has done, and which has meant so much, I think this House dare not longer deny her the right which, in my opinion, should have been granted many ; ears ago. T believe that in supporting this measure, as I propose to do, I shall be unanimously endorsed by the electors whom I represent.

I am unequivocally in favour of the principle of this Bill. Among the many reasons I have for supporting this Bill, the first is that my mother was a woman, my wife was a woman, and the old Queen Victoria was a woman, and so was Queen Elizabeth; and if there are any two individuals on the earth who have [DOT]demonstrated the fact that women can exercise public functions wisely it is these two great queens who have given to their several
eras their names-so that we speak of the Elizabethan period and the Victorian era.
I think there is no question as to the capacity of women to exercise the functions which the franchise will confer on them. Slavery always degrades, and woman has been a slave in this country, in a political sense, until the western provinces gave the franchise to women. Giving the franchise to women will develop public spirit, on the same principle that it developed public spirit in the non-property owner. I am surprised at some of my hon. friends telling us we ought to go back and listen to what the French people andi the English people did away hack in the night of time. We need not go back to the night of time. It is only a very few years ago that the Roman Catholics in this, country and in all the British possessions did not have the franchise.
There is another thing I want to point out. If you give the franchise to any section of the Dominion, it does not follow that the women have to' exercise the franchise. The greater includes the less. It is not as if we were taking something away from them; we are giving something to them, which they can use if they like, and if they don't like they can stop home. There is nothing compulsory about it. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Fournier), I think, made use of a fallacy. He was afraid the birth rate would decline if we gave the franchise to women, tout at the same time he told us that in old France they did not give the franchise to women. I am speaking of this to show that giving or withholding the franchise has nothing whatever to do with the birth rate. The people of old France, in my judgment, are the first and the only people who have solved the great question of modem civilization in regard to the birth rate. The people of Quebec have followed quite a different policy; they have been increasing their birth rate while the French in the old country have decreased theirs; and there were political reasons for that, and not only political reasons but scientific and national and social reasons.
I say that the great French nation, so far as civilization is concerned', stands ahead of every nation in the world. People of this country do not seem to realize thalt our present civilization and our present democracy are absolutely new. Why, the world has only been fit to live in for about fifty years as a matter of fact. The reason we have this democracy and this civilization is [DOT]because of the ^relief of the congestion of
0C3

the populations of Europe by the discovery of America, and the giving room for the people, and giving them time to think. The man who is pressed against the limit in the matter of subsistence cannot become civilized. The man who gets up in the morning and looks for a snake for his wife's breakfast cannot become civilized. Our present civilization depends upon our present democracy, and our present democracy is absolutely the result of immunity from pressing want. But what has happened? What induced this war? This war is more or less the direct result of over-population. The Empire of Germany in my time-and I am not a very old man-and in' the lifetime of nearly every hon. gentleman sitting in this House has doubled its population. Since the Franco-Prussian War, 40 odd years ago, their population has doubled. Now, remember the population increases in a geometrical ratio. I am using that term in contradistinction to an arithmetical ratio. Take Germany as an illustration. The German population in forty years rose from forty millions to eighty millions. In the next forty yeaTs it will be one hundred and sixty millions and the following forty years it will 'be three hundred and twenty millions. What about the forty years following ! It would be six hundred and forty millions. North of the boundary between the United States and Mexico, at the beginning of this century, we had one hundred million people, in Canada and the United States. In thirty years that population will be doubled, and we will have two hundred millions; in sixty years, four hundred millions; in ninety years eight hundred millions. Given peace, plenty and immunity from epidemics, and there will be nearly twice that many, if Quebec keeps at it at the present Tate. According to Malthus, the population of the Anglo-Celtie people, given peace, plenty and immunity from epidemics, will double itself every twenty-five years. Get to work with your pencils and paper and figure out what that means, arrd think of what the future has in store for the civilized nations of the world. At the same time, remember that I am not discouraging the increasing population. I do not want to do that; Canada is a new, great country, almost illimitable, in one sense of the word, and the first duty of Canadian statesmen is to occupy that land, and make it a white man's country. Another duty we owe, and especially we owe it to the people of this country immediately after the war, is to get as many people in here as we possibly can, so that they will divide up the tremendous public debt, and thereby 
lessen the debtb per capita, otherwise, we will all have to go out of the country. These are little suggestions, but I should like the House to sit up and take notice, and look to the future, because, as a matter of fact, we do not want to live on a smouldering volcano and not know it is there.
There are some other little points made. Some gentlemen said that women were not the equal of men. Why 'is that? Simply because they have not the franchise. If you give the women the franchise, I venture to say that in twenty years they will have just as much public spirit as the men, and be just as capable of exercising the franchise, because there is nothing like freedom, nothing like liberty, and nothing like giving people their rights, if you want to develop their character, but you must develop it along lines of self-reliance and not make slaves of them, because slavery always degrades.
Speaking about the influence that the church will have upon women, give them the franchise, and that will obviate the very difficulty that my hon. friend feared; because once the women get the franchise, they will develop the same as the men. It is because women have been driven out of public life and out of faking an interest in the affairs of the country, that they have been driven to patronize the theatre matinee and the five o'clock tea, when they would be a great deal better out of such places. At the same time, I want to draw the attention of the hon. leader of the Government to a principle which I think he would be well advised, and the Government be well advised, to recognize, and that is they should not be showing too many red rags to a bull. The Quebec people are sensitive; they are 'as fine a class of people as there are to-day in Canada, or any part of the world for that matter, but they are sensitive, and when they see a measure before this House, whether it is a conscription Bill, or Woman's Suffrage Bill, at an inopportune time, they necessarily think that it is aimed at Quebec, particularly if it has that colour. That is what it looks like to a good many of my friends*. They feel this, legislation is aimed primarily at the province of Quebec, because they dto not happen to have women suffrage or for some other reason, il am not going into the generic reasons, because you will recognize the situation as well as I do. That is one of the principal reasons why hon. gentlemen on -this side of the House criticise the Bill more severely than they would if my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition had introduced

it. I want to warn the Government to be careful and not irritate any class' of people in this country. _ The truth of the matter is this is a young country, and the inhabitants are not homogeneous. But they will become so if you leave them alone. And another thing, if you want to crystallize certain- things that you think are evils, persecute the people, because persecution defeats the very end the persecutors have in view. You cannot get a better illustration of that than Old Ireland, where the southern part of Ireland has been, persecuted

Mr. Chairman, I have
never been a believer in the divine right af kings, nor am I a believer in the divine right of men to the franchise. I think women hav-e just the same right to the franchise as -men ha/ve. It ha.s always been my belief that when Ad-am gave his rib for the creation of Eve he lost the best rib he had and possibly a good deal of his backbone with it. We are going to give women the franchise. We have no right to withhold it fro-m them and never had. My hon.
lessen the debt per capita, otherwise, we , favour of the Bill; so are any number of gentlemen on this side. The ho-n. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) was not justified in suggesting -that the opposition to the Bill was actuated by a political motive or in talking about eighty- . five members on -this side of the House defeating a hundred and Ifilfty members on the other side. That was only talking to the gallery, or the press, or his constituents. There is no good reason to my mind why wo-men should not have the franchise. They are just as intelligent and as capable of voting as men are. The women of the constituency which I represent polled a very large vote in the last election.
I g-o-t more votes in the last election than the combined votes of the candidates in the previous election; so that the women must be voting intelligently. That is another argument that is- very much in favour of woman -suffrage. I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member from East York (Mr. Foster) when he was explaining the inner workings of the Tory mind and suggesting that it was a good thing to offer -the women this inducement.
I am .satisfied that the women, being honest and honourable, will naturally turn to the ho-nest party in the country -and of course this measure mus-t be of great benefit to the Liberals o-f Canada.

Mr. Chairman, a moment ago I heard the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) express his astonishment that the province of Quebec should he opposed to granting women the franchise. I appreciate his position-which is of a very particular nature-and if the hon. member fails to fully grasp our objections to this Bill, it may result from the fact that he is in the very midst of his honeymoon.
Mr. Chairman, we are not opposed to women obtaining the vote in the other provinces; on the contrary, we believe their mind to be ripe for this reform, as folks are pleased to call it. And if we are opposed to this law it is not because we consider the women of Quebec less intelligent than those in the other provinces; on the contrary we are convinced that they are just as well able as any one to judge political -questions at their true value and will use their ballot with both enlightenment and intelligence. But we are opposed to this law because we fail to see, clearly, in what way, from a social point of view, it will improve the situation in our province.

We may well ask ourselves, in the first place, whether or not the women of Quebec have any desire to be admitted to the voting-booth. To this question, Mr. Chairman, we are in a position to give an exact reply, because we have just come from meeting with our constituents in every county of the province, and we may state, in full sincerity, that all the women of the province are strongly opposed to being saddled with the responsibility of the ballot, a burden which they find too heavy for their delicate shoulders.
During the last election campaign we had the opportunity to ascertain whether or not the franchise does improve woman's status, socially. Well, what took place? When the Patriotic Fund was organized, in the very first days of the war, it had been understood that the Fund, which was subscribed to by all the citizens of Montreal, irrespective of race or party, would in no way interfere with forthcoming election contests. That is to say: the Patriotic Fund was entirely neutral in the matter of politics. Now, what happened? At the December elections we saw women, who belonged to this organization, soliciting votes for the Government; we even saw them go from door to door and some of them went so far as to offer money. More than that, Mr. Chairman, on the very day of the election, they organized, a Unionist masquerade. In the district of St. Henri-Westmount we saw a certain group of women, who were entitled to vote, spend nearly the whole day in the different polls so as to prevent citizens from voting, bv making them believe that the polls were overcrowded with people awaiting their turn to mark their ballots.
Such, gentlemen, are the results of the first trial o,f this granting to women the privilege of the ballot. Now, we are opposed to this proposal of woman suffrage because we find that it is contrary to the character and the temperament of our women in the province of Quebec.
We believe that the sentimental side of their nature is so developed that this would expose them to many dangers.
I will cite only one instance to show that the sentimental side of woman can often be at fault. Last winter, I believe it was, we witnessed an association of women, moved by the imperialist spirit, decreeing, after due deliberation, that an honest citizen, who was exercising his right of free speech,-that is what iMr. Armand Lavergne was doing,-should be thrown into prison.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I ask you, was this young man, in taking advantage of his free-

dom to express his opinions, doing anything else than these women themselves?
He was their best friend, and they wanted, at the time to encroach on his liberty. I wish to draw their attention to the fact that the principles of Armand Lavergne were their own principles in 1911, that he has always been consistent in his manner of reasoning and in 1918 continues to profess the opinions he expressed in 1911. Which all goes to show that nerves are at times unduly influenced and that it is not prudent to grant them a privilege like the franchise.
Now, we are told, as an argument, as a reason, that this is being done all over the world, that it is a well-established current of opinion, in a word, that we need something new in this country. I will admit that we do not require novelty; but, at this time, when thousands of our Canadians are falling on the fields of Flanders; at this time, when those who return to us are disabled, mutilated or contaminated, it is at least strange that we should be presented with this, proposal of replacing the family spirit in our country by the spirit of the hustings.
No, Mr. Chairman, it is not by making speeches, it is not by writing articles in the newspapers, nor with lectures, nor with poetry, that, under the present * circumstances, the family spirit, which iis certainly the most precious for us to nurture, can be replaced.
I must draw your attention to the fact that in the province of Quebec we are not relying on immigration to increase our population; besides I find this hope unfounded even in the other provinces. I must tell those who hear me, that at the present time the gates are closed against immigration. It is not the United States who, after the war, will allow their subjects to come and colonize a depopulated Canada; it is not France nor England assuredly; and still less, devastated Belgium and ruined Serbia. No, Mr. Chairman. Moreover, a barrier will surely be established in this Dominion.
We have a last hope: the immigration of the yellow races; but we fear the yellow peril. If our friends in the other provinces are hankering after this immigration, that is their own affair; but, for our part, we are opposed to having this race enter the country. We claim that the French Canadian cannot be replaced by a Chinaman; and neither can the English Canadian be replaced in this Dominion by a Chinaman.
Mr. 'Chairman, I will not go on very long, as the hour is late and a number of speakers have eloquently dealt with the subject;

but I must say that, to my mind, politics and the home are two incompatible things.
By granting the franchise to women we will, in a way, oblige them to become well-informed so as to cast their vote in an enlightened manner; in a way we will force them, in order to gather this information, to read all sorts of things; we will oblige them to desert their homes and go to clubs in search of information; we will oblige them.to be present at meetings; and we, who have the habit of considering our women with the greatest respect, will be pained to see them set off, bound for those common meeting-places where, perchance, they will leave a little of their reputation.
I do not shaTe the opinion of the English philosopher, Stuart Mill, who maintains that the role of woman throughout her whole life is to drag the chains put on her by her husband, for this opinion is absolutely false.
However, <1 do not .say that such a thing could not happen amongst those who are not really married.
This Bill is presented to the House in the shape of a reward. I do not see, Mr. Chairman, how we can accept this reward when it means the imposition upon woman of a heavy responsibility which will force her to leave her home to go to rallies, to leave her family, to leave her household duties, so as to fulfil a duty which is far too arduous for her character, her habits and her delicate temperament.
Now, if I understand aright, this Bill is presented to the House as a reward or as a token of gratitude for the services rendered by Canadian women to the divers organizations having for their object the relief of our soldiers and of their families during the present war.
I wish to point out to the hon. Prime Minister that, if such be the end he has in view, there are other means of proving his gratitude to the women of our province, means far more effective than the ballot, which will never dry the tears of so many bereaved mothers, nor soothe the deep wounds left in their hearts by the absence of their sons on the firing-line. This franchise will not console our old men who, because their sons have gone, are forced to bend their backs to labour so as to earn, by the sweat of their brow7, a bit of miserable war-bread. No, Mr. Chairman, if the Prime Minister wishes to reward the devotion of our Quebec women to patriotic undertakings, let him give them back their sons, the object of all their tenderness and their sole interest in life. I may assure him that
this form of reward from the .Government would be much more appreciated by them.
So I say, in closing, that I am opposed to this Bill, first because it is against Nature, and next because it turns the established social order upside down. Each tree must bear its own fruit and no otheT. The mission that woman is called upon to fulfil is absolutely incompatible with the r61e which this Bill seeks to foist upon her.
I make bold to hope that the observations made against the Bill will be accepted in good part by the Government. As regards myself, I am convinced that the province of Quebec is not ready to accept this change. Things may be different in the other provinces and against that, we, in the province of Quebec have no objection; but we maintain that it is for the provincial governments exclusively to decide this question. To them belongs the privilege of preparing the voters'1 lists; and when the province of Quebec is ready to adopt such a radical change she will not fail to take advantage of this privilege, which will put her on the same footing as the other provinces. For the time being, I do not hestitate to say that this Bill shows a very bad policy and constitutes an abuse of power, since it takes a prerogative away from the provinces and gives it to the central authority.
Mr. J. E. ILiESLAGE (Hochelaga): Mr Chairman, it was not my intention to say anything on this subject, but I think it is a dtity to my constituents to express my opinion on the Bill. There have been many arguments for and against this measure which have their value and deserve great consideration. I do not think it is necessary to cover the subject as thoroughly as many of the preceding speakers, but I merely want to call attention to certain details, and to explain the reason why I am against this Bill. This question of franchise, if you will look at it in a political way, may suit some localities and certain persons, but I do not think you can advance any reason which will modify in any way the nature of women. I have seen in the United States women elected on school boards. I can very well understand the reason for that, but there I think you will admit they were elected by the people as mothers, not as politicians, in order that they might come in closer contact with the children in the schools. I understand that in that sphere they were very useful following up the work which they had begun at home. In all ages we have found women in hospitals as nurses; we find them in this war taking care of the wounded soldiers at the front, but always

as women, not as politicians. It was within their sphere to follow these, different occupations and to perform work appropriate to women. They have done more. It has been mentioned here that they have taken the place of men in the field and in the factory. I can understand' that very well. It was the duty of everybody to do what was possible to help win the war. The women did it willingly, they are still doing it in many places, hut I am very sure that it was more because of the compulsion of events, and that they will he glad to be relieved when their duty is over and to return where they belong, in the home. It is all very good, 'Mr. Chairman, -to talk of privileges and to bring forward the argument that, because they have done so much for the country, they deserve the right to vote. I believe the natural franchise which belongs to them, and the only one for me is the franchise at home. One hon. member has told us that politics stirs up passion and emotions. The two go together. I believe that if politics leads to these ends, we had better keep our wives at home and the passion there with them. In the province of Quebec, I know very well, as has been stated here, there has not been any particular movement or demand for this franchise. I am sure that the women would exercise it in that province as well as they would anywhere else. But there is one thing sure: if men feel political life to be a burden sometimes, and find that it is a sphere in which one goes deeper and deeper, if you give women the privilege of voting and deciding upon political questions I am much afraid that the privilege will expand a great deal further than it is supposed to do, and I think there will be a revolution in our ideals which will be incompatible with ideals of home life. And that is one reason why I do not agree with the principle of this Bill. I remember that a candidate in one of the counties in Quebec in a certain election was very surprised at being defeated, and all his friends toldl him after the election: "We loved you so much that we wanted to keep out at home." I love the women so much that I want to do likewise. Allow me to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that in my business I am in close daily contact with them; I know that they want to be respected, and that they should be respected, and1 I believe I would vote against the Bill, to keep them at home. I have nothing more to add; but, as the hon. member for Brorne (Mr. McMaster) stated, as an argument for the Bill, that the emotion was so great at one time in his last 
campaign that even women with little babies came to political meetings, I am of opinion that that is an argument against the franchise. I do not believe that common decency would allow that as an argument for a Bill. There is a limit to everything. It shows an abuse that should be corrected. I do not think that women, enjoying all the rights and) privileges which they do, should1 expect to have the right to vote at this moment.
