speechtext: I promised the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) that I would see him next.
The only reason I desire to speak is that reference has been made to me this evening

Mr. Chairman, I will be 'brief. The reason I rise at this late hour is 'because I come from a province where the women may rightly be termed electors. At the time of the last election, I want to point out to the 'Government these women in the province of Saskatchewan and ,in the constituency which II have the honour to represent who had been privileged to exercise the franchise in June of last year and were denied that privilege in December of the same year, do not feel very kindly toward the Government who put them in that position. I notice that the hon. member for Brorne (Mr. McMaster) attached some significance to the fact that in clause 2 of the Bill there is a reference'made to the Wartime Elections Act. Personally, I am content to accept the- statement made by the Prime Minister the other day about this matter in connection with the War-time Elections Act. If I thought that by endorsing this Bill I was in any way endorsing the War-time Elections Act, my vote would certainly be registered against it.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I come from a province where the women have the franchise in the provincial sense at the present time. I was struck with the remark made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). He said that if .a candidate in the province of Quebec could be sure of the support of the women he would be all right. That remark carried some little significance to my mind; that the hon. gentlemen to the left of you, Mr. 'Chairman, who have been opposing this Bill are not in the happy position of commanding the support of the women of the province of Quebec. But my

mind was disabused of that thought by the explauation given to the committee by the member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), who showed us that in his constituency the women had been enfranchised to a considerable degree, and that they used the franchise.
The women of Saskatchewan-I speak only for those in my own constituency-are looking for just such a measure as this. To my mind they are entitled to it in every sense of the word, and should have had it at the last election, if, for no other reason than as a reward for good citizenship, proof of which we have seen ever since this great war began. As evidence of the unfairness of the enfranchisement of some of our women as against the enfranchisement of all, I may point out that nearly all the women of the small village in which I live who have given their time to war work have no sons to send overseas. They worked hard; they burned midnight oil, doing all they could in the way of Red Cross work, knitting soc?ks, and so on; but they were not permitted to cast their vote in the election of last December, while those who happened to have sons overseas and were not in a position, perhaps, to do so much war work, were enfranchised. These things brought home to fair-minded men and women the unfairness of the War-time Election Act.
Some at least of those who oppose this measure must do so from a selfish motive. Often when a man marries a woman he expects her to bury her individuality and merge it with his. But we cannot build up a strong citizenship in this Dominion by building up one-half of our people; we must build up all classes in order to make the development complete. I am guided in my support of this Bill by the old axiom, " Equal rights to all; special privileges to none," and I believe that hon. gentlemen who have opposed the Bill have not been acting in the best interests of the whole of Canada. I hope that when the time comes I shall have the privilege of voting for this Bill, and also of voting to wipe off the statute book of Canada the War-time Elections Act. The people whom I represent have sent me here to do that. Other matters, I have been told, are to rest in abeyance during the war, and I shall not take up the time of the Committee by discussing them now. I am heartily in favour of this Bill.

Mr. Chairman, were it not for the anxiety that seems to prevail among a number of hon. gentlemen on the
other side, I should not have attempted to say anything to-night. Hon. gentlemen opposite, however, seem to have been living in an atmosphere of terror almost ever since the opening of this session. They seem to dread the effeot of every measure that is proposed, and I wish to attempt to relieve their minds with regard to what they deem to be the probable effects of the legislation which we iare now considering.
In Saskatchewan, women have voted in provincial and Dominion elections, and I have been unable to detect any trace of difficulty. If domestic affairs have been adversely effected by giving women the vote, the difficulty lies not with the woman but with the man of the household. Up to the present time the male electors have been giving the franchise to the women, and if they turn round and create trouble in the household, surely it is their own fault.
The member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) laid particular stress on provincial autonomy. I agree that we should have provincial autonomy wherever it is advisable, but there is a point where we must draw the line. II desire to emphasize this fact: in all our provinces there have been cesspools of iniquity for the removal of which the vote of the women is necessary. In this respect, then, the limit of provincial autonomy is reached; the Dominion Government must step in and provide legislation whereby such cesspools may be prevented or removed. Our experience in western Canada is conclusive proof that the extension of the franchise to women has been the means of clearing up some of these cesspools of iniquity. I may refer, in the first place, to the almost entire removal of the liquor traffic from Canada. This movement started in a province where the women had the franchise; to the female electorate of the western provinces must go the main credit for this reform. Had the franchise been fextended to the women of the province of Quebec two or three years ago there would have been no such evasion of the prohibition law of Ontario as has been evidenced by the traffic across the Ottawa river. The Ontario law did prohibit very largely, but a new vessel was created- called the " self-container," I believe- which worked continuously between the two provinces its particular path being across the bridge that spans the Ottawa river. I shall just go a step further, although this may not be very pleasing to the members of the Cabinet at the present time. Had we had women representatives, not only in this House, but in the Cabinet,



this nefarious trafficking in that, I was going to say, damnable stuff-because it is nothing else-would not have been given another lease of life as it was about a month,ago. Recently I spent a week end in an Ontario city where I have some friends who are in business and who require the services of draymen to conduct their business. They told me it was absolutely impossible for them to secure the services of draymen because every possible conveyance that could be secured was being used in the distribution of liquor that had been ordered before the first day of April and it had to be delivered before the first of May. They further told me that the draymen had a full month's business. One of these people had a boy under sixteen years of age who is a particular friend of my friends and who comes of a splendid family. If his people had known in what occupation he was engaged, he would not have been allowed to remain there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. gentleman to come nearer to the subject-matter of the Bill under discussion. I can understand references to temperance legislation by way of illustration, but I do not think the hon. gentleman ought to go into matters connected with the liquor traffic.
I shall take it all back. I should not like to get the hon. member in wrong with the ladies. The hon. member said that political meetings were not fit places for ladies.
I never said that.

That statement was
made by one of the hon. members.

I do not want it fastened on me.
Mr. MAiHARG: During the recent election campaign, I attended a few political meetings, at practically all of which we had ladies present. At one meeting a gentleman had the nerve to make a silly interjection, and one lady in the meeting silenced him to eueh an extent that he did not open his mouth during the rest of the meeting. If we had had a lady or two like that present at some of the meetings in some parts of the Dominion of Canada, who could have silenced similar interjectors as well as she did1 this one it would have been a good thing. I think the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MoMaster) stated that in Quebec the men had a partnership with their wives. He put that forward to show that the electors of the province of Quebec had done more for the women than the electors of some of the other provinces. I would inform the hon. gentleman that we have similar legislation in our western provinces. We have our dower lawe there, and the women are very well satisfied with them. Moreover, they did not have to secure the franchise in order to get those laws; they had them before they received the franchise. I will leave the War-time Elections Act- alone for the present_ as there will probably be another opportunity to discuss that measure.

I do not rise for the purpose of discussing this Bill, although I have the right if I want to, but I do not desire to do so. I have never been very much enamoured of the granting of the franchise to women, but any doubts I had in my mind have been settled by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Maharg). I am going to support the Bill, but I would prefer to have the franchise come from the different provinces. Some of the provinces, have already granted the franchise to women, and I understand that legislation will be passed by the New Brunswick legislature next session giving to women the vote. I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question on section 1.
43J

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think it would be better, now that the principle of the Bill has been discussed, to take the Bill up clause by clause, it being well understood that the debate on the second reading is now over, and that we will confine our remarks to the clauses as they come up for discussion.
On section 1-women to be entitled to vote:

In the province of New Brunswick it is not one official, but a board of revisers, of three officials., that makes up the lists. I see that paragraph (c) of subsection 2 of section 1 says that a woman may vote if she is otherwise qualified and " obtains and presents to the official in charge of the preparation or revision of the voters' lists." If the statement was filed with just one of the officials it might not get before the board of revisers at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think under the interpretation clauses the singular includes the plural wherever necessary, but we could put in after the word official the words " or officials." I beg to move that after the word " official " the -words " or officials " be inserted.
Amendment agreed to.

In the province of Quebec the lists in rural municipalities are made up by the clerk of the municipality from the assessment roll and revised by the council sitting as a Court of Review after the lists have been posted for a certain time. We have no enumerators except .by virtue of the War-time Elections Act, and if a woman wanted to get on the roll she would have to appeal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have explained three or four times already what perhaps my hon. friend has- not observed, that so far as the Dominion Elections Act is concerned, we must provide additional machinery, but that is no urgent at the moment; we need not do that at this session. So far as the War-time Elections Act is concerned the machinery is there, but before using the Dominion Elections Act again we must undoubtedly provide the machinery.
Mr. BUREAU; That machinery would apply only to women voters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The machinery necessary to enable women to be put on the lists.
I thought it might be as well to put the machinery in the Act that gives women the franchise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right, except that the Dominion Elections Act will not come into operation before another session, andl therefore we nedfl not trouble about that this session. It would require a good deal of consideration as to how' that is to be -worked out in the different provinces. We may have to embody in the Dominion Elections Act some such provisions as those which are now in the War-time Elections Act. but probably those could be improved and1 simplified. We did not want to cumber this Act, which is designed to affirm and carry into effect the principle of giving to women the vote, with the provision of machinery which will not be necessary until the next session of Parliament at least.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that the word "said" at the commencement of line thirty is superfluous, and I move that it be struck out.
Amendment agreed to.

Why would a certificate as to age be required from a judge of a Superior Court? That is the case of a woman who had become a British subject by marriage, or who had become a British subject, her father being an alien, and naturalized while she was a minor. I do not see how a judge would be in a position to decide such a case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It would be a matter for the judge to determine, on such evidence as he might hear. We are following the provisions of the Naturalization Act.
I understand a certificate would give the lady in question the title of British subject. She is entitled to be considered a British subject, but will not really be one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If I correctly apprehend the hon. gentleman, I may tell him that this really provides that women who have been naturalized in one of two ways-that is by marrying a British subject, or by the naturalization of the father while the women was herself a minor- shall not be entitled to vote by virtue of that naturalization until they themselves fulfil what would be required by the Naturalization Act, if they made application in their own right. Do I make myself clear?

Yes, but that is not the point. Take the case of a lady born in Germany coming to this country. She has been here five or six years. She is alone,

unmarried, and over twenty years of age. She goes to the judge and asks for a certificate proving she has fulfilled all the requirements of the Naturalization Act. She gets a certificate that she is entitled to British citizenship, and then stops. She does not go through all the procedure required by the naturalization laws. She gets a certificate, and her name is put on the voters' list. A year or so later she goes back to Germany, or some other country, and subsequently returns to Canada. She has not lost heT first status, and has the right to vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: She has not the right to vote in the case the hon. gentleman puts, because she has never become a naturalized British subject.
And the necessary requirements are just surplusage?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It seems to me very plain. She is entitled to vote if she is a British subject whether by birth or by naturalization made on her own application. But if she has become naturalized by reason of naturalization of her husband, by reason of having married a man who was a British subject, or by the naturalization of her father while she was a minor, she must conform to the qualifications set forth.
Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before going to the preamble II would like to add a sec-

tion. I move, seconded by Mr. Sifton, that the following section be added to the Bill:
3. Notwithstanding anything in this Act contained, it shall not be necessary by reason of any of the provisions thereof, to prepare new voters' lists for the purpose of any byelection to be held before the 1st day of January, 1919, and in the case of any such bye-election any lawful lists available therefor may be used for the purposes of such byelection to the same extent and with the same validity as if this Act had not been passed.
The intention is that this Act shall go into immediate operation, so far as the preparation of lists in the ordinary course is concerned, but inasmuch as there are lists available for by-elections, it was not thought desirable that it should1 be necessary under this Act to prepare new lists for by-elections before the first day of January, 1010. In the meantime, I think, in most of the provinces, new lists will have been made, and the Act will have its operation after the preparation of those lists, but new lists are not considered necessary in the case of by-elections.
What is the meaning of this new amendment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If there are lists available for any by-election between now and the first of January, it shall not be necessary to make up new lists for the purpose of this Act.

Then the
women would not have the right to vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They would not have any additional right at any by-election between now and the 1st of January.
Supposing new lists were made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It merely says it shall not !be necesary to make new lists by reason of anything this Act contains. If they are made in the meantime, well and good, but it shall not be necessary by reason of this Act to make specially any new lists for by-elections before next January.
Suppose by-elections are held in the province of Quebec, the women would not be entitled to vote until January, 1919?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Except in so far as they are upon the lists now available.

Amendment agreed to.
Bill reported.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.

speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. J. D. Reid, (Minister -*f Railways and Canals) the House
went into committee on the following resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That It is expedient to provide that an employee in the service of His Majesty who is injured, and the dependents of any such employee who is killed, shall be entitled to the same compensation as the employee, or as the dependent of a deceased employee, of a person other than His Majesty would, under similar circumstances, be entitled to receive under the law of the province in which the accident occurred, and- the liability for and the amount of such compensation shall be determined in the same manner and by the same Board, officers or authority, or by su®h other Board, officem or authority or by such Court as the Governor in Council shall direct; and any compensation awarded shall be paid to such employee, or dependents, or to such person, as may be directed by the Board, officer, authority or Court, who may award costs as in cases between private parties in the province where the accident occurred; and any compensation or costs so awarded may be paid by the Minister of Finance out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I wish to introduce a Bill, after this resolution is passed, placing not only the employees of Government railways, but all employees in the Government service under the same laws as other railway employees are under in so far as compensation for injury or loss of life is concerned. The Bill will provide that the compensation is to be the same as under the law of the province where the accident occurred.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I think the object of the resolution is a very proper one. I have no objection to the principle, but I must take decided objection to the manner in which the compensation is to be fixed. It is to be determined
-in the same manner and by the same Board, officers or authority, or by such other board, officers or authority or by such court as the Governor in Council shall direct.
This is another instance in which the Governor in Council is assuming jurisdiction which he should not exercise. The board which is to determine the compensation should be fixed by law. However, it is late and I shall not press the point now, but I shall press it upon the second reading of the Bill.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
If I understood the minister aright, this law will apply only to provinces where they have a Workmen's Compensation Act. I Ibelieve there are four provinces in Canada where there are no such Acts. There is one in Quebec, one in Ontario, I believe one in Manitoba, and one in another of the western provinces. I believe that Nova Scotia and New Bruns-

wick have no Workmen's Compensation Acts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: There is such an Act in Nova Scotia.	.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Perhaps it is in New Brunswick in which there is no such Act. There are certainly three or four provinces where there is no such Compensation Act.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: What are the provinces which have no Compensation Acts?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: They have one there under which the amount is decided by arbitration and the real object of this resolution is to provide for the appointment of a hoard in Prince Edward Island instead of submitting the matter to arbitration. All the other provinces have Acts of some kind.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I was told by a gentleman in one of the labour unions that there are four provinces in which there is no such Act.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: There are four provinces in *which the Acts are practically identical; there are four provinces which have Acts that they prefer; but all the other provinces have some kind of an Act.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The object of this resolution is to bring workmen employed on Government railways under the Workmen's Compensation Act of the province. I object to any provision that will require the submission of the case of a man injured on the Canadian Pacific railway to a different court from that to which will be submitted the case of a man injured1 on the Canadian Northern.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
That is an alternative only.
Mr. BtJREAU: I object to the alternative. I want the same court to try every case whether the accident happens on one line or on the other. These two lines run parallel in my constituency for about twenty-five miles, but, notwithstanding that, a case affecting a man employed on the Canadian Northern will be tried before a different tribunal from that which will hear the case of a man injured on the Canadian Pacific.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: That is not the intention of the Bill at all.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: That is what the resolution says.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
The intention is that the case affecting a workman employed on

a Government railway shall be tried by the same court that will try the case of a man employed on the Canadian Pacific.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
If that is the intention it is all right.
Mr. MeMASTER:	I trust that the Bill,
when 'brought down, will contain a saving clause to protect all causes of action which have already arisen from the operation of the Act. I have knowledge of one case which is 'being dealt with by my office. My partner is negotiating with one of the departments to get what we consider an adequate recompense for a widow whose husband was killed. The department had offered just about the amount that they would be liable to under the compensation law of Quebec. We did not think the compensation allowed was sufficient in this case [DOT]and we have been trying to get a larger [DOT]allowance. I would not like our rights, or *the rights of our clients, to be prejudiced by any legislation adopted in a House of which I was a member.
>
Mr. J. D. REID: The railway employees would like a Dominion Compensation Act, but that would take a considerable amount of time and I thought it would :be well to [DOT]simply 'bring in a Bill for this session putting Government railways in exactly the same position as the other railways. When the resolution is passed the Bill will be introduced and it will be printed so that every one will have an opportunity of looking it over. That is the reason I would like *to get the resolution through to-night.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Will this apply to pending litigation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: There is no pending litigation.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
There is one point in
connection with this Bill that will have to receive very careful consideration. Disputes have arisen between different classes of labouring .men in the different provinces in regard to interference with common-law rights by reason of compensation Acts. Under the Compensation Act in the province of Ontario, if a workman is injured in the course of his employment lie is brought under the Compensation Act, his Tight to the common law remedy is taken away from him, and his damages are limited to the amount which is fixed by the Act.
Mr. MeMASTER:	It is practically the
same in Quebec.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
There is an Act before the legislature of Alberta over which there

6T9
is the same discussion. Last year, the province of Saskatchewan undertook to amend their Compensation Act along that line, and it was thrown out. My personal opinion is that any Compensation Act w'hich interferes with the common-law rights of the labourer is wrong in principle, because the Compensation Acts fix definitely the amount of damages which can be recovered, and they are fixed in some cases as low as $2,500 in the event of death, and the dependents receiving compensation under that Act are barred from their remedies under the common law. Now, if this Government brings railway employees under the Workmen's Compensation Acts of the various provinces, they should certainly put in a clause which will safeguard to those employees the rights which they have at common law. Until we have the particulars of the Bill before u3, it will be unnecessary to discuss this matter, but I want to point this out to the Minister of Railways, because I feel that, if he takes away the common-law rights from the railway employees of Canada he will be introducing legislation which "will 'be very unsatisfactory to them and will, I think, work injustice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Possibly my
hon. friend has not quite grasped the purpose of the resolution. I have had the advantage of discussing it with some-not all-of the labour organizations, and they are exceedingly anxious that it should be passed. More than that, this legislation would not take away any common-law right at all; it is not taking anything away, it is giving something. And in g'ving the right to compensation, it has been thought desirable, for the present at least, to follow the same lines which have been established under the laws of the several provinces. There is nothing given away, but a right is conferred.	[DOT]
Resolution reported without amendment and read the first and second time.
Hon. J. D. REID thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 51, to provide compensation where employees of His Majesty are killed or suffer injuries while performing their duties.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid, (Minister of Railways and Canals) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Department of Railways and Canals Act, Chapter 35 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, by providing that the stores account of the Canadian Government Railways shall be debited with the cost of materials, equipment and stores purchased, and of work preformed and expenses incurred in connection therewith, together with the cost of establishing, maintaining and conducting the railway stores; and shall be credited with the values of materials, equipment and stores as issued and charged to proper appropriations, or otherwise disposed of; and that the balance to the debit of the said stores account shall not at any time exceed six million dollars.

The Railway Act of 1906 contained a section, No. 20, which reads a3 follows:
Stores accounts as heretofore established in connection with the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway shall, respectively, be debited with the cost of materials, equipment and stores purchased and of work performed and expenses incurred in connection therewith, together with the cost of establishing, maintaining and conducting the railway stores, and shall be credited with the values of materials, equipment and stores as issued and charged to proper appropriations, or otherwise disposed of.
Since that time we have taken over the Transcontinental railway and the International railway, that is to say we have increased the magnitude of the Government railway system. We propose to amend the clause I have just read so that it would apply to the enlarged railway system. Section 21 of the Act reads as follows:
The balance of the debit of the respective stores acounts so established, shall not at any time exceed, for the Intercolonial Railway the sum of one million five hundred thousand1 dollars, and for the Prince Edward Island Railway the sum of one hundred thousand dollars.
The object of this Bill is to increase the quantity of the stores that we can have on hand. Owing to the high price of coal and other necessary supplies, it is an impos-siblity to operate the roads with the quantity of stores which $1,500,000 will purchase, and', of course, under the Audit Act, We cannot purchase without haVing a sufficient credit. For that reason, this resolution proposes to increase the amount which may be invested in stores from $1,500,000 to $6,000,000. Of course, the system now requires supplies from Port Arthur to Sydney. We have to keep a supply of coal at Port Arthur, for instance, and 100,000 tons at that point at $5 or $6 a ton represents in itself a large proportion of the amount we are asking.

That explanation seems reasonable enough, Mr. Chairman. I hope the hon. minister at a later

stage will give us some statistics showing why he has selected the amount of $6,000,000 instead of $2,000,000 or $4,000,000.
I shall give a detailed statement showing the stock on hand at the present time.
Has the Minister of Railways and Canals lost the Canadian Northern railway again? He does not mention it.

In the clauses of the Act read by the minister I notice that specific amounts are allocated to the two railways mentioned, $1,500,000 to the Intercolonial, and $100,000 to the Prince Edward Island railway.
We have now a much larger mileage embraced in the Canadian Government Railway system.
Will a certain proportion of the six million dollars be divided amongst the different roads, so much to the Canadian Northern, and so on?
The Canadian Northern railway is being operated under its own charter. This resolution applies only to the railways operated by the Canadian Government and covered by the Railways and Canals Act.
But the Canadian Northern is the property of the Canadian Government.

Only when it comes to the matter of making payments.
Resolution reported without amendment, and read the first and second time.
Mr. J. D. REID thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 52, to amend the Department of Railways and -Canals Act.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House adjourned at 12.19 a.m. (Friday).
